meta.promotionRule: Metadata, free full text, claim-level scope, limitations and category-specific quality score are verified; gap-only records are retained solely for explicit prior-art bounding.

sources.title: SAGA: A Security Architecture for Governing AI Agentic Systems
sources.publisher: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium

access.accessNotes: The NDSS landing page, proceedings PDF, slides and implementation/formal-model repository were live and freely accessible on 2026-08-30. The repository license file is Apache-2.0; setup metadata still carries an MIT classifier.

evidence.summary: SAGA is the strongest reviewed technical design prior art against broad Warrantor claims about agent-specific authorization and bounded revocation. It supplies a user-controlled provider/registry architecture, agent discovery, lifecycle registration, access-control policy, cryptographic inter-agent tokens, expiry and request-count budgets, an implementation, formal protocol analysis and systems evaluation. The design distinguishes long-lived identity keys, medium-lived access-control material and one-time keys used in token derivation. An initiating agent obtains receiver information and key material through the provider; the resulting token is intended to be accepted only within the policy, time and request quota encoded by the protocol. This is directly relevant to W3 and W6, and it constrains W4 wherever Warrantor proposes an agent-specific policy plane. Pinned artifact review materially narrows the implementation claim: a controlled two-thread schedule admitted two requests from quota one because validation and decrement use separate critical sections, and contact-policy results changed when the same specific and wildcard rules were reversed. The formal models cover selected secrecy and authentication properties in a Dolev-Yao network-attacker model, not those state and concurrency properties. They also do not prove exact correspondence between an authorized request and its real external effect, complete mediation, multi-principal authority intersection, receipt completeness, durable release consistency or non-bypassability after host compromise. SAGA should therefore be consumed as an essential design baseline and adversarial comparator, not as a strict revocation-SLA implementation or drop-in Warrantor replacement.
evidence.technicalContribution: A concrete security architecture for user-governed agent lifecycle and inter-agent communication, with cryptographically derived access tokens intended to be bounded by expiry and maximum request count, provider sharding/replication, a public implementation and formal models for selected token-secrecy and authentication properties. The reviewed Python path does not make request validation and consumption atomic.
evidence.methodology: The authors define a threat model and protocol, implement user/provider/agent components, encode registration and communication handshakes in ProVerif and Verifpal, implement eight malicious-agent behaviors within the stated threat model, measure primitive and protocol overhead, run multi-agent calendar/email/writing tasks over local and hosted models in multiple geographies, and test provider throughput, sharding and Raft replication. This project pinned commit 7372111bea150e32cee390a616849316d2780bfc, compiled the Python tree, exercised token round-trip and negative validation paths, permuted contact-policy rules, deterministically scheduled concurrent quota validation/consumption, tested current and flake-era Verifpal versions, and inspected the formal queries, dependency metadata, CI and data-seeding path. A full distributed deployment and independent ProVerif run remain pending.
findings: The ProVerif model establishes the paper's selected token-secrecy and communication-authentication queries under a symbolic Dolev-Yao attacker, not comprehensive authorization correctness.

The evaluated cryptographic work is small relative to agent task time; the paper reports approximately 7 ms of local cryptographic setup in its protocol-overhead model and under 0.6% end-to-end overhead for its fastest task configuration.
Request quota and expiry create an explicit security/performance trade-off at the design level: larger quotas reduce provider contacts while increasing residual exposure after compromise.

Provider operations scale with sharding in the reported experiments, including over 40,000 registrations per minute and nearly 20,000 one-time-key refreshes per minute in the cited high-sharder configurations.

The source disproves a broad design-level claim that no open, formally analyzed, count-budgeted authorization mechanism for agents exists, but it does not establish a strict implementation or service-level bound.
A controlled two-thread check admitted two requests from an initial quota of one because `token_is_valid` releases the token lock before `receive_conversation` reacquires it to decrement.
The documented most-specific contact-policy rule is order-dependent in the reviewed implementation because the matcher never updates its selected `best_pattern`.
The pinned Verifpal model parsed under flake-era 0.27.4 but did not complete in the bounded run; current 1.3.6 rejected the legacy `G` syntax.
limitations: Formal verification is scoped to cryptographic secrecy/authentication and reachability, not policy-language soundness, non-bypassability, complete mediation or outcome correctness.
The provider, registries, user authentication, TLS, public reachability and key custody remain important trust/availability boundaries.
An adversarial agent can share credentials or tokens with another adversarial agent; the protocol does not make a compromised endpoint trustworthy.

Request count is intended to bound protocol messages, not every downstream effect or action through an unmediated channel; the reviewed concurrent implementation can overshoot even that message budget.
Token quota state is held in process-local dictionaries; restart, multiple receivers, replication, failover, partitions and release-consistency behavior are unspecified.
No native automated unit/integration suite or security CI was located at the pinned commit; the documentation workflow and interactive experiment script do not fill that role.
The current formal-tool incompatibility and non-terminating bounded historical Verifpal run prevent independent reproduction of the repository's formal result in this wave.
Reported paper performance, adversary and scaling results remain author-run; a full isolated CA/Provider/MongoDB/TLS/LLM deployment was not executed.
incentives: Academic authors have incentives to emphasize novelty and evaluation success, but peer review, explicit assumptions, open artifacts and quantitative detail make the claims unusually inspectable.
No material product-sales incentive is apparent in the source.

quality.rationale: Top-tier peer review, explicit protocol/threat model, open implementation, formal models, multi-part evaluation and exceptional Warrantor relevance keep this essential. Reproducibility is reduced because no native automated suite was found, current Verifpal rejects the model, the historical version did not terminate in the bounded run, and controlled tests contradicted atomic quota and policy-precedence semantics.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt SAGA as the minimum design prior-art and empirical comparator for W6, but reject its separate check-then-decrement and order-dependent policy paths. Differentiate on linearizable durable consumption, measured residual-action and propagation bounds, multi-principal intersection, complete mediation, action-effect binding and proof-to-code correspondence.
options: Consume compatible token/registry ideas while replacing quota and policy enforcement with an atomic, durable and permutation-tested Warrantor profile.
Use SAGA only as a benchmark and implement a separate standards-aligned token profile, accepting higher duplication and proof burden.
Reject execution-count tokens in favor of time leases only, accepting a weaker residual-action bound.

architecture: Define whether the W6 algebra strictly subsumes or composes with SAGA's policy, expiry and request quota.
Specify enforcement points needed to make the count cover attempted external effects rather than only protocol messages.
Define consistency, availability and residual-action behavior during partitions, restart and failover.
implementation: Implement token validation and consumption as one linearizable transaction bound to an idempotent immutable operation.
Create differential tests for concurrent quota exhaustion, policy-rule permutation, replay, retry, crash/restart, key rotation, registry partition, endpoint compromise and token sharing.
Reproduce ProVerif in the exact pinned environment and preserve machine-readable proof output; do not treat the bounded Verifpal non-result as a proof.
business: Do not market execution-count bounds as unique; position measured end-to-end residual-action guarantees as the value.
regulatory: Use SAGA as technical evidence for bounded authorization, not as proof of compliance or legal delegation.
academic: Publish an independent extension/evaluation only if Warrantor adds clearly formalized multi-principal or complete-mediation properties.
content: Produce a fair SAGA-versus-Warrantor explainer centered on guarantee boundaries instead of first/only claims.

verification.notes: NDSS landing page, full proceedings PDF, slides and GitHub artifact were verified. Pinned commit 7372111bea150e32cee390a616849316d2780bfc compiled; token positive/negative checks ran; policy-order and concurrent-quota failures were reproduced; current Verifpal failed to parse; flake-era Verifpal parsed but did not terminate in the bounded run. ProVerif and the full distributed deployment remain pending. See artifact-review-saga-ndss-2026.md.

sources.title: SentinelAgent: Intent-Verified Delegation Chains for Securing Federal Multi-Agent AI Systems

access.accessNotes: The arXiv abstract, full text, source archive and MIT-licensed repository were freely accessible on 2026-08-30. The repository README's IEEE TDSC badge points to a TBD DOI and its IEEE citation was not verified; this record credits only the arXiv preprint.

evidence.summary: SentinelAgent is direct, open W6 and machine-checked-invariant prior art with a seven-property Delegation Chain Calculus, an HTTP Delegation Authority Service, HMAC-signed and hash-linked tokens, scope/API/output checks, cascade revocation, an authored 516-scenario benchmark, sentence-transformer intent experiments, a TLA+ model and multiple attack/robustness scripts. Artifact reproduction confirmed meaningful positive evidence: Python compilation passed; the deterministic benchmark blocked 150/150 authored attacks with 0/366 benign false positives; robustness reported 29/29; a five-fold NLI run reached 86.7% ± 4.1 malicious recall with 12.3% ± 5.7 benign false positives; and direct TLC v1.7.4 exploration completed 2,744,789 generated and 1,145,473 distinct states without an invariant violation. The same review sharply bounds the claims. The TLA+ specification checks finite subset, copied-policy, arithmetic-parent-link and atomic revocation-set properties; it does not model real API calls, output values, cryptography, time, policy evaluation, partitions, persistence, complete mediation or Python-code refinement. Controlled tests found that output authority is omitted from the token signature, expired tokens continue to pass API/output checks, permitted output tags are pooled across scopes, empty tags pass, missing ancestors yield a successful partial reconstruction and a token identifier alone can request delegation without holder authentication. The actual sentence-transformer workflow evaluation achieved 21/27 accuracy, detected 0/4 malicious intents and produced 2/23 benign false positives, while the static integration path achieved the more favorable headline. SentinelAgent therefore defeats unqualified absence claims and usefully illustrates narrow formal slices, but it is not a production authorization boundary or proof of Warrantor's composed invariants.
evidence.technicalContribution: A concrete delegation-chain research prototype combining deterministic scope, API-manifest, policy-copy, output-tag, chain and cascade-revocation rules with probabilistic intent entailment, executable federal scenarios and a bounded TLA+ state model. Its strongest contribution to Warrantor is inspectable design and counterexample evidence rather than deployment-ready enforcement.
evidence.methodology: The paper defines seven delegation properties, describes a trusted non-LLM authority service and threat assumptions, evaluates authored attack and benign scenarios, fine-tunes an NLI model on 190 labeled examples, provides red-team and robustness scripts, and model-checks six deterministic properties. This review pinned commit b7b1add07b7485e99aa3b91882a3f8f879f2e357; compiled all Python; ran the deterministic benchmark, both red-team files, robustness, fault-tolerance, executable-theorem, static DAS/LLM, sentence-transformer simulation/workflow and NLI fine-tuning paths; inspected authorship and dependency provenance; ran official TLC v1.7.4 directly against the medium configuration; mapped every checked property to actual TLA+ state; and executed controlled negative tests for signed-field coverage, expiry, scope/output binding, empty output evidence, reconstruction completeness and delegation-holder authentication. The paid live-provider path was deliberately excluded because it requires an external key and mutable provider/model behavior.
findings: Direct TLC reproduction matched the headline generated-state scale: 2,744,789 states generated, 1,145,473 distinct, depth seven, zero queued and no reported invariant violation.

The formal model is a narrow bounded design model: P3 copies policy unchanged, P4 uses integer arithmetic rather than cryptography, P5 revokes a finite descendant set atomically, and P6/P7 model child-set narrowing rather than real actions or output content.
The token HMAC omits output_schema, so post-issuance mutation can expand P7 authority while the original signature remains valid.
API and output checks omit expiry enforcement; a correctly signed expired token remains usable for those decisions even though further delegation is blocked.
P7 unions tags from every scope independently of the P6 decision, enabling a call under one scope to use a tag authorized only by another scope.
An empty caller-provided output-tag set passes, so omission is treated as conformance rather than incomplete evidence.
Chain reconstruction returns a truncated list without error when a parent-hash lookup is missing and does not verify every link, signature or expected root.
The delegation endpoint has no caller authentication or proof of possession; the reviewed path authorizes a request based on the parent token identifier and fields alone.

The static 516-scenario benchmark reproduced 100% authored attack recall and zero benign false positives, but actual sentence-transformer workflows reproduced 0/4 malicious-intent recall and 2/23 benign false positives.
Five-fold NLI fine-tuning reproduced 86.7% ± 4.1 malicious recall, 81.5% ± 4.7 malicious F1 and 12.3% ± 5.7 benign false positives; a 100% full-data result is training fit, not held-out evidence.

The file labeled an independent red team shares the repository and author provenance; its summary also subtracts three benign steps from the attack count and prints inconsistent 42/45 and all-45-blocked conclusions.
The TLA+ wrapper filters output without pipefail and prints verification success unconditionally; direct checker execution is necessary for a trustworthy release gate.
limitations: Single-author preprint; no independent peer review, audit, deployment study or independently authored attack corpus was verified.
The README advertises IEEE TDSC and a DOI placeholder, but only the arXiv publication was verified.
The core service uses a hard-coded shared HMAC secret, mutable in-memory objects, eight-character UUID prefixes, one process and no durable or distributed state.
The HTTP decision and delegation endpoints have no application authentication/TLS configuration and do not mediate or forward the actual external action.
Policy identifiers are signed and copied but are not evaluated by the API/output enforcement functions.
Audit records are a mutable in-process list rather than signed, hash-chained, independently witnessed or reconciled evidence.
The fault-tolerance experiment simulates three HMAC signers in one process with shared state; it is not threshold cryptography, consensus or failure-isolated replication.
Dependencies are unpinned lower bounds; no lock, CI, environment image, SBOM or archived model digest makes the ML runs bit-reproducible.
The formal state space is bounded to small finite sets and three tokens in the reproduced configuration, with no proof that the Python or deployment refines the model.
The live LangChain/provider experiment was not executed because it needs external credentials and a mutable hosted model path.
incentives: The author benefits from novelty, benchmark-success and formal-assurance framing; shared paper, code, benchmark and red-team provenance increases correlated-evidence risk.
Open MIT artifacts, candid acknowledgement that P2 is probabilistic and extensive executable material make the work unusually inspectable despite the absence of independent review.

quality.rationale: The open DAS, evaluation scripts, training data and directly reproducible TLC model provide unusual depth and high Warrantor relevance. Authority and independence are low because this is a single-author preprint with same-author benchmarks/red teams and an unverified IEEE citation. Reproducibility remains strong but not complete: most paths executed, while unlocked dependencies, metric inconsistencies, the excluded live-provider path and multiple controlled implementation defects prevent a higher band.

recommendation.preferredAction: Use SentinelAgent as supporting W6 design prior art, a formal-assurance caution and a source of mandatory negative vectors. Reimplement the useful calculus over signed immutable authority, proof-of-possession, atomic expiry/revocation checks, scope-bound operations and outputs, complete chain validation, durable enforcement and an explicit TLA+-to-code conformance layer; do not adopt the reviewed service as production code.
options: Consume its property taxonomy and test corpus while independently specifying and implementing the W6 intersection state machine.
Contribute fixes and independent tests upstream, then reassess only the narrow prototype after holder, signature, expiry, output and completeness defects close.
Use the source solely as a benchmark/formal-method comparator if Warrantor adopts an emerging IETF or capability-token profile instead.

architecture: Define authority as an exact multi-principal intersection rather than only parent-child set narrowing.
Bind principal, holder key, scope, policy, exact operation, canonical arguments, output contract, expiry, revocation and chain/root commitment in one immutable signed object.
Separate deterministic authorization, probabilistic intent risk and non-bypassable enforcement into explicit assurance layers.
Treat complete reconstruction and expected-set reconciliation as first-class states rather than returning partial evidence as success.
implementation: Add regression vectors for unsigned output schema, expired use, cross-scope output laundering, empty tags, truncated reconstruction and bearer delegation.
Require proof-of-possession and authenticated workload identity on every delegation and decision endpoint.
Validate the actual output payload or typed no-output assertion at the same operation boundary as the authorized call.
Invoke model checkers directly, preserve full exit/output/state evidence and connect model transitions to production events through conformance vectors.
Lock dependencies, seeds, folds and model digests before using ML results as release evidence.
business: Do not position basic delegation narrowing or bounded TLA+ checking as unique; position independently tested multi-principal composition and proof-to-enforcement correspondence.
Treat the reproduced live-intent error rates as a deployment-cost and user-friction input rather than citing only the deterministic benchmark headline.
regulatory: Do not infer NIST or federal compliance from copied control identifiers or federal-domain scenarios.
Require attributable holder identity, immutable evidence, complete audit state and documented human escalation before using probabilistic intent gates in regulated workflows.
academic: A strong paper opportunity is an independent differential evaluation of delegation calculi that separates abstract invariants, code refinement, enforcement bypass and deployment faults.
Publish exact formal statements and counterexamples for Warrantor's twelve invariants rather than claiming broad full-system verification.
content: Produce a technical explainer showing how a valid bounded model check can coexist with runtime defects, using guarantee boundaries rather than dismissing formal methods.
Compare authored benchmarks, held-out intent evaluation and enforcement conformance as distinct evidence classes.

verification.notes: Full paper, source archive and repository were inspected. Pinned commit b7b1add07b7485e99aa3b91882a3f8f879f2e357 compiled; deterministic, red-team, robustness, fault, theorem, sentence-transformer and NLI paths were run; official TLC v1.7.4 reproduced 2,744,789 generated and 1,145,473 distinct states; and six controlled authorization/evidence failures were reproduced. See artifact-review-sentinelagent-2604-02767.md.

sources.title: Chasing Shadows: Pitfalls in LLM Security Research
sources.publisher: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium

access.accessNotes: The official 19-page NDSS proceedings PDF, extended arXiv version and reproduction repository were freely accessible on 2026-08-29.

evidence.summary: Chasing Shadows is the methodological control source for the entire Warrantor evidence program. Fifteen researchers define nine LLM-specific or LLM-intensified pitfalls across data collection, pre-training, fine-tuning, prompting and evaluation: data poisoning, label inaccuracy, data leakage, model collapse, spurious correlations, context truncation, prompt sensitivity, surrogate fallacy and model ambiguity. They systematically review all 72 LLM-centric papers meeting their criteria at selected leading security and software-engineering conferences during 2023–2024, use a shared labeling process, and find at least one identified pitfall in every paper; only 15.7% of observed pitfalls were explicitly discussed. Four empirical case studies demonstrate concrete effect sizes or reproduction failures, including performance inflation from test leakage, large portions of vulnerable functions exceeding common token windows, and materially different results from model snapshot/quantization ambiguity. The value for Warrantor is not the headline prevalence number. It is the operational instruction that an evaluation receipt is scientifically weak if it merely signs a score while leaving the exact model snapshot, quantization, prompt, context handling, dataset lineage, label process, judge identity and contamination checks ambiguous. It also prevents the source library from equating peer review with claim validity. Every Warrantor benchmark, attack corpus, evaluator, agent-security comparison and content claim should carry a pitfall checklist and report which items do not apply. The paper's sample is bounded: it covers selected 2023–2024 LLM-centric security/software-engineering papers rather than all venues or the 2025–2026 agent-authorization literature. A pitfall label also does not automatically invalidate a paper. The correct use is claim-level scrutiny and experiment design, not a blanket quality penalty.
evidence.technicalContribution: A nine-pitfall taxonomy, systematic prevalence review of 72 selected papers, four empirical impact studies, reporting guidance and open code/data/reproduction materials for evaluating validity and reproducibility in LLM security research.
evidence.methodology: The team scraped papers from IEEE S&P, NDSS, ACM CCS, USENIX Security, ICSE, ISSTA, FSE and ASE, applied inclusion criteria for LLM-centric security work published in 2023–2024, developed detailed labels, reviewed papers using a collaborative agreement process, and ran four experiments on model ambiguity, data leakage, context truncation and recursive synthetic training. Code, datasets and reproduction instructions are public.
findings: Every one of the 72 sampled papers had at least one identified pitfall, but pitfall presence is not equivalent to invalidity.
Only 15.7% of the pitfalls identified by the reviewers were explicitly discussed in the source papers.
In the leakage case study, adding 20% of test data to fine-tuning increased F1 by roughly 0.08–0.11 in the tested setup.
Approximately 49% of vulnerable functions in the context-truncation case exceeded a 512-token window and 29% exceeded 1,024 tokens, showing how preprocessing can silently remove decisive evidence.
Model snapshot and quantization differences can materially change security metrics, so model name alone is not adequate provenance.
Signed evaluation receipts must preserve experimental identity and validity inputs, not only final outputs.
limitations: The prevalence sample is restricted by venue, year and topic and should not be generalized to all LLM or agent-security research.
Taxonomy coding involves judgment; the study's shared process improves consistency but does not remove construct-validity questions.
The four case studies demonstrate possible impact in selected settings rather than estimating universal effect sizes.
The taxonomy is oriented toward model/evaluation research and does not replace systems-security checks for complete mediation, protocol state, race conditions or host compromise.
incentives: The work is academic and openly reproducible; authors benefit from demonstrating widespread methodological weaknesses, so prevalence claims must remain tied to their inclusion criteria and labels.
No direct commercial product incentive is evident.

quality.rationale: The combination of top-tier peer review, a defined sampling frame, multi-researcher review, empirical case studies and open artifacts makes this the strongest cross-cutting methodology source found. Its main limitation is bounded external validity beyond the selected 2023–2024 paper population.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt the nine-pitfall checklist as a mandatory experiment and source-review control for every Warrantor benchmark, evaluation receipt, attack corpus and research paper.
options: Use the checklist directly and add systems/protocol-specific validity fields.
Reference it only in academic papers, accepting weaker consistency across engineering and marketing claims.
Develop an independent checklist, creating avoidable duplication and comparability loss.

architecture: Evaluation receipts should bind exact model/version, prompt, context policy, dataset/label provenance, evaluator and preprocessing configuration.
implementation: Add machine-readable pitfall applicability and mitigation fields to evaluation bundles.
Require frozen artifacts or content hashes where providers expose mutable model names.
business: Do not use benchmark headlines in sales material unless the pitfall review and scope are visible.
regulatory: Treat reproducibility metadata as assurance evidence, not proof that an evaluation is legally sufficient.
academic: Use the taxonomy in preregistration, artifact evaluation and threats-to-validity sections.
content: Build an evidence-led series on why signed scores are not automatically trustworthy evaluations.

verification.notes: Official NDSS PDF was inspected; DOI, author list, 72-paper sampling frame, key prevalence results and artifact links were verified. Artifact reproduction remains pending.

sources.title: OpenID Continuous Access Evaluation Profile 1.0 Final

access.accessNotes: The final normative HTML specification was live and freely accessible on 2026-08-29.

evidence.summary: CAEP 1.0 Final is the principal current standards baseline for signaling continuous changes in access-relevant state across cooperating systems. It profiles the Shared Signals Framework and defines interoperable security-event types including session revoked, token claims changed, credential changed, assurance level changed, device compliance changed, session established/presented and risk level changed. Events can identify simple or compound subjects and carry timestamps, initiating entities and human-readable reasons. For Warrantor, CAEP should be treated as a transport/event vocabulary to consume, not a competing execution-bound revocation mechanism. A CAEP transmitter can tell a receiver that a session, credential, claim, device posture or risk state changed. The specification does not guarantee how quickly the event is delivered, how quickly each receiver applies it, whether every enforcement point is subscribed, whether in-flight work is fenced, how many residual actions occur, or whether a malicious endpoint used an unmediated path. Those are precisely the properties W3 and W6 must add and measure. The strongest architecture is therefore layered: use CAEP/SSF for cross-vendor state-change notification; translate relevant events into Warrantor authority-version or epoch changes; propagate them to every policy, tool and network enforcement point; fence stale work; and emit receipts measuring event time, receipt time, enforcement time and residual actions. This avoids inventing a proprietary revocation transport while preserving a defensible Warrantor contribution: a tested end-to-end bound across the action path.
evidence.technicalContribution: A final, vendor-neutral set of continuous-access event types and claims carried through the OpenID Shared Signals Framework, with normative semantics and examples for session, credential, claim, assurance, device-compliance and risk changes.
evidence.methodology: Consensus-oriented specification work under OpenID Foundation process. The document uses normative requirements, registered event-type URIs, structured subjects and examples. It specifies event semantics rather than reporting a performance study or proving receiver enforcement behavior.
findings: Session revocation and state changes have standardized event identifiers and can target simple or compound subjects.
The profile supports timestamps and initiating-entity classifications that can be preserved in Warrantor evidence.
CAEP standardizes notification semantics but does not define an execution-count or end-to-end latency bound.
Receiver enforcement, delivery guarantees and complete coverage of enforcement points remain deployment properties.
A proprietary Warrantor revocation event format would duplicate established cross-vendor work without solving the harder enforcement-bound problem.
limitations: The profile does not mandate Warrantor-style complete mediation, stale-work fencing, tool/network acknowledgement or action receipts.
Event delivery and receiver action are governed by SSF deployments and local policy, so a signal is not proof of enforcement.
The event taxonomy is continuous-access oriented and needs a carefully versioned mapping for agent delegation epochs, warrants and action chains.
Adoption and conformance evidence must be evaluated separately from normative quality.
incentives: OpenID Foundation participants benefit from interoperable identity/security-event standards; individual vendors may favor mappings compatible with their platforms, but the final cross-vendor process and explicit normative scope improve transparency.

quality.rationale: This is the authoritative final specification for its event vocabulary and an essential consume decision. It loses points because it is not an enforcement architecture, does not measure end-to-end revocation, and conformance/adoption evidence is separate.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt CAEP/SSF as the external revocation and access-state signal baseline, then define and measure Warrantor's stricter translation, propagation, fencing and residual-action guarantees.
options: Implement a CAEP receiver/transmitter profile plus Warrantor-specific event mappings.
Consume CAEP through enterprise identity connectors while keeping a private internal bus, accepting mapping and observability complexity.
Create a proprietary revocation protocol, gaining control but losing interoperability and duplicating mature standards work.

architecture: Separate notification semantics from enforcement guarantees.
Version-map CAEP subjects/events to authority epochs, delegation chains and affected enforcement points.
implementation: Record event occurrence, receipt, policy update, acknowledgement and last accepted stale action.
Test loss, duplication, reordering, partition, replay and delayed receivers.
business: Interoperability lowers enterprise integration resistance and supports identity-platform partnerships.
regulatory: CAEP events can contribute to control evidence but do not prove timely revocation without measured enforcement receipts.
academic: A defensible research contribution is an end-to-end agent-action bound layered over CAEP, not another event vocabulary.
content: Explain the difference between revocation notification and proven revocation enforcement.

verification.notes: Final status, authors, date, event taxonomy, examples and security-consideration scope were checked in the official OpenID specification. Implementation/conformance review is a separate queued source.

sources.title: Notarized Agents: Receiver-Attested Confidential Receipts for AI Agent Actions

access.accessNotes: The abstract page, full text, TeX source and linked reference implementation were freely accessible on 2026-08-29.

evidence.summary: Sello is the best reviewed counter-design to Warrantor evidence generated solely by the acting agent or its operator. It moves the signing role to the receiving service: after observing a call, the service constructs and signs a fixed-format receipt, encrypts it to an owner public key bound into the authorization token, and publishes the encrypted object to a witnessed Merkle transparency log. The owner discovers and decrypts receipts by token reference. The design combines COSE signing, HPKE confidentiality, token-bound ownership, service-key discovery/revocation and a witness-cosigned append-only log. Its central contribution is trust-boundary inversion: compromising the agent/operator is not automatically sufficient to forge what an honest receiver says it observed. That directly changes W1/W2 design. Producer receipts remain valuable for local intent, policy and pre-execution evidence, but material external effects should support receiver, gateway, TEE or witness corroboration. Sello also clearly exposes what signatures do not prove. It provides integrity for an individual receipt, not completeness of the receipt set. An agent may use an uninstrumented path, a receiver may collude, publication/query interfaces may suppress entries, and real deployments must solve service identity, owner key recovery, log availability, privacy, multi-log consistency and incentives. The reported performance evidence is a first-party laptop microbenchmark using an in-process mock log; it does not establish hosted-log latency or production operating cost. The paper candidly reports no adoption at publication, making it useful evidence for an ecosystem problem: independent receipts create integration cost for receivers that may not capture the value. Warrantor should adopt the corroboration model while avoiding claims that Sello already provides production-grade completeness.
evidence.technicalContribution: A receiver-signed, owner-encrypted action-receipt protocol using COSE Sign1, HPKE, authorization-token owner-key binding, service-key discovery/revocation and witness-cosigned Merkle-log publication, with a reference implementation and cryptographic microbenchmark.
evidence.methodology: The author defines an adversary controlling the agent and operator, specifies the receipt and discovery flow, analyzes security properties and known attacks, compares adjacent receipt/provenance protocols, implements Sello, and benchmarks cryptographic operations on a laptop against an in-process mock log. No peer review, independent reproduction or production deployment is recorded.
findings: Receiver signing can provide evidence independent of a compromised agent/operator when the receiver, keys and log path remain honest.
HPKE can keep publicly logged receipts confidential to the owner while a witness log protects append-only publication structure.
Per-receipt authenticity does not prove that every material action produced a receipt or that query results are complete.
Receiver collusion, off-network actions, suppression, key loss, service identity and incentive alignment remain material open problems.
The source reports zero adoption in 2026, so protocol elegance must be paired with deployment incentives and gateway/standards strategies.
limitations: Single-author preprint without independent review.
The benchmark uses an in-process mock transparency log and does not measure hosted network, storage, indexing or multi-log costs.
The protocol cannot force a malicious agent to use an instrumented receiver or prevent an authorized receiver from colluding.
Discovery and publication can omit receipts unless deployments add authenticated completeness proofs, full-log audit or redundancy.
Production identity bootstrap, key lifecycle, recovery, privacy policy, adoption incentives and failure behavior need further design.
incentives: The author created the protocol and implementation and therefore benefits from emphasizing novelty; the paper also explicitly reports limitations and lack of adoption, improving incentive transparency.
No established commercial deployment is identified.

quality.rationale: Technically detailed, unusually relevant, open and candid about limitations, but still a single-author unreviewed v0.1 design with only first-party microbenchmarks and no adoption. It is strong design prior art and a required implementation experiment, not definitive evidence.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt Sello's receiver/witness corroboration as an optional Warrantor evidence profile, but add explicit completeness, multi-log, identity, failure and incentive requirements before treating it as an assurance mechanism.
options: Require receiver receipts for high-impact effects, maximizing independence but raising adoption cost.
Use gateway receipts as the deployable default and receiver/TEE witnesses for high-assurance profiles.
Retain producer-only receipts, accepting a materially weaker trust model and procurement story.

architecture: Separate per-receipt integrity from receipt-set completeness.
Define corroboration profiles for receiver, gateway, TEE and external witness evidence.
implementation: Reproduce cryptographic vectors and benchmark.
Test suppression, service collusion, multi-log split view, key rotation/recovery and registry compromise.
business: Create value for receivers through standard middleware, reduced liability or shared assurance rather than expecting uncompensated integration.
regulatory: Independent receipts may improve evidence credibility but do not automatically satisfy legal admissibility or record-completeness duties.
academic: Receipt completeness and incentive-compatible adoption are stronger research questions than another signature envelope.
content: Explain why who signs an agent receipt changes its trust value, and why even receiver signatures are incomplete.

verification.notes: arXiv metadata, full text, reference implementation link, stated protocol, adversary, limitations and evaluation boundary were inspected. Repository execution remains pending.

sources.title: Mandato: Protocol-Level Enforcement of Digitally Signed Mandates on AI Agent Actions with Cryptographically Chained Audit Trails

access.accessNotes: The abstract, five-page PDF and source metadata were freely accessible on 2026-08-29. No completed reference implementation artifact was verified from the source record.

evidence.summary: Mandato is highly relevant design prior art but currently weak empirical evidence. It proposes an MCP-transparent governance proxy that requires a digitally signed, machine-readable mandate before an agent can invoke tools. The mandate binds agent identity, authorized tools, parameter constraints, contextual conditions, validity, quotas, oversight class and delegation rules. The proxy evaluates each tool call, records permit/deny decisions and evidence in a hash-chained log, and proposes periodic anchoring through qualified timestamps. A deliberately closed constraint language aims to keep decisions deterministic and auditable. This overlaps W1, W2, W4 and W6 closely enough that Warrantor should compare schemas and semantics field by field. The paper is also unusually explicit about legal/audit legibility, mapping its design to EU accountability concepts. Those mappings are hypotheses and engineering aids, not legal validation. The paper is five pages and describes implementation status plus a future quantitative evaluation plan; it does not report completed enforcement-overhead, fault-injection, audit-completeness, verifier-cost or human-factors results. End-to-end demonstration and qualified trust-service integration are roadmap items. Its authority model is principally single-authority; cross-domain composition, conflicting quotas, multi-proxy behavior and revocation remain open. The source therefore receives a gap-only score below 70. It is retained because it narrows novelty and supplies concrete design questions, but it must not be cited as proof that the design works, scales, is non-bypassable or has established legal effect.
evidence.technicalContribution: A protocol-level design for principal-signed agent mandates with a closed constraint language, inline MCP proxy enforcement, delegation attenuation, quotas, validity, oversight classes and cryptographically chained decision logs intended for external timestamp anchoring.
evidence.methodology: The paper specifies a mandate model, decision semantics, proxy architecture, regulatory mapping, implementation status and planned quantitative evaluation. It does not report a completed comparative experiment, independent artifact reproduction, production deployment or formal proof.
findings: A signed mandate can make principal authorization a first-class inspectable artifact rather than implicit application code.
Closed constraints and per-call mediation create a plausible deterministic policy boundary for MCP tool calls.
Hash-chained decisions and external timestamps can improve tamper evidence but do not prove action or log completeness.
The current source does not establish measured performance, bypass resistance, multi-authority composition or legal effect.
The work directly narrows any Warrantor claim that principal-signed mandates, delegation attenuation or protocol-level MCP enforcement are absent from public prior art.
limitations: Single-author, five-page preprint without peer review or verified complete implementation.
Quantitative evaluation is a plan rather than reported evidence.
The design primarily assumes one authority and leaves multi-domain proxy composition, conflicting quotas and cross-domain revocation unresolved.
A transparent proxy mediates only traffic routed through it; host, direct network and alternate-tool bypasses need separate controls.
Legal and regulatory mappings are interpretive and qualified trust-service integration is future work.
incentives: The author proposes the design and benefits from novelty framing. The source labels several items as future work, but its abstract still uses broad absence language that requires independent prior-art review.

quality.rationale: The design is exceptionally relevant and concrete for a five-page preprint, but empirical results, formal proof, independent review and a verified artifact are missing. It is retained solely as prior-art and design-gap evidence and is not recommended as an implementation authority.

recommendation.preferredAction: Retain Mandato as gap-only prior art, compare its schema and decision semantics with Warrantor, and defer adoption claims until an artifact and completed evaluation can be reproduced.
options: Reuse selected mandate fields and align terminology after a compatibility review.
Collaborate on an interoperable signed-mandate profile if implementation and governance mature.
Treat it only as a citation and independently formalize Warrantor's multi-principal model.

architecture: Document how Warrantor differs on multi-principal intersection, complete mediation, revocation and receiver/outcome evidence.
implementation: Do not copy unverified mechanisms; first obtain or build a testable reference and run failure-path evaluation.
business: Do not present Mandato as a mature competitor or validation of enterprise demand.
regulatory: Treat EU-law mappings as hypotheses for counsel review, not compliance evidence.
academic: Use unresolved multi-authority and completeness properties as research questions.
content: Describe it as emerging design prior art with planned evaluation, not a deployed product.

verification.notes: arXiv metadata and full five-page text were inspected. The record explicitly separates specification and planned evaluation from demonstrated results; no artifact reproduction is claimed.

sources.title: Attestable Audits: Verifiable AI Safety Benchmarks Using Trusted Execution Environments
sources.publisher: ICML Workshop on Technical AI Governance
sources.venue: ICML 2025 Workshop on Technical AI Governance

publication.version: arXiv v1 and ICML TAIG 2025 workshop paper

access.accessNotes: The arXiv abstract/PDF and ICML TAIG workshop copy were freely accessible on 2026-08-30. A bounded title, author and repository search did not locate public prototype source code, so artifact reproduction is not claimed.

evidence.summary: Attestable Audits is direct implemented prior art against any broad claim that AI evaluation results cannot be cryptographically tied to the model, evaluator and evaluation data. Its three protocols prepare an optionally quantized model, execute audit code and data with the model inside a trusted execution environment, and let a user verify that later inference uses the audited model. The audit attestation binds hashes of the quantized model, audit code and audit dataset to the aggregate result and publishes the evidence to a transparency log; the interaction attestation additionally binds the model, prompt, response and prior audit result. Security goals cover model and audit verifiability, confidentiality, transparent measurements, stateless sessions and output integrity. The threat model includes network tampering and privileged or physical attacks such as memory snapshots, rollback and side channels, while denial of service is excluded. The authors implement the design in Rust with llama.cpp on AWS Nitro Enclaves using a 4-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model. They run 500 prompts per benchmark across MMLU, summarization and ToxicChat in four deployment configurations. This is substantially stronger than a paper-only receipt sketch, but it is not a production-ready general evaluator standard. The measured CPU path is slow and expensive, the experiment excludes model-copy overhead from decoding metrics, the tested model is quantized, the design ultimately trusts AWS hardware and firmware, and no public prototype repository was located in the bounded search. Most importantly, attestation can establish which measured code, model and data produced a result under its hardware assumptions; it does not establish scientific validity, benchmark representativeness, fairness, receipt-set completeness, or that every real deployment path used the audited environment.
evidence.technicalContribution: A TEE-backed three-stage protocol that confidentially binds model preparation, audit code, audit data, aggregate benchmark result and later inference responses to remotely verifiable measurements published through a transparency log.
evidence.methodology: The paper defines six security goals and two adversary classes, specifies KEM/AEAD and attestation-based protocols, implements them on AWS Nitro Enclaves, and evaluates a quantized Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model with 500 prompts per benchmark across MMLU, a summarization task and ToxicChat under enclave, CPU and GPU configurations. It records token counts and decoding latency but excludes non-decoding work such as the up-to-two-minute model copy into the enclave. Results are author-run and the prototype code was not publicly located for independent execution.
findings: The audit attestation binds the measured model, audit code, audit data and aggregate result; the later inference attestation binds the audited model and result to a specific prompt and response.
The paper reports 1.84 tokens per second and USD 5.80 per 100,000 tokens for its enclave configuration versus 202 tokens per second and USD 0.12 for its L40S GPU baseline.

CPU inference is reported as roughly 100 times slower and 21.7 times the cost of GPU inference; enclave deployment adds roughly a two-times cost relative to the CPU comparison because of instance sizing or reserved cores.

Four-bit quantization and context/precision differences affect benchmark results, so a valid attestation to the tested model does not imply equivalence to the provider's larger or unquantized production model.
The work directly defeats a nonexistence claim about pinned, verifiable audit execution but leaves an interoperable, evaluator-neutral and completeness-aware receipt profile open.
limitations: Workshop publication and author-run prototype rather than an archival systems paper, standard, independent evaluation or production service.
No public implementation repository was located in the bounded artifact search; reproducibility rests on paper detail rather than executable evidence.
The design trusts the confidential-computing vendor and measured base; firmware compromise, vendor-key failure and side channels remain material assumptions.
The prototype uses CPU inference, a quantized 8B model and a single-vendor Nitro environment; GPU-capable and multi-vendor deployments are future work.
Attestation does not prove benchmark validity, model quality, fairness, complete routing, absence of omitted results, correct policy selection or legal sufficiency.
The paper's suggested production GPU overhead near five times is an expectation, not an observed result.
incentives: Academic authors benefit from novelty and feasibility framing. Explicit costs, limitations, trust assumptions and workshop review make the work inspectable, but independent artifact review is absent.

quality.rationale: A concrete protocol, explicit threat model, real prototype and quantitative evaluation make this high-quality direct prior art. Workshop status, missing public code, single-vendor hardware, quantized small-model evaluation and major production gaps keep it below essential.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt TEE-measured execution as an optional high-assurance Warrantor evaluation profile, while keeping the base receipt portable and adding multi-vendor appraisal, replay/key lifecycle, authority binding and receipt-set completeness properties that the paper does not supply.
options: Require TEE attestation for every evaluation, maximizing measured-execution confidence but imposing vendor, performance, capacity and availability costs.
Use signed portable receipts by default and require a TEE, receiver or external witness only for high-impact or confidential evaluations.
Use gateway signatures alone, minimizing cost but retaining trust in the signer and no proof of provider compute.

architecture: Separate receipt-envelope integrity, measured-execution identity, external witness and receipt-set completeness into explicit assurance profiles.
Bind the warrant/authority, evaluator code, grader/rubric, model, dataset, preprocessing, prompt, result and limitations without making TEE evidence mandatory for every profile.
implementation: Build verifier adapters for at least two attestation ecosystems and record appraisal policy, firmware status, nonce, measurement, key validity and transparency inclusion.
Test replay, model/rubric substitution, stale measurements, omitted results, evaluator crash, log outage, quantization mismatch and direct non-attested bypass.
business: Offer TEE-backed verification as a premium assurance tier rather than making the most expensive trust profile the product baseline.
regulatory: Describe attestation as evidence of measured execution under stated roots of trust, never as proof that an evaluation is fair, correct, complete or legally sufficient.
academic: Compare portable signatures, gateway corroboration, TEE evidence and multi-witness completeness under a common threat model and cost model.
content: Publish a precise explanation of what verifiable evaluation execution proves, what it cannot prove, and why benchmark validity remains a separate governance question.

verification.notes: Abstract, full 13-page paper, workshop venue, security goals, protocols, benchmark method, reported performance and limitations were inspected. A bounded exact-title, author and GitHub search found no public prototype repository; no artifact reproduction is claimed.

sources.title: Making AI-Assisted Grant Evaluation Auditable without Exposing the Model

access.accessNotes: The abstract and full 12-page preprint were freely accessible on 2026-08-30. The paper contains no prototype or code reference, and a bounded title/arXiv/GitHub search did not locate an implementation.

evidence.summary: This preprint supplies unusually concrete schema-level prior art for an attested AI evaluation bundle, but it is an architecture proposal rather than evidence that a system has been built or tested. It models an applicant, grant-evaluation agency, model provider and auditor or appellate board. Its threats cover applicant gaming, prompt injection, post-hoc output tampering, substituted model or rubric, input silencing and infrastructure-operator compromise. The proposed pipeline hashes the original submission before canonicalization, records the canonical representation, measures the runtime/model/rubric/prompt configuration, constructs the complete model input, hashes the output, signs an evidence packet inside a TEE with an ephemeral attested key, obtains an RFC 3161 timestamp and writes the bundle to an append-only Merkle log. A verifier checks the hardware chain, reference manifest, model/rubric/prompt/runtime measurement, original and canonical input hashes, output hash and trusted time. The paper correctly separates the AI recommendation from the human funding decision and states that attestation does not prove model quality, calibration, bias, scientific correctness, rubric validity, human-review quality, canonicalization completeness or freedom from TEE flaws. It also identifies governance risk if the agency controls the reference manifest. These details strongly narrow Warrantor novelty, especially the fields Horig, Hcan, HI, HO, M, A, timestamp and output. However, there is no prototype, experiment, performance measurement, public code, independent review or deployment evidence. Assertions about prompt-injection mitigation and TEE properties are architectural hypotheses dependent on implementation details. The record is retained below the promotion threshold only because it directly bounds a critical nonexistence claim and provides field-level design input; it must never be presented as a working comparator.
evidence.technicalContribution: A five-layer TEE evaluation architecture and signed evidence packet binding original/canonical input, full prompt, measured model/rubric/runtime, output, hardware attestation and trusted time, with separate human-decision evidence.
evidence.methodology: The author defines principals and six threats, specifies a canonicalization/attestation/inference/signing/logging pipeline, walks through security properties and limitations, and proposes future formal and empirical work. The paper does not implement or evaluate the architecture and reports no code, dataset, benchmark, performance result or deployment.
findings: The proposed bundle E contains original and canonical submission hashes, complete input and output hashes, the measured configuration, attestation, trusted time and output; B signs E with an ephemeral key certified by the TEE attestation.
The reference manifest pins the approved model, rubric, prompt template and runtime, making manifest custody and version governance part of the trust boundary.
Recording both original and canonical inputs exposes some silent transformations, but correctness and completeness of parsing/sanitization remain unresolved security problems.
The AI evaluation artifact is explicitly separated from the final human decision, avoiding the false implication that a valid receipt proves the legal or normative outcome.
The source directly narrows a novelty claim at the design level but provides no evidence that the architecture works, scales, resists bypass or has been independently reproduced.
limitations: Single-author preprint with no peer review, prototype, code, experiment, benchmark or production evidence.
Remote attestation proves measured execution only under hardware, firmware, certificate and verifier assumptions; it does not prove model or rubric quality.
Canonicalization and prompt-injection screening are informal and cannot enumerate all document or steganographic channels.
An agency-controlled reference manifest creates a conflict of interest; independent custody is proposed but institutionally unresolved.
Performance, cost, TEE bootstrap, storage, verification and operational failure behavior are unmeasured.
Legal/accountability discussion is analytical framing rather than jurisdiction-specific legal authority.
incentives: The single author benefits from novelty framing. The paper's unusually explicit limits reduce overclaiming, but there is no independent review or artifact evidence to counterbalance author incentives.

quality.rationale: The bundle is directly relevant and more field-specific than most proposals, but an unreviewed architecture without code or empirical results cannot support implementation, efficacy or scalability claims. It is retained only to bound prior art and inform schema design.

recommendation.preferredAction: Use the paper as design prior art and a field checklist, especially its separation of original, canonical, full-input and output hashes plus human-decision evidence; do not adopt or cite it as an implemented system until a prototype and evaluation exist.
options: Borrow the field decomposition inside a broader interoperable Warrantor profile and independently implement/test it.
Build a faithful research prototype and publish results before incorporating the architecture into product claims.
Retain it only as a novelty-bounding citation, accepting less schema input but avoiding premature design commitment.

architecture: Keep raw artifact, canonical representation, full evaluator input and output as distinct commitments.
Separate evaluator receipt, reference-manifest governance, human acceptance/override and final business decision into linked artifacts.
implementation: Treat canonicalization as versioned executable code with conformance vectors rather than an informal sanitizer.
Test parser differentials, hidden content, prompt injection, manifest substitution, timestamp failure, key rotation, omission and human-record mismatch.
business: Do not describe the proposal as a deployed competitor; use it to show why a field-complete and independently tested Warrantor profile is necessary.
regulatory: Preserve contestability and human-decision linkage, while obtaining jurisdiction-specific counsel before claiming legal sufficiency.
academic: A reproducible implementation with formal canonicalization bounds and cross-agency schema portability is publishable work not supplied by this preprint.
content: Use it to explain why a signed model output is not the same as a complete, contestable decision record.

verification.notes: Author, affiliation, arXiv date, all 12 pages, threat model, evidence fields, limitations and future-work sections were inspected. The paper contains no prototype or code reference and a bounded artifact search located none.

sources.title: ATTESTATION-v1, ACTION-v1 and Reference Verifiers

publication.version: Stable v1 wire formats and verifier 1.2.2 at commit 9daac5dc7fb88ef626cfabb82d933972b5c5487a

access.accessNotes: The specification is CC-BY-4.0 and code is Apache-2.0. The repository was cloned, pinned and executed on 2026-08-30. The managed Seal gateway is not part of the open repository.

evidence.summary: Aqta's open repository is the strongest artifact-level evidence in this wave that signed AI gateway decisions and agent-action authorizations already have implementable receipt formats. ATTESTATION-v1 signs a canonical JSON record containing the organization, request hash, named model, outcome, applied policies, timestamp and issuer key. ACTION-v1 signs the proposed tool, canonical arguments hash, session/intent binding, policy and allow/block decision before execution. Both require an out-of-band pinned Ed25519 issuer key; verification against the embedded key alone is explicitly labeled integrity-only because it does not establish issuer identity. The repository provides Python and TypeScript verifiers, reference issuers, test vectors, CI, cross-language checks, differential fuzzing, an RFC 6962-style transparency implementation and unusually candid threat documents. At pinned commit 9daac5d, 92 Python tests and 29 TypeScript tests passed; the basic cross-language path passed; the differential fuzz run reported 329 checks and zero divergences; and the ACTION-v1 interop sweep was clean. This is meaningful reproducible engineering evidence, but the guarantee is deliberately narrow. A valid receipt proves that the holder of the pinned gateway key signed those fields. It does not prove that the named provider ran the stated model, that an allowed action subsequently executed with those arguments, that all traffic passed through the gateway, that the issuer told the truth, or that the disclosed receipt set is complete. Production-gateway operation and five-of-six issuer-adversary mitigations are first-party claims because the managed Seal gateway is closed. The draft ACCEPT-v1 profile links a recorded human acceptance/override/escalation to a machine record but explicitly does not verify reviewer identity or authority and is not yet frozen or cross-language complete. Aqta therefore bounds Warrantor's base receipt layer and offers useful negative tests, while leaving measured compute, independent witnesses, verified authority, outcome evidence and completeness as defensible Warrantor targets.
evidence.technicalContribution: Stable Ed25519-signed model-call and agent-action decision formats with strict canonical JSON, pinned-key offline verification, reference issuers/verifiers, adversarial vectors, differential cross-language testing and transparency-log components.
evidence.methodology: Repository-level inspection at a pinned commit plus local execution of both verifier suites and cross-implementation scripts. Python ran 92 tests; TypeScript ran 29; the issuer-to-verifier interop path passed; 329 differential mutations produced zero divergences; the ACTION-v1 cross-language sweep was clean; and the generated base conformance report showed 27 of 27 vector agreement/correctness. The managed production gateway and real traffic were not available for independent examination.
findings: Pinned-key verification is required by default; embedded-key-only verification is explicitly untrusted, closing a common self-signed-evidence error.
Strict fields, canonical number/string behavior and cross-profile rejection are exercised by negative vectors and differential tests rather than documented only in prose.
ACTION-v1 binds an issuer's authorization decision to a declared tool and argument hash but explicitly does not prove execution or verified agent identity.
ATTESTATION-v1 names a model and gateway outcome but does not bind the receipt to provider compute, evaluator code, grader/rubric or benchmark data.
The repository treats issuer equivocation, omission, backdating, reordering, key substitution and selective disclosure separately; omission remains explicitly unsolved.
ACCEPT-v1 is relevant human-decision prior art but remains a draft and records caller-asserted reviewer identity/authority rather than verifying it.
limitations: Vendor-authored source and vendor-operated production claim; no independent deployment, adoption, traffic, latency or failure-rate evidence was located.
The open repository excludes the managed gateway, so its enforcement placement, key custody, full failure behavior and five-of-six issuer-adversary claim cannot be reproduced here.
Per-record signatures do not establish issuer truthfulness, provider execution, complete mediation, receipt-set completeness or legal admissibility.
ATTESTATION-v1 is canonical JSON rather than a conforming SCITT COSE_Sign1 profile; the repository itself identifies re-envelopment and public transparency-service integration as unbuilt.
The receipt embeds a public key but depends on external key pinning and a durable key-history process; signing-key compromise remains a critical boundary.
Python and TypeScript surface coverage is not fully symmetric: draft ACCEPT-v1 is exercised in Python but not yet a frozen cross-language verifier profile.
incentives: Aqta benefits commercially from adoption of its Seal gateway and formats. Open licenses, runnable code, explicit negative claims and reproducible tests improve credibility, but managed-service assertions remain first-party evidence.

quality.rationale: Runnable multi-language verifiers, strict specifications, adversarial vectors and reproduced differential tests make this unusually strong vendor engineering evidence. First-party production claims, low independent adoption and a narrow gateway-assertion trust boundary keep it in supporting rather than high-quality.

recommendation.preferredAction: Use Aqta as a mandatory receipt-format and negative-test comparator, reuse compatible vectors or interoperate where licensing and semantics permit, and differentiate Warrantor above it with verified authority, evaluator/runtime binding, receiver or TEE corroboration, outcome evidence and completeness reconciliation.
options: Implement an Aqta-compatible adapter for base gateway/action decisions and add Warrantor assurance extensions as linked evidence.
Reuse its test ideas but define a standards-native DSSE/in-toto/SCITT profile, accepting more implementation work for broader ecosystem alignment.
Build an unrelated proprietary envelope, maximizing format control but duplicating solved canonicalization and verifier work.

architecture: Model assertions by provenance: caller-declared, issuer-observed, issuer-attested, receiver-attested, TEE-measured and externally witnessed must not collapse into one signed object.
Design receipt-set completeness through reconciliation or monitored transparency, because signatures and TEEs cannot expose events that never enter the evidence path.
implementation: Adopt cross-language differential vectors for number/string canonicalization, key pinning, profile confusion, unknown fields, malformed encodings and wrong-key cases.
Add execution-result, authority credential, external time, key-history and provider/receiver reconciliation tests beyond Aqta's base profiles.
business: Treat Aqta/Seal as a possible interoperability partner and narrow competitor; do not claim signed gateway decisions are an empty category.
regulatory: Keep claim wording at issuer-authenticated decision evidence unless independent identity, time, workload and completeness controls are actually verified.
academic: Study the gap between envelope conformance and history/evidence completeness across mutually distrustful issuer, provider, receiver and auditor records.
content: Use Aqta as a fair example of honest receipt boundaries: a signature proves who asserted fields, not that every field or omitted event is true.

verification.notes: Cloned and inspected commit 9daac5dc7fb88ef626cfabb82d933972b5c5487a. Locally passed 92 Python tests, 29 TypeScript tests, issuer/verifier interop, a 329-case zero-divergence fuzz sweep, the ACTION-v1 cross-language sweep and the 27-vector base conformance report. Managed gateway behavior was not independently verified.

sources.title: Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit

access.accessNotes: The MIT-licensed repository and documentation were cloned and inspected at the pinned commit. The core Rust policy-engine workspace was compiled and tested with the same checksum-verified OPA 0.70.0 prerequisite used by repository CI.

evidence.summary: Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit (AGT) is the most consequential open implementation comparator found for the former broad Warrantor governance portfolio. Version 5.0.0 is a large public-preview monorepo spanning Python, Rust, Go, TypeScript and .NET, with policy, identity/trust, delegation, application sandboxing, kill-switch/SRE, audit/compliance, MCP, framework adapters, conformance fixtures and supply-chain controls. The pinned snapshot contained 4,790 files, 1,070 test files, 42 GitHub workflows, ten component specifications, 35 ADRs and 21 recorded security audits. Its Agent Control Specification core supports deterministic intervention points, Cedar and Rego/OPA policy execution, transforms, escalation/approval, resource limits, failure normalization and cross-SDK fixture concepts. A CI-matched local run compiled and passed the entire Rust policy-engine workspace when the repository's checksum-verified OPA 0.70.0 prerequisite was placed on PATH. This is strong evidence that the core artifact is inspectable and executable; it is not independent proof of every package or claimed benchmark. AGT's own documentation sharply bounds the overlap. It is application middleware rather than OS/kernel isolation. Many components can share a process with the governed agent. Retaining an unwrapped tool reference is explicitly tested as a host-contract bypass. No-policy/permissive initialization can allow actions. Audit is best effort and can fail open; records describe attempted/allowed actions rather than independently verified external outcomes. Individual allowed actions are not automatically analyzed as a malicious sequence, knowledge provenance/flows and credential persistence are incomplete, and high-assurance deployments still need containers, network policy, identity and external append-only storage. These boundaries leave a defensible Warrantor role in below-model complete mediation, default-deny network egress, authority-to-execution binding, independently corroborated receipts, outcome evidence and cross-stack conformance. They eliminate any credible claim that open-source policy, identity, delegation, kill-switch, audit or cross-language agent governance is an empty field.
evidence.technicalContribution: A broad, MIT-licensed, multi-language agent-governance implementation with a deterministic Agent Control Specification core, Cedar/Rego policy dispatch, pre/post action interception, identity/trust and delegation facilities, audit/SRE modules, MCP/framework adapters, extensive specifications, conformance fixtures and supply-chain automation.
evidence.methodology: Repository review pinned commit 46463ef8689433817fcc0c582a7881f515d4df15, inspected README, SECURITY, architecture, limitations, error handling, specifications, feature matrices, governance, workflows and source/test structure. A shallow clone was compiled locally. An initial Rust workspace run without OPA failed closed at a Rego allow test; the prerequisite was traced to CI. A second run that set both PATH and ACS_OPA_PATH changed one negative test's expected error provenance. The decisive run matched the Rust CI job exactly by putting checksum-verified OPA 0.70.0 on PATH with ACS_OPA_PATH unset; the entire policy-engine workspace then passed. Other language suites, benchmark reproduction and adversarial bypass testing remain pending.
findings: The repository is a serious implementation and governance project, not a marketing-only launch: it includes multiple language SDKs, extensive tests, specifications, ADRs, security audits, supply-chain workflows and a current public-preview release.
The Rust Agent Control Specification workspace compiles and passes its full test suite in a CI-matched environment at the pinned commit.
The artifact explicitly tests that a retained unwrapped tool reference is a host-contract bypass, confirming that wrapper/middleware coverage is not complete mediation by itself.
AGT documents application-layer and same-process boundaries and recommends container/network/IAM layers for production isolation.
Audit failure can be configured or documented as best effort/fail open, and current audit semantics emphasize action attempts/decisions rather than independently verified world-state outcomes.
The no-policy default and permissive configuration can allow actions; reliable governance therefore depends on strict initialization and effective-policy verification.
Sequence-level malicious workflows, cross-session knowledge flows, credential persistence and physical-agent safety remain explicit gaps or roadmap items.
The repository directly challenges broad W1–W6 absence/novelty claims but does not remove Warrantor's narrower complete-mediation, egress, evidence-independence and conformance opportunities.
limitations: Public preview: APIs and semantics may change before general availability.
The artifact review reproduced the Rust policy-engine workspace, not every Python, Go, TypeScript and .NET package or published benchmark.
Most performance, production and adoption claims are first-party; the adopters file is self-reported and includes entries that require independent verification.
Application middleware can be bypassed by unwrapped references, alternate clients, direct sockets, child processes or a compromised host unless deployment controls mediate those paths.
Same-process keys, trust state and audit components weaken isolation under agent/host compromise; external sidecars/stores are recommendations rather than universal defaults.
Attempt logs and Merkle/chained records do not establish complete external-effect evidence or receiver-independent truth.
OPA is a real runtime/test prerequisite for Rego paths; the top-level local Rust test instruction can fail closed without making the prerequisite immediately visible.
incentives: Microsoft and maintainers benefit from ecosystem adoption and strong production-quality framing. The repository's explicit limitations, open implementation, security history and reproducible core tests materially improve transparency but do not substitute for independent evaluation.

Linux Foundation/AAIF governance material appears in the repository, but current hosting/governance status and independence should be verified from the receiving organization rather than inferred from project-authored documents.

quality.rationale: Exceptional implementation breadth, documentation, tests, explicit limitations and successful pinned core reproduction make AGT a high-quality engineering source. Vendor authorship, public-preview change risk, first-party performance/adoption claims and incomplete independent multi-language/bypass evaluation keep it below essential.

recommendation.preferredAction: Treat AGT as a mandatory build/consume comparator: evaluate selective reuse or interoperability with its Agent Control Specification and adapters, while keeping Warrantor differentiation below the middleware boundary in complete mediation, default-deny egress, independent receipts, outcome binding and end-to-end conformance.
options: Consume or contribute to compatible ACS schemas/core adapters and layer Warrantor assurance beneath/around them, minimizing duplication but accepting upstream preview churn.
Implement an ACS-compatible Warrantor target while retaining an independent internal representation and verifier, increasing control and conformance cost.
Build an incompatible full governance stack, maximizing ownership but creating the highest novelty, maintenance and adoption risk.

architecture: Define Warrantor's enforcement boundary where AGT explicitly stops: kernel/network mediation, wrapper-bypass closure, action-effect evidence and independent witnesses.
Make strict initialization, effective-policy state and audit durability explicit invariants rather than optional deployment advice.
implementation: Create an AGT/ACS compatibility and differential-conformance adapter at a pinned version.
Test unwrapped references, direct sockets, child processes, audit outage, no-policy startup, permissive mode, stale work and external outcome mismatch.
business: Treat AGT as competitor, partner and open-source substrate; do not claim the broad category is empty.
Sell assurance guarantees and evidence that remain missing after middleware governance, not another undifferentiated policy SDK.
regulatory: Use AGT audit/control data as inputs; do not equate toolkit compliance mappings or attempted-action logs with regulator-accepted outcome evidence.
academic: A publishable comparison should evaluate complete mediation, evidence independence and cross-language semantic drift against AGT/ACS rather than restating its feature list.
content: Publish a technically fair boundary analysis: what AGT already solves, what its own docs say it does not solve, and what Warrantor will prove additionally.

verification.notes: Cloned and inspected commit 46463ef8689433817fcc0c582a7881f515d4df15. The decisive Rust workspace run matched repository CI with checksum-verified OPA 0.70.0 on PATH and ACS_OPA_PATH unset; it passed. Other language suites and independent performance/bypass evaluation remain pending.

sources.title: Every Eval Ever: A Unifying Schema and Community Repository for AI Evaluation Results

publication.version: arXiv:2606.14516 plus schema 0.3.0 and repository 0.2.3rc1 at commit 687b7a36902c01db8a80f0b719d8861d6494f550

access.accessNotes: The paper, MIT-licensed repository, schemas, generated Pydantic models, validation code and converters were freely accessible. Commit 687b7a36902c01db8a80f0b719d8861d6494f550 dated 2026-08-28 was cloned and exercised on 2026-08-30.

evidence.summary: Every Eval Ever is the strongest reviewed source for evaluation-result semantic interoperability and directly changes Warrantor's W2 build decision. It defines a source-agnostic aggregate schema plus an optional instance-level sidecar that can represent results from papers, leaderboards and execution frameworks.
