The records cover source provenance and evaluator relationship, model identity and access mode, evaluation library/version, generation configuration, benchmark and dataset source, metric semantics, uncertainty, LLM-judge configuration and result details. Instance records can retain raw and formatted inputs, references, outputs, reasoning, messages, tool calls, answer attribution, scoring, token usage and performance across single-turn, multi-turn and agentic interactions. The paper reports 22,235 models, 2,273 unique benchmarks and 31 input formats; those scale figures are coalition-reported and were not independently recounted here. The repository includes converters for Inspect AI, HELM and lm-eval-harness plus many leaderboard/source adapters, schema validation, duplicate detection, provenance reports and content-addressed raw capture. At pinned commit 687b7a3, a local Python 3.13 run exercised 1,043 collected tests: 997 passed, 45 skipped and one presentation-layer assertion failed because capture-disabled output did not contain the expected ANSI red escape code. The converter, schema, semantic-validation, provenance, checksum, raw-capture and duplicate-handling paths otherwise passed. EEE does not execute evaluations, authenticate a producer, attest runtime compute, prove all events were submitted or recover source metadata that never existed. Its UUID-based run identity is not a canonical receipt fingerprint, and searched code did not expose a native DSSE, in-toto, Sigstore or equivalent signer-authenticated evaluation artifact. Warrantor should therefore consume or losslessly map EEE semantics, not compete with them, while placing those records inside an authority-linked assurance envelope with explicit evaluator/grader identity, signatures, optional measured execution and reconciled completeness.
evidence.technicalContribution: A community-governed, source-agnostic schema for aggregate and instance-level AI evaluation results; converters from heterogeneous harnesses and leaderboards; semantic validation and provenance accounting; and a public community repository designed to make results comparable and reusable.
evidence.methodology: The paper derives a shared representation from heterogeneous evaluation sources and demonstrates it through converters and a community datastore. This review inspected the full paper, aggregate and instance schemas, converter implementations, validation and raw-capture paths at a pinned commit. Local reproduction used uv and Python 3.13.11. The normal captured pytest invocation found no tests before failing during output-capture cleanup in the mounted environment; rerunning explicitly against tests with capture disabled collected 1,043 tests and produced 997 passes, 45 skips and one ANSI-color assertion failure. No semantic or converter test failure was observed.
findings: EEE already supplies the broad cross-harness semantic layer Warrantor would otherwise need to invent; building an incompatible general schema would create avoidable standards and adapter debt.
Aggregate and instance schemas preserve far more than headline scores, including model, library, generation, source, metric, uncertainty, judge and optional message/tool-call details.
Validation establishes type, required-field, enum, path, aggregate/sidecar consistency and selected semantic rules; it does not establish that a source, evaluator or model provider told the truth.
Content SHA-256 values and duplicate fingerprints support integrity checks, raw-source capture and deduplication but are not key-authenticated producer signatures.
Fresh UUIDs preserve distinct run records but shift semantic duplicate detection to later analysis; a Warrantor receipt needs a separate canonical predicate digest and explicit rerun lineage.
Framework-level provenance remains necessary because a converter cannot reconstruct metadata that the native artifact omitted, and conversion may be lossy unless field coverage is measured.
The source explicitly leaves multimodal, human-preference and multi-agent coverage less mature than text/single-model evaluation and does not replace evaluation execution frameworks.
limitations: Preprint and coalition-authored artifact; reported repository scale, coverage and first-of-kind language have not undergone independent recounting or archival peer review in this wave.
Text and single-model evaluations receive the strongest representation; multimodal, preference, human and multi-agent formats remain partial or evolving.
The schema cannot force source systems to record complete model, dataset, prompt, grader or runtime provenance and cannot always diagnose why nominally identical evaluations disagree.
Validation checks conformance and selected consistency properties, not authenticity, measured execution, benchmark validity, complete routing, receipt-set completeness or legal admissibility.
Community contribution and maintainer review improve governance but leave participation, curation, correction, repository and maintainer trust dependencies.

The single local failure was presentation-specific and does not invalidate schema semantics, but the suite was run on Python 3.13 in this mounted environment rather than the maintainers' complete CI matrix.
incentives: The coalition benefits academically and institutionally from adoption of its schema and repository. Broad authorship, open code, explicit limitations, public contribution workflows and reproducible tests improve transparency, but first-of-kind and scale claims remain first-party evidence.

quality.rationale: A detailed source-agnostic schema, unusually broad converter surface, public datastore, explicit limitations and a nearly clean 1,043-test local reproduction make EEE essential for Warrantor's evaluation interoperability design. Preprint status, first-party scale claims, partial non-text coverage and absence of authenticated assurance keep it below the highest scores.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt EEE as the semantic interoperability baseline, contribute missing agentic and assurance fields upstream where possible, and define Warrantor as a lossless EEE-compatible DSSE/in-toto assurance profile rather than a competing general evaluation schema.
options: Use EEE objects as the Warrantor predicate subject and add linked authority, signer, attestation and completeness blocks in a versioned assurance profile.
Maintain an internal Warrantor predicate with a provably lossless bidirectional EEE mapping, gaining tighter control but accepting ongoing conformance cost.
Invent a separate schema, gaining maximal ownership while duplicating community work and creating the highest interoperability and credibility risk.

architecture: Separate semantic normalization from assurance: EEE answers what an evaluation record means; DSSE/in-toto, credentials, attestation and reconciliation answer who asserted it and what was observed.
Define a canonical Warrantor predicate digest, rerun/supersession lineage and population-completeness block without replacing EEE's source/run identifiers.
implementation: Build Inspect-to-EEE-to-Warrantor first, then garak, PyRIT and AgentDojo adapters, and emit field-coverage reports that fail closed on unclassified loss.
Contribute reusable agentic/tool-call, grader/rubric and provenance improvements upstream before forking semantics.
business: Position Warrantor as the assurance and operating layer over an emerging neutral evaluation schema, reducing buyer fear of format lock-in.
Treat EvalEval as a standards and research partner rather than a product competitor.
regulatory: Use EEE-normalized records as technical evidence inputs only; attach identity, authority, time, retention, jurisdiction and completeness evidence required by a specific assurance case.
academic: A defensible paper should measure cross-harness information loss and the security properties added by authenticated, corroborated and reconciled profiles, not claim the first shared schema.
content: Publish an evaluation-evidence stack explainer that distinguishes result semantics, provenance, signature authenticity, measured execution, validity and completeness.

verification.notes: Paper, schemas and code were reviewed at commit 687b7a36902c01db8a80f0b719d8861d6494f550. An explicit capture-disabled test run collected 1,043 tests: 997 passed, 45 skipped and one ANSI-color presentation assertion failed. The initial default-capture invocation encountered a mounted-environment capture cleanup error before collection and is not counted as a semantic test result.

sources.title: AERF — Agent Evidence Receipt Format v0.2.0-draft.1

access.accessNotes: Specification, JSON Schema, threat model, verifier, conformance vectors and adversary simulator were all freely accessible and inspected at the pinned commit.

evidence.summary: AERF is the closest open wire-format prior art for Warrantor's basic signed agent-action receipt. Its v0.2 draft authenticates a receipt, parent receipt signature and policy-decision input, binds context and policy hashes, records allow/deny or in-policy results, and can carry a transparency-log inclusion proof. The project is unusually explicit about what a receipt cannot establish. It labels tag stripping and common-mode poisoned context as known accepted limits; allows replay for its EVIDENCE profile; leaves identity and key acquisition out of scope; and states that receipts are evidence rather than enforcement. This makes AERF useful both as an interoperability target and as a negative design control. It is not an adequate Warrantor core substrate by itself because its bespoke JCS/Ed25519 format overlaps more mature DSSE, in-toto, COSE and SCITT standards, the draft remains unstable, and the repository's top-level documentation is version-inconsistent. The right posture is to consume its test ideas and offer a bounded adapter while keeping Warrantor's canonical assurance profile standards-aligned.
evidence.technicalContribution: A compact JSON/JCS/Ed25519 receipt format with explicit parent and PDP signatures, context and policy hashes, optional log inclusion proof, JSON Schema, Python and Go verification paths, conformance vectors, threat model and executable adversary scenarios.
evidence.methodology: The project defines schema and verification rules, publishes positive and negative vectors, and supplies an adversary simulator. This review pinned commit 59fce60f and ran the project tests with uv-provided Python and an explicit Go path: all 12 vector expectations, 16 schema cases and 11 adversary outcomes matched, including the two intentionally accepted known-limit cases.
findings: The v0.2 draft materially strengthens v0.1 by authenticating parent receipt linkage, the PDP decision and hashes of decision context and policy.
All 12 conformance vectors, 16 receipt-schema cases and 11 adversary scenarios matched their expected outcomes in the controlled local run.
Tag stripping and common-mode poisoned context are correctly exposed as accepted known limits rather than misreported as prevented attacks.
AERF establishes strong format-level prior art but no proof of complete mediation, enforcement-before-execution, complete event capture or independent deployment.
limitations: The specification is explicitly a draft and the README/compliance material still advertises v0.1 while core files implement v0.2.
EVIDENCE receipts accept replay; identity bootstrap, key acquisition, endpoint compromise and enforcement are outside the format.
The Go verifier does not yet verify RFC 3161 timestamps or multi-receipt chains.
The small project has no located independent security audit, interoperability report, production deployment or broad adoption evidence.
incentives: The project benefits from adoption of its format and therefore may emphasize novelty or completeness; open schemas, executable vectors and unusually candid known-limit documentation make the claims inspectable.

quality.rationale: AERF earns strong rigor and reproducibility credit for explicit threat boundaries, schema, vectors and executable adversary tests, but remains a small unstable draft with inconsistent documentation, incomplete verifier functions and no independent adoption or audit evidence.

recommendation.preferredAction: Consume AERF's threat vectors and provide a versioned import/export bridge, but retain DSSE/in-toto as Warrantor's canonical envelope and SCITT or another VDS layer for transparency; do not fork AERF's bespoke wire format into the core.
options: Contribute missing timestamp, chain and version-consistency fixes upstream and certify an AERF compatibility profile.
Map AERF receipts losslessly into a Warrantor in-toto predicate and preserve original bytes as evidence.
Adopt AERF as the core format, gaining simplicity but accepting draft instability, duplicated standards and a smaller ecosystem.

architecture: Keep receipt authentication separate from authority appraisal, enforcement and completeness.
Define explicit adapter behavior for known-limit and unsupported fields.
implementation: Import the AERF vectors into Warrantor conformance tests.
Fail closed if conversion loses parent, PDP, context, policy or log-proof bindings.
business: Treat AERF as an ecosystem interoperability opportunity, not as evidence that the category is empty.
regulatory: Use AERF records only as technical evidence inputs; they do not constitute compliance or legally effective authorization.
academic: Compare standards-aligned and AERF-native profiles under identical omission, replay, collusion and conversion attacks.
content: Publish a candid receipt-versus-enforcement explainer using AERF's own accepted attack cases.

verification.notes: Pinned at 59fce60fe30bde35318812f502a55ab4bace4650. Controlled test run passed all 12 vector expectations, all 16 schema expectations and all 11 adversary outcomes; tag stripping and common-mode poisoning were expected KNOWN_LIMIT outcomes, not test failures.

sources.title: in-toto Attestation Framework v1.2
sources.publisher: in-toto project and Cloud Native Computing Foundation
sources.venue: CNCF-governed open specification and language bindings

access.accessNotes: Release notes, envelope/statement/predicate/bundle specifications, predicate catalog and Go/Python/Rust/Java bindings were freely accessible; the current implementation was inspected and tested at a pinned post-release commit.

evidence.summary: in-toto v1.2 is the strongest reviewed general attestation substrate for Warrantor. It separates an authentication envelope, a subject-bound Statement, a URI-typed predicate and an optional multi-attestation Bundle. DSSE is recommended; envelopes must support multiple signatures, and v1.2 clarifies ITE-5 requirements and alternative envelope compatibility. The framework has mature governance, a broad predicate ecosystem and language bindings in Go, Python, Rust and Java. Warrantor should consume this layer rather than invent another generic signed JSON format. The decisive limit is completeness. The JSONL Bundle is a collection of independently authenticated envelopes but is not authenticated as a whole, so an attacker or operator can omit valid attestations, replay an obsolete set or inject irrelevant records. Statement subjects are matched purely by digest, independent of content type, and generic predicates do not supply Warrantor's authority, pre-commit, effect, evaluator, or reconciliation semantics. Therefore Warrantor needs a domain predicate plus a signed manifest/reconciliation layer rather than assuming an in-toto Bundle proves a complete receipt population.
evidence.technicalContribution: A layered, extensible attestation framework with authenticated envelopes, digest-bound subjects, typed predicates, bundle conventions, parsing/extension rules, vetted supply-chain predicates, runtime-trace and test-result models, and generated multi-language bindings.
evidence.methodology: The working group maintains normative specifications, schema and protobuf definitions, generated language libraries and CI tests. This review inspected the v1.2 spec and current commit 2dcd055e, then reproduced Go, Rust and Python tests: Go packages passed, Rust passed 12 unit and 4 documentation tests, and Python passed 12 tests in a controlled capture-disabled run after installing declared test dependencies.
findings: v1.2.0 is the current stable release and DSSE remains the recommended envelope while alternative formats must meet multi-signature and authenticated-type requirements.
The predicate URI provides extensibility without requiring a new envelope, making a Warrantor-specific authority/evidence predicate technically appropriate.
Bundle membership is not authenticated as a whole; valid per-attestation signatures do not prove that every expected attestation is present or current.
The Runtime Trace and Test Result predicates are reusable baselines but do not themselves prove synchronous observation, complete routing or detailed cross-harness evaluation semantics.
Controlled Go, Rust and Python test paths passed at the pinned current implementation.
limitations: Subject matching is digest-only; consumers that require type or role binding must enforce it in policy or predicate semantics.
The Bundle permits omission and replay risks unless an external authenticated manifest or monotonic policy supplies set-level expectations.
An attestation authenticates an assertion, not its truth, execution environment, policy legitimacy, completeness or non-bypassability.
Some generated predicate packages have no dedicated tests, and the project states that tooling and integration continue to evolve.
incentives: The CNCF/in-toto ecosystem benefits from broad attestation adoption, but open governance, public versioning, explicit compatibility rules and multi-language artifacts substantially improve auditability.

quality.rationale: Current stable versioning, CNCF governance, normative detail, multi-language bindings, a broad predicate ecosystem and successful local tests make this essential. Set-level completeness gaps and continued tooling evolution prevent treating it as a complete assurance system.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt DSSE plus the in-toto v1 Statement/predicate model as Warrantor's canonical portable attestation base, then add an authenticated set manifest, authority profile and reconciliation proof instead of relying on Bundle membership for completeness.
options: Contribute Warrantor's evaluation and action predicates to the in-toto ecosystem and keep extensions monotonic.
Maintain private predicate URIs with public schemas and conformance vectors, gaining release control while accepting ecosystem coordination cost.
Use SCITT/COSE as the sole statement format, improving one ecosystem alignment while losing direct compatibility with the dominant DSSE/in-toto supply-chain path.

architecture: Separate envelope authentication, predicate semantics and population completeness into independently testable layers.
Bind subject content type, role and expected set membership explicitly in Warrantor policy.
implementation: Generate Go, Rust, Python and TypeScript conformance vectors from one schema source.
Add deletion, replay, obsolete-bundle and irrelevant-injection tests before claiming complete evidence.
business: Standards alignment lowers procurement and integration friction and avoids a proprietary-signature narrative.
regulatory: Map in-toto statements to evidence controls, but do not equate signed provenance with legal or control effectiveness.
academic: Evaluate the security and cost of set-level completeness mechanisms layered over independently authenticated attestations.
content: Explain the four layers—envelope, statement, predicate and set completeness—so buyers do not overread a signature.

verification.notes: Stable release v1.2.0 and current implementation commit 2dcd055e9f72e746687c306e35f4e59720ff45be were inspected. Go tests passed with GOTOOLCHAIN=local; Rust passed 12 unit and 4 doc tests; controlled Python execution passed 12 tests. The default mounted-environment pytest capture failure occurred before collection and is recorded as environment setup, not a project failure.

sources.title: Dead Simple Signing Envelope v1.0.2
authors: Secure Systems Lab and DSSE contributors

access.accessNotes: The tagged protocol, envelope, background and implementation links were freely accessible; v1.0.2 remains the current stable revision consumed by the in-toto v1.2 framework.

evidence.summary: DSSE is a deliberately small authentication envelope for arbitrary serialized payloads. Its pre-authentication encoding signs the exact payload bytes together with the UTF-8 payload type, avoiding JSON canonicalization and cross-protocol type-confusion dependencies. The recommended envelope carries base64 payload bytes, an authenticated payloadType and one or more signatures; threshold verification can require t valid signatures from n distinct trusted keys. This is a strong canonical base for Warrantor because semantics can evolve in an in-toto predicate without changing the envelope. DSSE also imposes critical verifier discipline. keyid is explicitly unauthenticated and cannot authorize a key. Algorithm and key trust are negotiated or configured outside DSSE. The application must receive the exact bytes that were verified rather than reparsing an attacker-controlled envelope. The envelope alone has no key discovery, PKI, time, revocation, transparency, semantic validation, execution measurement, policy legitimacy or set-completeness property. Warrantor should therefore adopt DSSE as one narrow layer and describe every additional guarantee separately.
evidence.technicalContribution: A serialization-independent signing protocol using PAE(payloadType, payload), a minimal multi-signature envelope, type-confusion resistance without canonicalization, and explicit verification invariants.
evidence.methodology: Normative protocol and envelope documents define signing, verification and serialization behavior, supported signature thresholds and security pitfalls. This review reconciled tagged v1.0.2 with in-toto v1.2 envelope requirements and inspected the reference protobuf definition and implementation links; implementation execution is covered by the in-toto artifact review rather than counted as an independent DSSE reproduction.
findings: PAE authenticates the payload type and exact serialized bytes, avoiding the need for a canonical JSON representation.
The envelope supports multiple signatures and threshold trust across distinct configured keys.
keyid is an unauthenticated lookup hint and must never be treated as an identity or authorization assertion.
DSSE proves only that accepted key material signed an exact typed payload; every semantic and operational guarantee remains external.
limitations: Key discovery, PKI, exclusive ownership, algorithm choice, trust roots, revocation, time and transparency are out of scope.
A verifier can nullify DSSE's security if it verifies one payload and then passes separately reparsed or mutated data to the application.
No receipt completeness, measured execution, truthful-producer, authority or enforcement property follows from the signature.
incentives: The authors and dependent ecosystems benefit from envelope adoption, but the specification's narrow scope and explicit exclusions make overclaiming comparatively easy to detect.

quality.rationale: Its precise scope, mature adoption through in-toto/Sigstore ecosystems, simple verifier invariants and durability make DSSE essential. It is intentionally not a complete trust or receipt protocol, so its high score reflects fitness as an envelope rather than assurance breadth.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt DSSE v1.0.2 as Warrantor's default portable envelope, require payload-type verification and exact verified-byte handoff, and define key, time, identity, authority, transparency and completeness in explicit profiles outside the envelope.
options: Offer COSE_Sign/COSE_Sign1 profiles for constrained and SCITT deployments while preserving equivalent predicate semantics.
Use DSSE only for external interoperability and a native COSE core, accepting dual-stack complexity.
Create a new signature envelope, gaining no decisive security property while multiplying review and integration cost.

architecture: Make envelope verification a small isolated component and expose verified payload bytes plus signer facts, never a trusted semantic object by default.
implementation: Add keyid-confusion, payload mutation, payloadType substitution and threshold-key-duplication vectors across all languages.
business: Standards reuse strengthens procurement credibility and ecosystem integration.
regulatory: A DSSE signature is provenance evidence, not proof of control effectiveness or legal authority.
academic: State DSSE as consumed prior art and evaluate only the novel profile properties layered above it.
content: Teach the difference between authentic bytes and trustworthy execution.

verification.notes: Tagged v1.0.2 protocol and envelope documents were reconciled with in-toto v1.2. This record does not double-count in-toto's multi-language test reproduction as independent DSSE evidence.

sources.title: RFC 9943: An Architecture for Trustworthy and Transparent Digital Supply Chains

access.accessNotes: The RFC Editor metadata and complete HTML standard were freely accessible; status, authorship, date, guarantees, exclusions, privacy and threat-model sections were inspected.

evidence.summary: RFC 9943 is the current IETF architecture for making single-issuer signed statements transparent. An issuer creates a COSE_Sign1 Signed Statement; a Transparency Service verifies it, applies a registration policy, commits it to an append-only non-equivocating Verifiable Data Structure and returns a universally verifiable receipt using RFC 9942. This is directly useful for Warrantor evidence publication, audit history and ecosystem interoperability. The RFC is also exceptionally valuable because it defines the guarantee boundary precisely. SCITT authenticates who made a statement, proves that a trusted service accepted and registered it, and enables consistent auditing of registered history. It does not make the statement accurate. An issuer can intentionally or accidentally lie, refuse to register, or submit only selected statements. The VDS order need not equal statement issuance order. Relying-party trust in issuers and services, key discovery, registration-client authorization and compromised-key revocation remain external. Therefore SCITT can corroborate inclusion and detect equivocation within a declared service, but cannot prove that every agent action or evaluation was routed to that service. Warrantor should use SCITT as an optional transparency layer over its semantic receipts and authenticated completeness manifests.
evidence.technicalContribution: A consensus architecture and COSE message profile for issuer-signed statements, transparency-service registration policy, append-only/non-equivocating sequences, receipts, auditing and accountable operation across heterogeneous supply-chain statement types.
evidence.methodology: The IETF SCITT Working Group developed the architecture through public review and IESG approval. This review performed section-level analysis of roles, message formats, registration flow, VDS requirements, privacy, key management and the explicit residual threat model, and reconciled it with RFC 9942.
findings: SCITT guarantees identifiable/authenticated issuer statements, independently auditable provenance/history and efficient proof of registration.
The transparency service must verify a statement, apply registration policy and commit it before returning a receipt.
The standard explicitly says registered statements can be false and issuers can selectively omit submissions.
Multiple independent transparency services reduce reliance on one service but leave the relying party responsible for selecting trusted issuers and services.
SCITT receipts are strong evidence of inclusion, not evidence of complete routing, accurate semantics or successful execution.
limitations: Issuer accuracy, issuer/service trust selection, key discovery, client authorization and key-compromise revocation are not standardized by this RFC.
Selective participation prevents the log from proving a negative about unsubmitted events.
Registration order cannot be assumed to be issuance order unless the service policy says so.
Full statements or even hashes and sequence metadata can expose confidential operational information.
incentives: The authors and implementers have an ecosystem incentive to promote SCITT adoption, but IETF consensus review, Standards Track status and unusually explicit exclusions support high confidence in the bounded claims.

quality.rationale: IETF consensus, precise message and threat-model boundaries, current publication and direct W1/W2 applicability make this essential. It is an architecture and profile rather than an independently benchmarked implementation, limiting reproducibility credit.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt SCITT as an optional registration and transparency profile for Warrantor statements, but retain DSSE/in-toto for the primary interoperable predicate path and add signed expected-set/reconciliation evidence because SCITT cannot prove submission completeness.
options: Re-envelope or bridge Warrantor DSSE predicates into SCITT COSE statements while preserving a cross-format digest.
Use a private consortium SCITT service for confidential enterprise deployments, accepting governance and availability duties.
Run only a public Sigstore/Rekor path, simplifying operations but narrowing statement and privacy choices.

architecture: Define issuer, transparency-service and relying-party trust separately from receipt semantics.
Never use log inclusion as a synonym for complete action capture.
implementation: Implement COSE/SCITT bridge vectors, selective-omission tests, key compromise recovery and multi-service consistency monitoring.
business: Standards-based transparency can improve audit portability, but service operation creates governance and cost obligations.
regulatory: Use registered evidence to support auditability and chronology while retaining privacy, retention and legal-validity controls outside SCITT.
academic: Study completeness protocols and cross-log accountability beyond inclusion proofs.
content: Publish a precise comparison of authenticity, transparency, accuracy and completeness.

verification.notes: RFC Editor metadata and full text were inspected, including Sections 5-9. The record preserves explicit limits on statement accuracy, issuer participation, ordering, trust decisions, key compromise and privacy.

sources.title: RFC 9942: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Receipts

access.accessNotes: The complete RFC and official metadata were freely accessible; VDS/VDP registries, usage, proof examples, privacy and security sections were inspected.

evidence.summary: RFC 9942 standardizes compact COSE receipts carrying signed proofs about a Verifiable Data Structure. The proof can establish properties such as inclusion, consistency, disclosure, non-inclusion or freshness, depending on the registered VDS and proof type. It defines COSE header parameters for receipts, VDS algorithms and VDS proofs, requires receipts to be COSE_Sign1, and gives RFC 9162 SHA-256 Merkle examples. This is the correct normative building block for a SCITT-backed Warrantor profile, but not a semantic receipt replacement. The proof states a property of a particular data structure at a particular state; it does not authenticate the original producer unless the surrounding object does so, validate evaluation or policy semantics, prove execution, or show that unsubmitted events never occurred. Proof formats are tied to their VDS, and the RFC explicitly warns against assuming cross-VDS interoperability. Validity periods and revocation/suspension status are outside scope. Warrantor should therefore consume RFC 9942 through a pinned profile with named VDS, algorithms, trust roots, status/freshness policy and a separate completeness mechanism.
evidence.technicalContribution: IETF registries and COSE encodings for signed VDS proofs, including inclusion and consistency receipts, common header parameters, tagged COSE_Sign1 representation and profiling rules.
evidence.methodology: IETF COSE Working Group specification with public review and IESG approval. The review inspected definitions, registries, RFC 9162 proof examples, interoperability warnings, privacy leakage, algorithm guidance, validity and status exclusions, and its role within RFC 9943.
findings: COSE Receipts can carry several VDS proof properties in a standard envelope while keeping the VDS algorithm explicit.
Receipts must be COSE_Sign1 and verifiers must validate registered VDS and proof identifiers.
Proof types are VDS-specific; interoperability and migration cannot be assumed.
The standard leaves validity-period expression and receipt revocation/suspension status to profiles or other mechanisms.
A proof of inclusion is not a proof that all required events were submitted, accepted or truthful.
limitations: VDS-specific representations create implementation burden and migration risk.
Log size, structure and header metadata can reveal sensitive operational facts.
The standard does not define receipt status, semantic truth, event completeness, key governance or application authorization.
COSE_Sign1 is single-signer, so threshold or multi-party assurance needs composition outside an individual receipt.
incentives: Authors and transparency implementers benefit from COSE Receipt adoption; IETF consensus and explicit proof/implementation limits support high confidence in the constrained interpretation.

quality.rationale: Consensus standardization, precise CBOR/COSE structures, proof registries, concrete Merkle examples and explicit security/privacy limits make this essential to W1/W2 transparency profiles. It does not supply application semantics or completeness.

recommendation.preferredAction: Consume RFC 9942 only through a Warrantor profile that fixes the VDS, proof types, algorithms, signer trust, validity, status and privacy rules; use it for verifiable registration properties, never as a substitute for semantic or population-completeness evidence.
options: Use RFC9162_SHA256 for maximum current compatibility.
Register a new VDS only if it supplies a measurable property unavailable in existing structures and budget for independent cryptographic review.
Use an external SCITT or Sigstore service and store its native proof bytes, reducing implementation surface while retaining provider dependencies.

architecture: Keep VDS proof verification pluggable but policy-pinned and return typed proof facts rather than a single generic valid boolean.
implementation: Test malformed proofs, wrong VDS identifiers, stale receipts, log forks, migration and privacy leakage.
business: Standards-based proofs improve audit portability but can add storage, monitoring and service cost.
regulatory: Document the exact proved property and avoid presenting inclusion as proof of control operation completeness.
academic: Measure interoperability and migration failures across proof structures and services.
content: Explain inclusion, consistency, non-inclusion and completeness as separate claims.

verification.notes: Official metadata and complete RFC were reviewed, including the cross-VDS interoperability warning, privacy considerations and out-of-scope validity/status mechanisms.

sources.title: RFC 9711: The Entity Attestation Token (EAT)

access.accessNotes: The current full RFC, metadata and reported errata were freely accessible. Core claims, evidence/result relationship, profiles, protection choices, trustworthiness and privacy sections were inspected.

evidence.summary: RFC 9711 defines EAT, the current Standards Track CWT/JWT claims framework for attesting the state and characteristics of a device, hardware component, software component or process. It supplies common identifiers and state claims, nonce-based freshness, nested submodules for layered/composite entities, detached claims sets and a profile mechanism that narrows the large option space for a use case. EAT maps cleanly to Warrantor's confidential-computing and measured-execution needs, but it is a framework rather than a security guarantee. The RFC allows every protection combination supported by COSE/JOSE/CWT/JWT, including an Unsecured JWT, unless a profile forbids it. It defines no message flow and no normative verifier rules. It explicitly imposes no security level on the entity, attester or claim implementation. A relying party must know how an attester protects keys and measurements and how a verifier appraised evidence against endorsements, reference values and policy. Warrantor should therefore define a full EAT profile with required signing, nonce/freshness, measurements, implementation identity, endorsement/reference-value provenance, verifier identity and appraisal-policy digest, and must keep Evidence distinct from Attestation Results.
evidence.technicalContribution: A JSON/CBOR attestation claims framework over JWT/CWT, common entity/state claims, nonce freshness, submodule and detached-claims modeling, security-envelope choices and a named profile mechanism for interoperable narrowing.
evidence.methodology: The RATS Working Group developed the Standards Track specification through public review and IESG approval. This review inspected the operational model, evidence-versus-result semantics, common claims, profiles, protection combinations, verifier-policy boundary, trustworthiness considerations and privacy consequences, and checked official metadata and errata visibility.
findings: EAT can represent both raw evidence and verifier-produced attestation results, but their meaning and trust path are different.
The profile mechanism is mandatory in practice for interoperability because the base standard deliberately permits many encodings, claims, algorithms and protection combinations.
Nonce claims can establish that signing occurred after a challenge, but they do not prove that every measured value was freshly collected at signing time.
The base framework allows unsecured tokens and requires no minimum defense level, so 'EAT present' must never be rendered as 'trusted execution'.
Claim trustworthiness depends on the implementation, key custody, endorsements, reference values, verifier and appraisal policy.
limitations: EAT does not define message flow, verifier algorithms, authorization decisions or implementation assurance.
Unsecured, MACed, signed and encrypted combinations are all permitted by the base; a secure application must publish a narrow full profile.
EAT signatures authenticate an attester's claim set but cannot alone prove hardware isolation, truthful measurements or complete execution observation.
Persistent identifiers, software versions, location and nested system state can create tracking and confidentiality risks.
incentives: Authors and RATS implementers benefit from a broadly reusable claims ecosystem; IETF consensus, explicit flexibility and unusually direct trustworthiness warnings make the bounded interpretation robust.

quality.rationale: Current IETF consensus, detailed claims and profile semantics, direct applicability to confidential computing, and explicit guarantee boundaries make EAT essential. Its flexibility is a strength only after Warrantor supplies a strict profile and validates implementations.

recommendation.preferredAction: Define a strict Warrantor EAT profile for measured-execution evidence and verifier results, require cryptographic protection and nonce/freshness semantics, bind the appraisal policy and reference-value set, and expose assurance level rather than a misleading trusted/untrusted boolean.
options: Use an existing platform-specific EAT profile and normalize results through RATS CMW, minimizing custom claims but accepting vendor variance.
Define one hardware-neutral profile plus vendor evidence adapters, maximizing portability while increasing appraisal complexity.
Embed raw vendor attestations only, reducing initial work but forcing every relying party to understand vendor-specific evidence.

architecture: Model Attester, Verifier and Relying Party as separate trust roles even when one deployment combines them.
Record evidence, endorsements, reference values, appraisal policy and result as distinct linked artifacts.
implementation: Reject unsecured tokens, ambiguous profiles, missing freshness and unknown critical claims.
Test stale nonces, nested-submodule substitution, verifier compromise, endorsement rollback and reference-value drift.
business: A vendor-neutral profile can reduce confidential-computing lock-in but requires maintained appraisal adapters and assurance disclosures.
regulatory: Expose what was measured, by whom, under which policy and when; do not represent token validity as proof of compliance.
academic: Evaluate cross-vendor equivalence, freshness race windows and verifier-policy reproducibility.
content: Publish an evidence-versus-attestation-result explainer and retire 'TEE-signed means trustworthy' language.

verification.notes: Official full text and metadata were inspected. The record explicitly incorporates Section 6.3.6 protection flexibility, Section 9.1 claim-trustworthiness limits, verifier-policy dependence and nonce/freshness boundaries.

sources.title: RFC 9334: Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS) Architecture

access.accessNotes: The complete architecture and official metadata were freely accessible. It is retained on the indispensable-foundations shelf because current EAT and CMW standards normatively depend on its role and conceptual-message model.

evidence.summary: RFC 9334 is the indispensable conceptual architecture for remote attestation. It separates an Attester that produces Evidence, a Verifier that appraises Evidence against endorsements, reference values and an appraisal policy, and a Relying Party that appraises Attestation Results under its own policy to make an application decision. That separation prevents a critical Warrantor category error: an authentic piece of evidence is not itself a trust decision, and a positive verifier result is not automatically an authorization. The RFC also distinguishes trust, a relying party choice, from trustworthiness, a quality used in that choice. It covers passport and background-check topologies, layered and composite attesters, verifier trust, privacy and several freshness mechanisms. Its limit is intentional abstraction. It does not define a wire format, claims schema, algorithms, concrete appraisal policies or implementation security level. Freshness narrows recentness rather than eliminating race conditions; evidence may contain old measurements that are only signed recently. Warrantor should adopt the RATS role/data model for confidential-computing evidence and record every appraisal input needed to reproduce a result.
evidence.technicalContribution: A technology-neutral architecture and vocabulary for Attesters, Verifiers, Relying Parties, Evidence, Attestation Results, Endorsements, Reference Values, appraisal policies, layered/composite systems, trust relationships and freshness.
evidence.methodology: IETF consensus architecture informed by representative remote-attestation use cases and existing technologies. This review inspected roles, trust model, conceptual messages, appraisal paths, freshness mechanisms, privacy and security considerations and reconciled them with current RFC 9711 and RFC 9999.
findings: Evidence is appraised by a Verifier; a Relying Party separately decides how to use the resulting claims or result.
Trust is a decision while trustworthiness is a property considered in that decision.
Attestation Result quality depends on the Attester, Evidence, Verifier, endorsements, reference values and appraisal policy.
Nonce, timestamp and epoch-ID approaches each narrow freshness differently and leave residual race or collection-age issues.
Composite trust requires appraising the relevant sub-entities and bindings, not merely accepting one top-level signature.
limitations: The RFC is Informational and protocol-neutral; it supplies no implementation, conformance suite or wire-level interoperability on its own.
Role separation does not make a verifier trustworthy or an appraisal policy correct.
Fresh evidence can describe measurements collected earlier, and state can change immediately after attestation.
Evidence, results, policies, reference values and endorsements can reveal sensitive system, defense and personal information.
incentives: The working group benefits from architectural convergence, but the document has no product-sales posture and repeatedly distinguishes conceptual roles from implementation guarantees.

quality.rationale: Although older and intentionally non-executable, RATS remains the authoritative architecture used by current EAT/CMW standards and prevents major trust-model errors. It belongs on the indispensable-foundations shelf, not in a recency-inflated main ranking.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt the RATS role and conceptual-message model as Warrantor's attestation architecture, require reproducible links from evidence through verifier inputs and policy to results, and keep the Relying Party's authorization decision distinct.
options: Operate Warrantor as both Verifier and Relying Party in a simple deployment while retaining logical role separation and audit fields.
Use third-party verifiers and accept their signed results, reducing vendor adapters but increasing external trust dependencies.
Expose raw evidence to every relying party, maximizing local control while multiplying sensitive-data, parser and vendor-integration risk.

architecture: Represent attestation as a graph of typed roles and artifacts rather than one token-valid boolean.
Bind composite sub-evidence and all appraisal inputs to the result.
implementation: Record verifier identity/version, policy digest, reference values, endorsements, freshness mechanism and result rationale.
Test verifier compromise, stale policy, submodule omission and post-attestation state change.
business: RATS alignment supports multi-vendor confidential-computing integration and clearer assurance contracts.
regulatory: Preserve explainable appraisal provenance and minimize sensitive evidence disclosure.
academic: Evaluate reproducibility and equivalence of attestation results across independent verifiers.
content: Center public explanations on evidence, appraisal and decision rather than hardware marketing labels.

verification.notes: The full architecture and current metadata were inspected. This older source is included solely as an indispensable foundation because current Standards Track RFCs build on it.

sources.title: RFC 9999: Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS) Conceptual Message Wrapper

access.accessNotes: The official July 2026 Standards Track RFC, encodings, protection options, examples, media-type registrations and security considerations were freely accessible and inspected.

evidence.summary: RFC 9999 supplies a typed wrapper for the protocol-agnostic conceptual messages defined by RATS: Evidence, Attestation Results, Endorsements, Reference Values and Appraisal Policies. It defines JSON/CBOR records and collections, CBOR tags, CWT/JWT claims, X.509 carriage, COSE/JWS protection options, media types and demultiplexing rules. This can give Warrantor a stable transport boundary for heterogeneous TEE and device evidence without making its core understand every vendor format. Its security boundary must remain explicit. The base wrapper is encapsulation, not a security format. A record's type and bytes do not prove authenticity, semantic correctness or freshness. An unprotected collection can be manipulated so that a verifier accepts a misleading composite; member-to-member or collection-level binding is the producer's and hosting protocol's responsibility. The hosting protocol must define which conceptual-message combinations are allowed and how protection fits its security model. Warrantor should consume CMW for interchange while requiring signed, typed collections and explicit bindings among evidence, endorsements, reference values, policy and results.
evidence.technicalContribution: Normative JSON and CBOR wrappers, collection structure, conceptual-message type indicators, COSE/JWS protection and transport registrations for carrying heterogeneous RATS artifacts across web, CBOR, PKIX and constrained protocols.
evidence.methodology: IETF public review and IESG approval produced a Standards Track interoperability specification. The review inspected record/tag/collection forms, conceptual-message indicators, demultiplexing, signing/carriage options, examples, media registrations and the collection/hosting-protocol security analysis.
findings: CMW allows a generic processor to route opaque attestation artifacts using precise type information without parsing every vendor format.
Collections can carry several RATS artifacts but need explicit integrity and inter-item binding.
The same conceptual messages can travel through CBOR, JSON, JWT, CWT, COSE, JWS, X.509, HTTP, MIME or CoAP integrations.
The base CMW is not a security format; the selected protection and hosting protocol determine authenticity, confidentiality and freshness.
Warrantor can use CMW to avoid a proprietary attestation transport while keeping policy and appraisal semantics in its own profile.
limitations: CMW does not define evidence semantics, appraisal algorithms, trust roots, freshness, key lifecycle or authorization.
Unprotected or inadequately bound collections permit substitution, deletion and misleading composite evidence.
The broad format/transport surface increases parser, profile and conformance burden.
The July 2026 RFC is too recent for strong independent deployment or interoperability evidence in this library wave.
incentives: The authors and RATS ecosystem benefit from wrapper adoption; IETF consensus and explicit responsibility transfer to profiles/hosting protocols make the core claims highly auditable.

quality.rationale: The newest IETF interoperability layer for heterogeneous attestation messages is directly relevant and normatively precise. Its recent publication and lack of independent deployment evidence limit reproducibility and durability confidence but not its importance as the consume target.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt RFC 9999 as Warrantor's external wrapper for heterogeneous RATS artifacts, require protected collections and explicit inter-item bindings, and publish a narrow profile defining allowed message combinations and hosting-protocol security.
options: Use CMW only at ingress/egress and convert to a typed internal graph, minimizing core parser exposure.
Retain native CMW objects end to end, maximizing fidelity while increasing policy and storage complexity.
Create a Warrantor-specific wrapper, simplifying immediate implementation but creating avoidable interoperability and standards debt.

architecture: Treat CMW type as routing metadata, not semantic validation or trust evidence.
Require a collection manifest that binds every expected artifact and role.
implementation: Build malformed-type, duplicate-item, substitution, omission, nested-collection and cross-encoding conformance vectors.
business: A standards wrapper improves hardware/vendor portability while reducing the appearance of lock-in.
regulatory: Apply data-minimization and access rules to opaque evidence because wrapper-level processing cannot infer sensitivity safely.
academic: Test cross-format semantic preservation and collection-binding failures across independent implementations.
content: Explain why interoperability wrapping and attestation assurance are separate engineering problems.

verification.notes: The July 2026 official full text and metadata were inspected. The record preserves the RFC's explicit statement that CMW is encapsulation rather than a security format and its warning about unprotected collection manipulation.

sources.title: Aevum: Open-source AI Agent Governance Kernel

access.accessNotes: The Apache-2.0 repository, release history, documentation, code, tests and conformance runner were freely accessible; the reviewed main revision and v0.9.0 release are separately identified.

evidence.summary: Aevum is the strongest fully reproduced independent implementation in this operational-trust wave. It implements a recorder-oriented governance kernel with SHA3-linked event history, Ed25519 and ML-DSA signing, COSE receipts, RFC 3161 timestamps, Merkle proofs, standalone verification, policy adapters and kernel-barrier integration. The pinned repository contains thirteen packages and unusually candid documentation of its trust boundaries. In a controlled run, 1,930 tests passed, 174 skipped and 10 were deselected; nine conformance checks passed and two optional Cedar checks skipped. This is substantial prior art for W1/W2 and a useful consume/comparator candidate for cryptographic record construction. It is not a complete Warrantor substitute: it does not prove complete mediation, authority intersection, event-population completeness or downstream effect truth. More importantly, its advertised Rekor v2 integration is not protocol-correct. The backend posts a Rekor v1 hashedrekord body to the v2 endpoint, expects a v1 UUID-keyed response map and tests against that mocked shape. When presented with a response shaped like the official Rekor v2 TransparencyLogEntry, the verifier raised an AttributeError. A green internal suite therefore cannot be treated as v2 interoperability evidence.
evidence.technicalContribution: A modular, independently verifiable agent-event recorder with signed hash chains, crypto-agile receipt generation, COSE portability, timestamps, Merkle inclusion material, policy and framework adapters, kernel barriers, verification tools and an executable conformance surface.
evidence.methodology: The review pinned the repository commit and release, inspected package boundaries, documentation, receipt and Rekor implementations, ran the project test suite with output capture disabled to work around a mounted-environment file error, ran the conformance harness, inspected mocked Rekor request/response fixtures and executed a controlled negative test with an official Rekor v2-shaped response. Findings distinguish reproduced internal behavior from external protocol interoperability.
findings: The pinned suite completed with 1,930 passed, 174 skipped and 10 deselected tests after a host-specific capture workaround; no product code was modified.
The conformance runner reported nine passes, zero failures and two optional Cedar skips across eleven checks.
Receipts and history combine useful primitives: SHA3 chaining, Ed25519/ML-DSA, COSE, RFC 3161 material, Merkle proofs and standalone verification.
The RekorV2Backend uses the v1 kind/apiVersion body at the v2 path and expects the v1 map response; its tests reproduce that mismatch instead of detecting it.
An official-shaped v2 response triggered an AttributeError in the controlled verifier path, so the claimed Rekor v2 integration is not interoperable as implemented.
Aevum is explicitly a recorder and governance research project; cryptographically valid records remain distinct from non-bypassable enforcement and complete event capture.
limitations: The repository describes a solo-maintained research project; no independent security audit, production deployment, ecosystem adoption or cross-implementation conformance report was found.
The controlled run did not exercise optional Cedar functionality, hosted Rekor, real RFC 3161 services, HSMs or distributed failure recovery.
Record signing and chaining cannot establish that all actions traversed the recorder, that recorded context was true or that the stated external effect occurred.
The Rekor v2 documentation and implementation mix v1 and v2 concepts and must not be used as a reference client without correction.
incentives: The maintainer has an incentive to demonstrate the novelty and breadth of Aevum, but open code, executable tests, candid known limits and a clear research-project label make the claims unusually inspectable.

artifacts.label: Rekor v2 client contract used for comparison

quality.rationale: A large reproduced implementation, unusually broad receipt surface and candid boundaries make Aevum high-quality comparator evidence. Solo maintenance, absent independent adoption/audit and the protocol-breaking Rekor v2 path prevent essential status.

recommendation.preferredAction: Consume Aevum's recorder, verification and conformance ideas selectively, contribute or require a protocol-correct Rekor v2 adapter, and retain Warrantor ownership of authority/effect binding, mediation conformance and expected-set reconciliation.
options: Contribute fixes and external v2 conformance tests upstream, then use Aevum as a receipt backend.
Reuse only test vectors and design patterns while implementing Warrantor predicates on DSSE/in-toto.
Adopt Aevum wholesale, accepting its recorder boundary, small-maintainer risk and current Rekor incompatibility.

architecture: Separate recorder integrity from enforcement, authorization and completeness guarantees.
Keep Rekor registration as a replaceable optional service with explicit API/version negotiation.
implementation: Add official Rekor v2 request/response fixtures, checkpoint and proof verification and negative cross-version tests.
Preserve Aevum native bytes and emit a field-level adapter-loss report into the Warrantor predicate.
business: Aevum reduces greenfield implementation cost but introduces solo-maintainer and assurance-review diligence requirements.
regulatory: Use signed records as evidence inputs only; do not present them as complete compliance or control-effectiveness proof.
academic: Study why mocked conformance suites validate obsolete external protocol shapes and propose contract-derived differential testing.
content: Publish a constructive recorder-versus-enforcement comparison and a reproducible Rekor interoperability case study.

verification.notes: Pinned code and tests were inspected and executed. The internal suite was reproduced, and the Rekor v2 API mismatch was demonstrated with a controlled official-shaped response; hosted service interoperability was not attempted.

sources.title: Sigstore Security and Threat Model

access.accessNotes: The official threat-model, security and trust-root documentation were freely accessible and inspected together with current root-signing targets.

evidence.summary: Sigstore's official threat model is an essential guardrail for every Warrantor use of signatures and transparency. It states the security properties at their real boundary: verification can establish control of a signing identity or workflow at a time under configured trust, while transparency makes events discoverable and tampering detectable under log and monitoring assumptions. It does not show that a signer was authorized for the action, that signed content is correct or safe, that every required event was submitted, or that an action passed through a non-bypassable enforcement point. The model assigns important duties to identity providers, certificate authorities, transparency logs, clients, TUF trust-root distribution, policy and monitors. This directly rebuts any architecture or product language that turns a valid signature or Rekor inclusion proof into a generic trust decision. Inspection of current Sigstore root-signing targets also found a deployment nuance: the default public signing configuration selected Rekor v1, while a separate opt-in Rekor-v2 configuration selected the v2 log first with v1 fallback. Warrantor must explicitly pin and attest the selected service, API and trust root rather than relying on the word Sigstore.
evidence.technicalContribution: A component- and attacker-oriented security model for identity-bound signing, certificate issuance, transparency, verification, monitoring, trust-root recovery and compromise response, including explicit non-guarantees for signed artifacts.
evidence.methodology: The review inspected official threat-model and security documentation, enumerated stated principals, threats, guarantees and operational dependencies, and compared the current TUF/root-signing configuration targets used for default Rekor v1 and opt-in Rekor v2 selection.
findings: A valid signature can establish possession/control of the accepted digital identity at signing time; it does not establish entitlement, intent, correctness or safety.
Transparency and monitoring make compromised or malicious signing discoverable but cannot prevent all signed malicious artifacts or prove complete submission.
TUF-distributed trust roots and recovery operations are part of the security boundary, not incidental deployment metadata.
Log and CA compromise assumptions require detection, monitoring and recovery plans; signature verification alone is not a full assurance case.
Current root-signing metadata separates the default Rekor v1 target from an opt-in v2-first target, so protocol selection must be explicit.
limitations: This is authoritative first-party documentation, not an independent audit or deployment study.
The threat model cannot establish that a particular Warrantor implementation correctly validates identity, timestamps, checkpoints, proofs or TUF metadata.
Public transparency can disclose identities, artifact metadata, timing and operational relationships; private use needs a separate privacy and governance model.
incentives: Sigstore benefits from adoption, but explicit non-guarantees, public design review, open implementations and separable components make the security claims auditable.

quality.rationale: This is the authoritative current guarantee boundary for a core proposed dependency and prevents consequential overclaims. It is essential despite first-party implementation context because the normative operational assumptions and non-guarantees are explicit and independently inspectable.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt Sigstore's threat model as Warrantor's mandatory signature/transparency guarantee vocabulary, pin every selected service and TUF root, and prohibit any inference from signature or inclusion directly to authorization, correctness, execution or completeness.
options: Use public Sigstore services for non-confidential release artifacts with monitoring and privacy acceptance.
Operate private components with equivalent root, monitoring, recovery and audit controls.
Use DSSE/in-toto with enterprise PKI and trusted timestamps while deferring transparency.

architecture: Expose separate facts for signature, credential, timestamp, log inclusion, checkpoint consistency, authorization and completeness.
Make the service URL, protocol generation, log ID and trusted root part of the signed assurance profile.
implementation: Verify exact signed bytes, certificate identity constraints, time evidence, checkpoint signature, inclusion proof and TUF metadata.
Add compromise-recovery and root-rotation exercises to release and notary operations.
business: Standards-aligned signing lowers buyer integration friction but does not replace control assurance or independent audit.
regulatory: Describe Sigstore outputs as provenance and integrity evidence with named limitations, not automatic compliance.
academic: Evaluate how signature/transparency status is misinterpreted by agent governance systems and verifier interfaces.
content: Publish a guarantee-boundary explainer: signed, transparent and authorized are three different claims.

verification.notes: Official threat-model, security and root-signing materials were inspected. The default-versus-opt-in Rekor selection statement is a dated configuration observation, not a promise about future defaults.

sources.title: Rekor v2: Tile-backed Transparency Log and Client Migration Contract
sources.venue: GitHub release and official client documentation

access.accessNotes: The official v2.3.0 release, code, API types, deployment material and client migration contract were freely accessible and inspected.

evidence.summary: Rekor v2 is the current tile-backed Sigstore transparency implementation and the exact generation named by Warrantor specifications. It is not a drop-in endpoint rename from Rekor v1. The v2 API wraps a hashedRekordRequestV002 containing binary digest, signature and verifier material; the response is a direct TransparencyLogEntry rather than the v1 UUID-to-record map. Clients must verify a signed checkpoint, extract its root hash and tree size, validate the inclusion proof and trust the configured log identity/root. v2.3.0 also removed the DSSE entry type, so DSSE statements are registered by digest while their semantic bytes and signatures remain in the Warrantor/in-toto layer. The integrated_time field is always zero and must be ignored; reliable time is delegated to RFC 3161 timestamp authority evidence. These facts contradict Warrantor's bundled v1.3.6 deployment and invalidate Aevum's nominal v2 adapter shape. Rekor should be an optional registered-history layer, never the source of action authorization, execution truth or event-population completeness.
evidence.technicalContribution: A horizontally scalable, tile-backed transparency log with a versioned hashedrekord API, signed checkpoints, inclusion proofs, multiple storage backends, year-sharded operation and explicit client migration and time semantics.
evidence.methodology: The review pinned v2.3.0, inspected release changes, client migration instructions, request/response types and verification responsibilities, compared them with Rekor v1 and Warrantor/Aevum clients, and inspected current Sigstore signing-configuration targets to determine whether v2 is selected by default or opt-in.
findings: Rekor v2 request and response objects are structurally incompatible with the v1 API used by Warrantor's bundled service and Aevum's adapter.
Clients are responsible for verifying the signed checkpoint and inclusion proof against the trusted log identity/root.
The v2.3.0 release removed the DSSE entry type; clients register hashedrekord material and preserve DSSE semantics elsewhere.
integrated_time is always zero and must be ignored; RFC 3161 timestamp evidence supplies time.
An inclusion proof establishes registration in a particular authenticated log state, not statement truth or complete submission.
limitations: As a first-party implementation and release source, it does not independently validate Sigstore's operational security or availability claims.
Public or shared logs can expose identity, timing and relationship metadata even when only digests are submitted.
The project is rapidly evolving; Warrantor must pin API, trust-root and release versions and exercise migration/restore paths.
Rekor does not supply Warrantor's authority, action/effect, enforcement-conformance or expected-set semantics.
incentives: Sigstore benefits from migration to the new implementation; open code, precise incompatible API types and explicit client duties make the migration claims reproducible.

artifacts.label: Current opt-in Rekor v2 signing configuration

quality.rationale: This is the authoritative current implementation contract for the protocol Warrantor names and is detailed enough to disprove two client integrations. Rapid evolution and limited independent production evidence keep it below essential status.

recommendation.preferredAction: Replace the bundled v1.3.6 stack with a pinned Rekor v2 or managed-service profile only after checkpoint, inclusion, RFC 3161 time, privacy, monitoring, backup, recovery and upgrade gates pass; keep transparency optional by assurance profile.
options: Operate a private pinned Rekor v2 deployment with independent checkpoint monitors.
Use a public or managed Rekor v2 service for non-confidential evidence.
Use a SCITT implementation for consortium registration while retaining the same expected-set and monitoring responsibilities.
Defer transparency and use trusted timestamps plus signed statements until operational maturity is demonstrated.

architecture: Preserve DSSE/in-toto statement bytes outside Rekor and register their digest.
Bind log ID, API generation, checkpoint, tree size, proof, trusted root and timestamp evidence in the Warrantor verification result.
implementation: Delete v1-shaped v2 mocks and test against official request/response fixtures.
Exercise split view, checkpoint rollback, unavailable TSA, missing proof, backup/restore and year-shard transitions.
business: Managed service reduces operations but creates metadata, residency, availability and third-party trust considerations for enterprise buyers.
regulatory: Classify log data and location; do not publish confidential prompts, identities or tenant relationships by default.
academic: Measure log/checkpoint witness assumptions and population-completeness failure modes for agent receipts.
content: Publish a Rekor v1-to-v2 migration guide focused on proof and time semantics rather than endpoint changes.

verification.notes: The v2.3.0 code and client contract were inspected and compared with local integrations. Docker was unavailable, so a v2 service was not deployed in this environment.

sources.title: The SPIFFE Standard: Workload Identity, SVIDs, Workload API, and Federation

publication.version: pinned commit dc4e9d9; current standards snapshot

access.accessNotes: The current standard index and a 2026-08-03 repository revision were freely accessible and inspected across SPIFFE ID, X.509-SVID, JWT-SVID, Workload API, trust-domain bundle and federation specifications.

evidence.summary: SPIFFE is the essential consume standard for portable workload identity beneath Warrantor. It defines stable SPIFFE IDs, rotating X.509 and JWT SVID credentials, workload-facing delivery through the Workload API, trust-domain bundles and federation. The distinction between identity name and credential is decisive for Warrantor evidence design. A receipt field containing only spiffe://muveraai.com/service records an asserted SPIFFE ID; it does not prove which SVID was presented, whether it chained to the accepted bundle, when it was validated, whether it was expired or revoked, or which validation policy ran. The Workload API streams the full authorized SVID set and trust bundles so clients can rotate without freezing credentials. X.509-SVID validation uses certificate-chain and SPIFFE rules, with revocation/status dependent on configured bundle and CRL behavior. SPIFFE authenticates a workload, not the human principal, delegated authority, requested action or actual effect. Warrantor should therefore consume SPIFFE/SPIRE for workload credentials and build its agent-specific mandate, authority intersection, action authorization and receipt appraisal above it.
evidence.technicalContribution: An implementation-neutral identity system defining URI workload identities, short-lived X.509/JWT credentials, trust bundles, a local streaming Workload API, trust domains and cross-domain federation.
evidence.methodology: The review pinned the standards repository, inspected identity, credential, validation, bundle, Workload API and federation requirements, compared them with Warrantor receipt schemas and both Go identity implementations, and separated normative standard properties from SPIRE deployment behavior.
findings: A SPIFFE ID is a stable workload identifier; an SVID is a rotating credential that carries or represents that identity.
Workload API clients receive streaming SVID and bundle updates and should stop using credentials that are removed or redacted from the authorized set.
X.509-SVID validation depends on RFC 5280 path processing plus SPIFFE-specific constraints and the accepted trust-domain bundle/status material.
SPIFFE authenticates workloads and federated domains but leaves application authorization and initiating-principal semantics to higher layers.
A receipt that stores only a SPIFFE ID cannot prove live-and-unrevoked credential validation at issuance.
limitations: The standards do not prescribe application policy, agent delegation, complete mediation, effect observation or receipt population.
Security depends on workload isolation, correct attestation and registration, protected local Workload API access, bundle distribution and federation policy.
Short-lived credentials reduce exposure but do not supply an execution-count revocation SLA or prove immediate invalidation at every relying party.
The standards are not evidence that Warrantor's manifests or Go modules are correctly integrated.
incentives: The CNCF/SPIFFE ecosystem benefits from broad adoption, but implementation neutrality, explicit boundaries and multiple implementations make the standard claims durable and inspectable.

quality.rationale: SPIFFE is the authoritative interoperable workload-identity contract already present in Warrantor's dependency graph. Its precise credential/identity boundary materially changes receipt semantics and prevents unnecessary reinvention.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt SPIFFE as the workload-identity and federation contract, use a supported implementation such as SPIRE, and extend receipts to record credential-validation evidence while keeping agent authority and action authorization in W6/W4.
options: Use SPIRE with upstream Kubernetes deployment and controller-manager patterns.
Use a managed or cloud workload-identity implementation with SPIFFE interoperability.
Use enterprise PKI initially and add a SPIFFE compatibility boundary later, accepting migration cost.

architecture: Model workload identity, initiating principal, delegate authority and action authorization as distinct facts.
Record SVID type/digest or serial, validity interval, bundle/version, validation time, status inputs and result rather than only a SPIFFE ID.
implementation: Consume streaming Workload API updates and test credential/bundle rotation, revocation/status, federation and socket authorization.
Never cache an SVID beyond the authorized stream state or label a self-signed local token SPIFFE-compliant without an explicit compatibility profile.
business: Standards-based workload identity improves enterprise integration and reduces proprietary identity-plane scope.
regulatory: Workload identity can support evidence attribution, but organizational accountability and legal authorization remain separate controls.
academic: Measure the gap between credential revocation and residual authorized agent effects across heterogeneous enforcement points.
content: Explain identity versus authority versus effect using SPIFFE as the concrete baseline.

verification.notes: The current standards and pinned repository revision were inspected. Assertions about Warrantor deployment failure are recorded separately because the standard itself does not validate an implementation.

sources.title: SPIRE 1.15.3: Production-ready Implementation of the SPIFFE APIs

access.accessNotes: The current release, code, configuration references and Kubernetes/controller-manager ecosystem were freely accessible. Official SPIRE 1.10.0 binaries were also used to validate Warrantor's pinned configuration.

evidence.summary: SPIRE is the mature consume implementation for the SPIFFE standard and the correct baseline for judging Warrantor's workload-identity deployment. It provides node and workload attestation, SVID issuance and rotation, the Workload API, trust-bundle distribution, registration, federation and operational plugins. The current release at review time was v1.15.3, while Warrantor pinned v1.10.0 and also used an unpinned latest agent image in Helm. An official v1.10.0 server binary rejected Warrantor's extracted configuration because bundle_endpoint and default_svid_ttl were unknown top-level server keys. Static comparison found additional blockers: the k8s_psat allow-list key is misspelled, projected token path and audience do not match configured/default expectations, parent IDs do not match actual node-attestor IDs, declared SPIFFEEntry/SPIFFEBundleEndpoint kinds are not the controller-manager CRDs, the agent init container starts a long-running agent and blocks the real container, and the Helm init path has no socket mount. Even a successfully fetched SVID would not itself create an ongoing mTLS data plane. SPIRE remains the recommendation; Warrantor's manifests do not.
evidence.technicalContribution: A production-oriented SPIFFE implementation with extensible node/workload attestation, key and data stores, SVID rotation, local Workload API, registration, bundle distribution, federation and Kubernetes integrations.
evidence.methodology: The review compared the current release and official documentation with Warrantor's server, agent, trust-domain and Helm manifests. The ConfigMap server configuration was extracted and checked with the official pinned v1.10.0 spire-server validate command; removing the two rejected keys allowed syntax validation, after which remaining token, selector, topology, CRD and mTLS-data-plane issues were assessed from the corresponding official contracts.
findings: The official pinned server validator rejected Warrantor's configuration due to unknown bundle_endpoint and default_svid_ttl keys.
Warrantor's k8s_psat option uses service_account_whitelist instead of the documented service_account_allow_list and does not align token path/audience with its projected token.
Static parent IDs omit the node or pod UID portion of the attested agent SPIFFE ID, so registration entries do not select the actual parent.
SPIFFEEntry and SPIFFEBundleEndpoint are not the official controller-manager CRD kinds; ClusterSPIFFEID, ClusterStaticEntry and ClusterFederatedTrustDomain are the relevant APIs.
The DaemonSet init container runs spire-agent as a long-running process and lacks the config, bundle and token mounts, blocking the intended agent container.
The Helm mTLS switch uses a floating latest image, an unmatched socket path and no shared socket volume; a one-time SVID fetch cannot terminate mTLS.
limitations: Docker, Kubernetes, Helm and kubectl were unavailable, so the reviewed manifests were not exercised in a live cluster.
SPIRE's first-party release materials do not independently establish the security of any particular deployment.
A corrected deployment must still test HA database/key management, recovery, upgrades, federation, socket isolation, attestor compromise and credential rollover.
SPIRE authenticates workloads; Warrantor still needs agent authority, action authorization, enforcement and receipt semantics.
incentives: The CNCF project benefits from adoption, while open code, strict validators, public documentation and multiple deployment integrations make its configuration contracts independently testable.

quality.rationale: A mature CNCF implementation, strict configuration validator and directly relevant Kubernetes contracts make SPIRE high-quality operational evidence. The source remains first-party and the latest release is too recent for this wave to establish independent durability.

recommendation.preferredAction: Consume a pinned supported SPIRE deployment through upstream Helm/controller-manager patterns, delete or quarantine the current manifests, and enable Warrantor mTLS only after clean-cluster identity, rotation, authorization and failure-path acceptance tests pass.
options: Adopt upstream SPIRE Helm plus controller manager and application-native go-spiffe mTLS.
