Use Envoy SDS/Workload API as the mTLS data plane while applications authorize peer SPIFFE IDs.
Use a managed SPIFFE-compatible workload identity platform.
Defer SPIRE and ship a narrowly documented enterprise-PKI profile for the first deployment.

architecture: SPIRE supplies workload credentials and federation; W6/W4 supply agent authority and action policy.
Specify the actual mTLS termination/data-plane component and peer-authorization rules instead of treating SVID retrieval as transport security.
implementation: Pin image digests and chart versions; use actual ClusterSPIFFEID/federation resources and matching service accounts/selectors.
Gate release on clean-cluster install, SVID/bundle rotation, node/workload rejection, federation, outage, restore, upgrade and socket-isolation tests.
business: Upstream deployment reduces bespoke operational risk, but production HA and support ownership still need costed enterprise plans.
regulatory: Document credential issuance, validation, rotation and administrative access as technical controls, not proof of legal authority.
academic: Publish an adversarial deployment-conformance corpus for SPIFFE agent systems and measure stale-credential residual effects.
content: Produce a corrected reference architecture showing Workload API, actual mTLS termination and Warrantor authorization as separate layers.

verification.notes: Current release and upstream APIs were inspected. The official v1.10.0 binary reproduced the deterministic server-config rejection; live-cluster behavior remains an explicit evidence gap.

sources.title: Open Agent Auth

access.accessNotes: The Apache-2.0 source, documentation, tests, workflows and history were freely accessible. The beta artifacts were not on Maven Central and were built locally from the pinned commit.

evidence.summary: Open Agent Auth is a substantial Java implementation comparator for agent operation authorization, workload identity/proof, policy evaluation, human consent, MCP mediation and signed audit context. A pinned 13-module build passed and yielded 6,510 executed passes out of 6,617 reported tests, with 107 default-skipped integration tests. Aggregate line coverage was 84.61% and branch coverage 67.61%. With six sample services live, the dedicated protocol profile executed 226 checks with no failure, error or skip. A separate broader live integration selection executed 107 tests and failed 13 across OIDC discovery, JWKS ETag/caching, PAR, authorization rejection/redirect and token-error behavior. Code inspection found that embedded delegation-record signatures are checked only for non-emptiness; layer-four identity consistency returns success when its optional binding store is absent; WPT does not bind the exact current-draft target/request; the MCP server API is a wrapper rather than demonstrated non-bypassable transport integration; default audit storage is deletable in-memory state; and the JWT evidence is not demonstrated to conform to W3C VCDM 2.0/current VC JOSE. Agent-to-agent authorization and delegation remain roadmap items. The artifact is therefore valuable supporting prior art and a negative-vector source, not a W6-equivalent production enforcement boundary.
evidence.technicalContribution: An integrated public Java framework combining WIT/WPT workload credentials, AOAT operation tokens, OAuth/OIDC flows, policy engines, consent rendering, MCP client/server helpers, audit records, sample services and large first-party test suites around an evolving IETF agent-operation authorization proposal.
evidence.methodology: The repository was pinned at commit d75da121a66f8b2ae5be009a98e050fd1dc4c1e6. Maven 3.9.16 and Temurin 17.0.20.1+1 were checksum-verified; the full aggregate build, per-module tests and coverage reports were executed. Six sample services were started under the mock-LLM profile inside bounded sessions. The protocol-conformance selection and the broader authorization/JWKS/security/five-layer integration selection were executed separately so skipped tests could not be counted as passes. A targeted 53-test delegation, identity-consistency and policy-registry selection also passed, confirming that the questionable placeholder-signature and no-binding-store outcomes are authored expectations rather than accidental untested paths. Relevant token, delegation, identity, policy, MCP, audit, VC, CI, version and support paths were inspected against current AOAT, WIMSE WPT and W3C VC specifications. OPA-live and browser E2E classes remain unexecuted because those external runtimes were unavailable.
findings: The clean 13-module build passed; 6,510 tests executed successfully and 107 integration tests were skipped by default.
The dedicated six-service protocol profile passed 226 of 226 checks, demonstrating substantial first-party self-conformance for its selected endpoints.

The broader live integration gate ran 107 tests and failed 13, including OIDC discovery 404s, absent JWKS ETag behavior, authorization requests returning unexpected 200 responses and malformed token requests returning 500.
Delegation-chain documentation says authorization-server signatures are verified, while the implementation accepts any non-empty as_signature and its unit tests use literal placeholder strings.
IdentityConsistencyValidator logs a warning, skips user/workload binding checks and returns success when BindingInstanceStore is not configured.
The WPT generator signs jti, exp, wth and optional token hashes but does not bind the target URI or exact HTTP request required for a complete evaluated-to-forwarded operation guarantee.
Agent-originated Rego can be registered without a trusted parse, type, semantic-equivalence or safe-built-in gate at registration.

The MCP surface supplies useful wrappers and policy inputs but no reviewed main-source transport hook proving every real MCP request is intercepted or that evaluated arguments equal forwarded arguments.
The default audit service uses deletable in-memory storage, so signed individual records do not establish durable, append-only or population-complete audit history.
The repository's VC-like JWT format is not demonstrated to meet current VCDM 2.0 JSON-LD and VC JOSE/COSE processing requirements.
Public-beta, changelog, Maven and security-policy version labels conflict, and current artifacts are not centrally published.
The README roadmap places agent-to-agent authorization/delegation, security-audit completion and richer audit monitoring in future work.
limitations: All implementation and evaluation evidence is first-party; no independent audit, formal proof, certification or second interoperating implementation was located.
The IETF Agent Operation Authorization and WIMSE WPT documents are evolving drafts, so compatibility is revision-specific rather than a stable-standard property.
The OPA integration suite was not run because no OPA service was available; the browser E2E suite was not run because Chrome/Chromium was unavailable.
Sample-service and mock-profile results do not establish production key custody, persistence, HA, disaster recovery, partition behavior, complete mediation or regulatory compliance.
Some broader integration failures may reflect profile or test drift; they remain failed authored requirements until the project identifies and fixes or retires the incompatible contract.
Strong unit count and line coverage do not measure authorization soundness, mutation resistance, bypass reachability, cross-implementation interoperability or production adoption.
incentives: Alibaba and project contributors benefit from adoption and standards influence; public code and tests make many claims inspectable, but product maturity and protocol-alignment claims remain first-party.
The repository's unusually large test surface is a positive transparency signal while still being co-designed with the implementation.

artifacts.label: W3C Securing Verifiable Credentials using JOSE and COSE

quality.rationale: Exceptional direct relevance, a large executable artifact and strong local reproducibility earn high technical-depth and reproducibility scores. First-party-only evidence, an evolving draft basis, ambiguous beta support, 13 live integration failures and material fail-open/bypass/semantic gaps prevent high-quality promotion.

recommendation.preferredAction: Track and implement interoperable profiles over the AOAT/WIMSE standards work, import Open Agent Auth protocol and negative vectors, and reject the reviewed beta as a production authority or MCP enforcement boundary until exact request binding, fail-closed identity, verified delegation, durable audit, second-implementation interoperability and all applicable live integration gates pass.
options: Consume only standards vocabulary and fixtures while implementing Warrantor's holder-bound authority and receipt layers independently.
Build an optional compatibility adapter to the beta behind strict version and conformance gates, accepting upstream draft churn.
Contribute missing security and interoperability fixes upstream, then reevaluate adoption after an independently audited stable release.
Fork the framework and own its security lifecycle, accepting a large Java, standards-tracking and support burden; not recommended.

architecture: Separate workload identity, user authority, delegation intersection, policy semantics, forwarding mediation and effect evidence as independently verified facts.
Bind target, method, canonical arguments/body, policy version, holder key, forward, response and effect under one immutable operation identifier.
implementation: Add garbage-signature, missing-binding-store, current-WPT-audience/replay, post-decision mutation, raw-MCP-bypass and audit-deletion vectors to release gates.
Require a typed policy IR and differential conformance instead of treating agent-originated Rego or policy IDs as trusted semantics.
business: Do not position signed agent-operation tokens, MCP authorization wrappers or semantic audit records as unique categories; sell independently measured complete-mediation and assurance properties.
regulatory: Treat cryptographic token/audit mechanisms as technical controls, not proof of user comprehension, legal authority, record completeness or compliance.
academic: Study protocol-revision drift, fail-open configuration, complete chain verification and evaluated-to-forwarded request correspondence against at least two implementations.
content: Publish a neutral AOAT/WIMSE/Open Agent Auth versus Warrantor boundary analysis with the green protocol and red broader-integration results shown side by side.

verification.notes: Pinned build, aggregate tests/coverage, six-service protocol profile, broader integration gate and targeted 53-test authority selection were executed. Protocol profile: 226/226 passed. Broader live integration: 94/107 passed and 13 failed. Targeted delegation/identity/policy registry: 53/53 passed, including tests that encode placeholder signatures and no-store success. OPA and browser E2E remain unexecuted. See artifact-review-alibaba-open-agent-auth.md.

sources.title: Authorization API 1.0

access.accessNotes: The OpenID Final Specification, approval announcement and public working-group source were live and free. The final was approved on 2026-01-12; the repository's final-publication preparation commit is dated 2026-01-11.

evidence.summary: AuthZEN Authorization API 1.0 is the essential cross-vendor PDP/PEP wire-contract baseline for Warrantor W4. It standardizes single and boxcar access evaluations using Subject-Action-Resource-Context, search APIs, HTTPS/JSON behavior and PDP discovery metadata. It intentionally leaves policy language, policy architecture, state management and API authentication out of scope. The PDP must trust the PEP to supply correct inputs and enforce the result; PEP authentication is recommended but its method and strength are not standardized. Decision responses may be signed, but signing is optional, and the base specification does not bind a decision to the exact bytes forwarded, atomically consume a permit, prove PEP coverage, preserve a delegation-chain intersection, emit a W2 receipt or reconcile external effects. The official repository has broad interop history and a detailed 2026 certification-scenario document, but no executable implementation of that new scenario was located in the pinned source. Warrantor should adopt AuthZEN as the public engine-neutral contract and build only the missing compiler-assurance, operation-binding, mediation and evidence layers.
evidence.technicalContribution: A final implementation-neutral API for interoperable access evaluation and permitted-subject/resource/action search between policy enforcement and decision points, including transport, discovery and optional response-integrity mechanisms.
evidence.methodology: The final specification and approval record were reviewed field by field; scopes, endpoints, status codes, request/decision semantics, boxcar defaults, search pagination, metadata, transport and security considerations were mapped to W1-W6. The public source was pinned at e94e0a26e52346d33fef56d28bce96bd34835705, its history was traced to the final-publication commit, and its certification scenario, CI rendering, interop result corpus and legacy gateway runner were inspected. The runner installation did not reproduce and no executable implementation of the new certification scenario was located.
findings: The final API gives W4 a stable external PDP/PEP boundary without choosing a policy language or engine.
A policy denial is HTTP 200 with decision false; HTTP 401 represents PEP authentication failure and must not be collapsed into a policy result.
The trust model depends on the PEP supplying correct SARC values and enforcing the returned decision.
Signed authorization responses and signed PDP metadata are optional and still do not prove the forwarded operation or external effect.
Search pagination is not an atomic authorization snapshot and may observe changes, repetitions or omissions across pages.
The repository's certification scenario covers protocol conformance rather than arbitrary policy correctness and is present as a document, not a located executable harness.
limitations: Policy language, architecture, state management and API authentication are out of scope.
The specification does not guarantee complete mediation, non-bypassability, decision-to-forward byte equality, atomic use, action receipts or effect completeness.
A positive decision does not by itself prove that the PEP understood or executed response context/obligations.
Interop event and participant result pages are ecosystem evidence, not independent hostile-input or production-assurance audits.
incentives: The multi-vendor working group and its members benefit from adoption and convergence; final-spec IPR process, public source, multiple implementations and explicit scope limits reduce but do not remove first-party ecosystem bias.

quality.rationale: Final OpenID standing, precise normative behavior, broad cross-vendor relevance and direct W4/W5/W6 impact make this essential. Reproducibility is bounded because the new certification scenario was not found as an executable harness, while independence is reduced because the ecosystem authors also supply implementations and interop results.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt AuthZEN 1.0 as Warrantor's primary external PDP/PEP contract while making PEP authentication, trusted-input provenance, exact-operation binding, atomic permit consumption, obligation profiles, complete mediation and receipts explicit Warrantor assurance layers.
options: Adopt AuthZEN as the public API over multiple internal policy targets; recommended.
Expose separate native Cedar/Rego/OpenFGA APIs and accept portability fragmentation.
Create a proprietary Warrantor decision API and accept avoidable integration and standards-tracking cost.

architecture: Keep the AuthZEN API separate from W4's typed policy IR and semantic-equivalence proofs.
Model a decision, enforcement event, receipt and external effect as distinct linked records.
implementation: Implement strict status/error handling, authenticated PDP/PEP transport and decision validation.
Add decision-to-operation digest binding and atomic consumption outside the base API.
business: Standards alignment reduces customer integration cost and weakens vendor-lock-in objections.
regulatory: Use AuthZEN decisions as technical control evidence, not proof of legal authority, policy correctness or complete enforcement.
academic: Evaluate cross-engine semantic equivalence and decision-to-effect integrity rather than proposing another general authorization API.
content: Publish an AuthZEN integration guide that clearly separates decision interoperability from enforcement assurance.

verification.notes: Final specification, approval announcement, public source and certification/interop materials were inspected. Repository pinned at e94e0a26e52346d33fef56d28bce96bd34835705. See artifact-review-authzen-coaz-mcp.md.

sources.title: Model Context Protocol Authorization — 2026-07-28

access.accessNotes: The versioned specification, changelog, schema and source repository were freely accessible. The inspected source commit was efb5cb3ecae3d5e185b49901a75a8fd5a551fc0f.

evidence.summary: MCP 2026-07-28 Authorization is the current essential transport-authorization baseline for Warrantor's HTTP MCP gateway. It defines OAuth/OIDC protected-resource discovery, client registration choices, issuer-response validation, resource indicators, audience-restricted token validation, step-up scopes, error behavior and security requirements. Authorization remains optional for MCP implementations; HTTP implementations should follow it when supported, stdio implementations should obtain credentials from the environment rather than use this flow, and alternative transports must apply their own security practices. The mechanism authenticates and scopes access to an MCP server at the transport layer. It does not standardize fine-grained parameter policy, server-authored semantic mappings, complete mediation, delegation-chain intersection, a signed permit bound to the exact forwarded JSON-RPC operation, receipt emission or external-effect reconciliation. Warrantor should adopt it beneath AuthZEN/COAZ and must not market OAuth conformance as complete agent authorization.
evidence.technicalContribution: A current OAuth 2.1/OIDC-derived authorization profile for MCP HTTP transports, including protected-resource and authorization-server discovery, registration, issuer validation, resource indicators, token audience handling and step-up scope challenges.
evidence.methodology: The versioned authorization text, current schema and 2026-07-28 changelog were reviewed against the previous 2025-06-18 candidate. Normative optionality, transport scope, discovery, registration, issuer, resource, token, scope and error requirements were extracted. The official current repository was cloned at efb5cb3ecae3d5e185b49901a75a8fd5a551fc0f and its current core method union was mechanically compared with COAZ-MCP Draft 1.
findings: Authorization is optional at the MCP implementation level and directly profiles HTTP-based transports.
Resource Indicators and audience validation reduce token passthrough and confused-deputy risk.
The 2026-07-28 revision adds issuer-response validation and changes registration preference toward Client ID Metadata Documents.
Scopes can be challenged and stepped up per operation, but the scope system does not define parameter-level semantics or cross-engine policy equivalence.
The standard does not bind a transport token or AuthZEN permit to the exact later-forwarded operation or its effect.
limitations: Authorization-server implementation remains out of scope.
Stdio deliberately uses environment credentials instead of this flow, leaving host/process isolation and secret handling as separate requirements.
Optional adoption prevents the standard itself from proving universal mediation.
OAuth tokens and scopes do not establish a human/agent delegation intersection, complete operation semantics or action receipts.
incentives: MCP maintainers and ecosystem vendors benefit from broad protocol adoption; public governance, versioned text, source schemas and explicit normative limits make the transport claims inspectable.

quality.rationale: This is the current normative authorization baseline for the protocol Warrantor intends to mediate and therefore essential despite optional adoption. It is versioned, source-backed and technically detailed; it remains ecosystem-authored and does not provide end-to-end enforcement evidence.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt MCP 2026-07-28 Authorization for HTTP transport identity, discovery, audience and token handling; add AuthZEN/COAZ for fine-grained policy and Warrantor-specific complete-mediation, delegation, operation-binding and receipt layers.
options: Implement the current standard plus Warrantor assurance extensions; recommended.
Use a gateway-vendor OAuth profile and accept portability drift.
Rely only on static API keys or environment secrets and accept weaker identity, rotation and discovery semantics.

architecture: Separate transport authorization from fine-grained action authorization and effect evidence.
Define a secure stdio/local-process profile because the HTTP flow does not apply there.
implementation: Test issuer mix-up, audience, resource indicator, registration, token forwarding, step-up and error paths.
Pin every gateway to an exact MCP core/extension version.
business: Current MCP compatibility is a procurement enabler; proprietary auth replaces rather than strengthens that baseline.
regulatory: OAuth evidence supports access-control narratives but does not prove delegated purpose, policy correctness or action outcome.
academic: Measure how transport authorization composes with parameter policy, delegation and complete mediation under extension/version drift.
content: Explain why MCP OAuth, AuthZEN decisions and Warrantor receipts solve different layers.

verification.notes: The current versioned authorization specification, release notes, changelog and source schema were inspected. See artifact-review-authzen-coaz-mcp.md.

sources.title: COAZ: A Framework for Mapping Information Models to AuthZEN Authorization Requests — Draft 1

access.accessNotes: The editor's draft and source were freely accessible. The HTML banner says 2026-02-13, while the current split framework source entered the repository on 2026-07-17; the pinned revision controls this record.

evidence.summary: The COAZ Framework is the best current consume baseline for W4's protocol-to-authorization projection layer. It defines JSON mapping envelopes for one or many AuthZEN evaluations, literal and expression semantics, CEL as the default expression language, binding-defined input variables, optional default/declared mappings, trust-anchored fields, discovery and a concrete binding-conformance checklist. Mapping errors, denials and PDP communication errors all fail closed, and every multi-evaluation item must permit. The framework correctly recognizes that a mapping may be supplied by the party being authorized and that non-anchored attributes remain untrusted. It remains a Working Group Draft without a located executable COAZ conformance suite. Trust-anchor choices are binding-specific, deployment coverage is validated rather than guaranteed, and the five-step map/evaluate/enforce sequence does not cryptographically or durably bind a decision to the exact forwarded operation, complete event set or external effect. Warrantor should consume the framework vocabulary and conformance shape while mandating trust sources, mapping identity/version, compiler limits and operation-digest binding.
evidence.technicalContribution: A protocol-neutral declarative model and conformance contract for projecting arbitrary operation information models through literal/CEL mappings into AuthZEN Access Evaluation or Access Evaluations requests.
evidence.methodology: The current Draft 1 source at e94e0a26e52346d33fef56d28bce96bd34835705 was reviewed section by section. Envelope, expression, absent/null, default/declared mapping, trust-anchor, discoverability, failure and conformance rules were mapped to W4/W5/W6 and compared with AuthZEN 1.0 and the concrete MCP binding. Repository history established that the current split framework landed on 2026-07-17. No executable framework conformance tests were located.
findings: The framework cleanly separates a protocol mapping language from the underlying policy engine and API.
Mapping errors, authorization denials and PDP communication errors all require refusal.
A binding must enumerate in-scope and pass-through operations so an absent mapping is not silently interpreted.
Trust-anchored fields can be verified or substituted from trusted inputs, while all other server/mapping-supplied attributes remain untrusted.
Deployment coverage and decision-to-forward integrity are not guaranteed by the framework.
limitations: Working Group Draft status and active source evolution reduce durability.
No executable COAZ framework conformance suite was located in the reviewed repository.
The framework does not prescribe CEL resource limits, mapping signatures/digests, cache invalidation, complete mediation, atomic permit use, receipts or effect reconciliation.
Trust-anchored fields are selected by each binding and can be too weak for high-assurance deployments.
incentives: The authors and working-group vendors benefit from a standard externalized-authorization ecosystem; open source, explicit untrusted-input language and separation from any one policy engine improve inspectability.

quality.rationale: The framework is technically precise, directly reusable and unusually candid about mapping trust and failure behavior. Draft status, date/version ambiguity and the absence of an executable conformance artifact prevent essential standing.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt COAZ envelopes and binding-conformance concepts through a strict Warrantor profile that mandates trusted-field provenance, mapping identity/digest/version, deterministic resource-bounded compilation, schema synchronization and exact-operation binding.
options: Profile and contribute to COAZ; recommended.
Use COAZ only at external adapters while keeping an independent internal mapping IR.
Invent a proprietary mapping language and accept duplicated semantics and ecosystem isolation.

architecture: Use COAZ as an adapter source language, not W4's entire semantic IR or policy language.
Preserve the distinction between untrusted semantic mappings and independently verified authority inputs.
implementation: Build type/cost/depth limits and deterministic test vectors around CEL.
Bind accepted mapping and compiler output digests to decisions and forwarding.
business: Standards participation can make Warrantor the assurance layer rather than another isolated policy product.
regulatory: Record mapping provenance and decision inputs so audit evidence can explain what policy question was actually asked.
academic: Study semantic completeness and malicious omission in server-authored protocol mappings.
content: Publish a COAZ mapping threat model and safe-profile guide.

verification.notes: Editor draft, pinned source and git history were inspected. No executable COAZ conformance suite was located. See artifact-review-authzen-coaz-mcp.md.

sources.title: COAZ-MCP: COAZ Binding for the Model Context Protocol — Draft 1

access.accessNotes: The editor's draft and source were freely accessible. The current split draft landed on 2026-07-17 and was patched on 2026-08-25 to remove MCP initialize; the banner date alone does not identify the reviewed content.

evidence.summary: COAZ-MCP Draft 1 is the closest standards prior art for mapping MCP JSON-RPC methods and parameters into cross-vendor AuthZEN decisions. It defines default mappings, server-declared tool mappings under x-authzen-mapping, token-anchored subjects, CEL projection, error behavior and fail-closed PDP handling. It is valuable W4/W5/W6 supporting evidence but is not production-current or an enforcement guarantee. Mechanical comparison with the MCP 2026-07-28 core ClientRequest union found only seven of ten methods mapped: `server/discover`, `resources/templates/list` and `subscriptions/listen` are omitted and would be denied by the draft's unknown-method rule. The draft still refers to removed or moved `ping`, `logging/setLevel`, resource subscribe/unsubscribe and old Tasks methods. It requires every `notifications/*` message to bypass the PDP, including current cancellation and future/extension state-changing notifications. A server can author the semantic mapping used to authorize its own tool; the draft classifies those attributes as untrusted but cannot detect omitted or false business semantics. It orders decision before forwarding without a canonical operation digest, signed consumed permit, immutable forwarding buffer, receipt or effect link. Warrantor should contribute a schema-generated current method profile and build the missing exact-operation assurance seam.
evidence.technicalContribution: A concrete COAZ binding that projects MCP operations and tool arguments into AuthZEN SARC evaluations, supports server-advertised declared mappings and specifies token, error and fail-closed behavior for gateways or servers acting as PEPs.
evidence.methodology: The pinned Draft 1 source and history were reviewed at e94e0a26e52346d33fef56d28bce96bd34835705. Default, declared, trust-anchor, error, security and deployment rules were mapped. Client-to-server request methods were mechanically extracted from the current MCP 2026-07-28 TypeScript schema at efb5cb3ecae3d5e185b49901a75a8fd5a551fc0f and compared with draft mappings. The official Tasks extension was pinned at 0d0a6bd4c258b35caa3c810a1dd506cf105b1501 and its four methods were compared with the stale task section. No executable COAZ-MCP conformance suite was located.
findings: Seven of ten current MCP core client requests have default mappings; three valid current methods are false-denied.
The draft's August 25 patch removed initialize but left other pre-2026-07-28 method assumptions.
Every notifications wildcard is pass-through, creating a fail-open future/extension namespace despite unknown request methods failing closed.
Default token anchoring is useful, but an unverifiable subject override is warned rather than universally rejected.
Server-authored mappings cannot be trusted to state complete or truthful business semantics.
No required canonical digest or durable consumption binds the evaluated request to the exact forwarded message or effect.
limitations: Working Group Draft with active revision and no located executable conformance suite.
Method-set drift produces false denials and stale authorization projections against the current MCP core and Tasks extension.
The notification wildcard permits control/state messages without a PDP decision.
At-least-one PEP deployment coverage is a should-level recommendation; no PEP means no COAZ authorization.
Server-initiated or MRTR input authorization, multi-hop delegation intersection, complete mediation, receipts and effect reconciliation remain out of scope or unspecified.
incentives: The working-group authors and their authorization vendors benefit from adoption and standards influence; explicit warning about untrusted server mappings is positive, while the lack of independent conformance and method drift limit confidence.

quality.rationale: Direct relevance, normative detail and a credible working group justify retention. Current method drift, wildcard notification bypass, no executable conformance, draft status and first-party ecosystem evidence prevent a high-quality score.

recommendation.preferredAction: Use COAZ-MCP only through a Warrantor-maintained versioned profile that maps every current core/adopted-extension method, denies unknown state notifications, verifies mapping provenance, and binds the exact evaluated operation to atomic forwarding and receipts; contribute these corrections upstream.
options: Contribute and consume a corrected current profile; recommended.
Use only default mappings and reject server-declared semantics for privileged tools.
Keep COAZ at the API boundary but implement an independent internal MCP authorization projection.
Adopt the draft unchanged and accept false denials and a notification bypass; reject.

architecture: Treat MCP core and every extension as independently versioned authorization surfaces.
Keep transport OAuth, AuthZEN decision, COAZ projection, W6 authority and W2 receipt as composable but distinct layers.
implementation: Generate/check the method table from pinned schemas and add post-decision mutation, mapping-swap and extension-notification vectors.
Content-address accepted mappings and include mapping/compiler digests in the permit and receipt.
business: Standards contribution can create ecosystem influence without claiming ownership of the underlying authorization category.
regulatory: Mapping provenance and exact-operation linkage improve audit explainability; draft conformance alone is not compliance evidence.
academic: Publish the method-drift corpus and a decision-bound-forwarding profile with independent gateway/PDP reproduction.
content: Write a constructive COAZ-MCP gap analysis showing false-deny, wildcard bypass and Warrantor's proposed interoperable fixes.

verification.notes: Full draft, current source and git history were inspected; MCP core and Tasks methods were mechanically compared. No executable COAZ-MCP conformance suite was located. See artifact-review-authzen-coaz-mcp.md.

sources.title: Cerbos PDP AuthZEN Authorization API Implementation
sources.venue: Cerbos open-source PDP repository and technical documentation

publication.version: AuthZEN introduced in v0.48.0; reproduced with v0.55.0 build 2901f6421b08bb544049bf0fae4e61ebfd52d59b

access.accessNotes: Apache-2.0 source, release assets, digest metadata and documentation were freely accessible. The official Linux x86-64 archive digest was verified before runtime testing.

evidence.summary: Cerbos PDP v0.55.0 is a current independent implementation of the final AuthZEN decision seam over a role/attribute policy engine. A digest-verified official binary exposed PDP metadata plus single and boxcar evaluation endpoints, accepted final `subject`, `resource.id`, `resource.properties` and `action` fields, and reproduced an allow decision under a live policy. The implementation is deliberately partial: search endpoints are absent, subject type is informational when explicit roles are supplied, action properties are reserved, and `cerbos.*` keys carry vendor-specific policy version, scope and metadata conventions. A controlled legacy `resource.name`/`attributes` request from Vengtoo was rejected with HTTP 400. Cerbos therefore demonstrates valuable wire interoperability but also proves that AuthZEN does not supply policy-semantic equivalence, complete PEP coverage, exact decision-to-forward binding, permit consumption, delegation intersection, receipts or effect evidence.
evidence.technicalContribution: A live AuthZEN 1.0 metadata/evaluation facade over Cerbos's policy-as-code engine, including explicit subject/principal, resource and context mapping and optional native response metadata.
evidence.methodology: Release metadata and official source/docs were inspected, including AuthZEN protobufs, service conversion code and mapping documentation. The v0.55.0 Linux release archive was checked against the GitHub release API SHA-256, started with a known policy, and exercised through discovery plus valid and legacy-mutated evaluation requests. The result was compared with OpenFGA v1.19.0 and the final AuthZEN specification. The complete Go suite was not executed because a Go toolchain was unavailable.
findings: The verified v0.55.0 binary returned final-shaped metadata and accepted a final AuthZEN evaluation request.
The same server rejected a gateway's legacy `resource.name` field before policy evaluation, demonstrating useful strictness and real interoperability failure.
Only metadata and evaluation endpoints are advertised; Cerbos documentation accurately calls the implementation partial.
Subject type, reserved properties, action properties and response metadata have target-specific meanings that W4 must expose as translation capabilities/losses.
A boolean decision is not bound to the exact later-forwarded operation and is not an enforcement or effect receipt.
limitations: Only a minimal live policy/evaluation case was reproduced; search is not implemented and the complete Cerbos test suite was not run.
Policy/API behavior remains first-party implementation evidence without an independent security audit in this wave.
PDP authentication, TLS, key custody, policy distribution, audit durability, HA and outage behavior are deployment-specific and were not production-tested.
Cerbos does not implement W6's proposed multi-principal intersection, holder proof, atomic quota consumption or W2 evidence-before-commit protocol.
incentives: Cerbos benefits from adoption of its PDP and commercial Hub. Public Apache-2.0 code, strict field handling and candid partial-implementation language increase inspectability but do not make product efficacy independent evidence.

quality.rationale: Current official code, a digest-verified live release, explicit mappings and direct W4/W5 relevance make this high quality. Partial API coverage, vendor-specific semantics and first-party-only assurance prevent essential standing.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt Cerbos as one supported AuthZEN PDP target through a strict Warrantor profile; retain Warrantor's typed IR, semantic-loss reporting, immutable operation binding, mediation, authority intersection and receipt layers outside the PDP.
options: Support Cerbos through final AuthZEN first and add a native gRPC optimization only after equivalence and performance tests; recommended.
Use only the native Cerbos API and accept vendor coupling at W4's public seam.
Exclude Cerbos and lose a useful non-Zanzibar differential target.

architecture: Treat AuthZEN as the public ABI and Cerbos as one target, not the internal policy language.
Declare every reserved `cerbos.*` field and trust source in a versioned target profile.
implementation: Pin and record policy version/scope, authenticate the PEP/PDP channel, and run the common negative corpus on upgrades.
Bind the returned decision to one immutable operation and atomically consumed permit outside Cerbos.
business: Cerbos compatibility can reduce integration friction for customers already using the PDP while preserving Warrantor's assurance differentiation.
regulatory: Use Cerbos decision and policy metadata as linked technical-control evidence, not proof of legal authority or complete enforcement.
academic: Use Cerbos as the ABAC/PBAC side of cross-engine semantic differential experiments.
content: Publish an explicit Cerbos target profile and decision-versus-enforcement boundary guide.

verification.notes: Official archive digest verified; v0.55.0 discovery and final-shaped evaluation reproduced; legacy Vengtoo shape rejected with HTTP 400. See artifact-review-authzen-pdps-mcp-gateways.md.

sources.title: OpenFGA AuthZEN API Implementation

publication.version: experimental AuthZEN API in v1.19.0 build 130c30aea5e73543e63b173dadfbd1ee519aa97a

access.accessNotes: Apache-2.0 source, implementation guides, tests, release artifacts, SBOM and digest metadata were free. The official Linux amd64 archive digest was verified before runtime testing.

evidence.summary: OpenFGA v1.19.0 supplies the strongest reviewed relationship-authorization implementation of AuthZEN 1.0. Its experimental, opt-in layer maps evaluation to Check, batch evaluation to Check/BatchCheck semantics, and search operations to native list APIs; discovery is store-scoped and constructed from a configured canonical base URL rather than the request Host. A digest-verified official binary created an in-memory store, authorization model and tuple, advertised all evaluation/search endpoints, and allowed the final-shaped `user:alice reader document:roadmap` request. The live endpoint rejected Vengtoo's missing `resource.id` shape with HTTP 400. OpenFGA explicitly documents important limits: AuthZEN cannot manage models/tuples, pagination, contextual tuples, signed metadata and decision explanations are absent, and the API is experimental. Its model-ID header is a valuable reproducibility seam, but default-latest behavior, property/context precedence and relationship semantics still require a Warrantor target profile.
evidence.technicalContribution: A store-scoped final AuthZEN evaluation, batch, search and discovery facade over a Zanzibar-style relation graph with explicit property-to-condition-context mapping and optional authorization-model pinning.
evidence.methodology: The v1.19.0 source, AuthZEN implementation/registry documents and server tests were inspected at current main and the release build. The official binary archive was checked against its published SHA-256, then used to create a store, model and relation tuple and to reproduce discovery, allow, subject-type error and legacy-shape rejection. The source's feature flag, validation, model header, property merge, batch/search and metadata paths were mapped to AuthZEN Final and W2/W4/W6. The complete Go suite was not run because Go was unavailable.
findings: The verified v1.19.0 binary accepted a final AuthZEN request and returned the expected allow decision for a stored relation.
Store-scoped discovery advertised single, batch and all three search endpoints with absolute configured URLs.
The selected authorization model ID appeared in the live HTTP response header, offering a decision-reproducibility input that the reviewed gateway ignored.
The legacy gateway body failed validation before evaluation, independently confirming non-interoperability.
Detailed official docs distinguish implemented, optional and absent capabilities and recommend native APIs for model/tuple lifecycle.
Property-to-context merging and action-as-relation semantics are not equivalent to Cerbos, so W4 needs capability/loss and differential evidence.
limitations: The AuthZEN API is experimental, disabled by default and may change before general availability.
Search pagination, contextual tuples, signed metadata and normal decision explanations are not implemented through this layer.
Default-latest model selection is not reproducible unless the PEP pins or records the model ID.
Request context has highest precedence over namespaced properties; trusted token/registry fields require an anti-override profile.
OpenFGA is a policy decision/data substrate, not proof of complete mediation, holder binding, atomic action consumption, receipts or effects.
Only a minimal runtime scenario was reproduced and no independent hostile-input audit was located.
incentives: OpenFGA and its commercial ecosystem benefit from adoption. Mature open code, detailed limitations, interop fixtures and production use of the native engine are positive signals, while AuthZEN efficacy and conformance evidence remain first-party and experimental.

quality.rationale: A current verified release, deep code/documentation/test surface, candid capability registry and live reproduction make this the strongest implementation source in the wave. Experimental status and first-party-only AuthZEN assurance keep it below essential.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt OpenFGA as the first relationship-authorization target for W4/W6 differential testing, use AuthZEN for decisions and native APIs for model/tuple lifecycle, and require store, model and consistency evidence on every security-critical decision.
options: Support OpenFGA through AuthZEN plus a governed native lifecycle adapter; recommended.
Use only native OpenFGA and accept a target-specific decision seam.
Treat OpenFGA as W6 itself and lose mandate, holder, consumption and receipt semantics; reject.

architecture: Separate relationship graph evaluation from W6's authority algebra and action permit lifecycle.
Carry store, model and data/consistency revision into decision and receipt records.
implementation: Pin the model ID, bound context precedence, authenticate the channel and run the common interop/adversarial corpus.
Use native writes/reads under governed change and provenance controls; AuthZEN alone cannot operate the graph.
business: OpenFGA compatibility addresses enterprises already invested in Zanzibar-style authorization without surrendering Warrantor's cross-target assurance layer.
regulatory: Record relationship-data provenance and consistency because an allow result without graph state is weak audit evidence.
academic: Use OpenFGA to study action-as-relation semantics, consistency and semantic loss across AuthZEN targets.
content: Explain the difference between graph authorization, delegation-chain intersection and evidence-before-commit.

verification.notes: Official archive digest verified; live store/model/tuple, store-scoped discovery and final allow reproduced; legacy Vengtoo request rejected with HTTP 400. See artifact-review-authzen-pdps-mcp-gateways.md.

sources.title: Cerbos FastMCP Authorization Middleware

publication.version: main 3bdaef615dd33ab18b20b48d311335459b52b54c; annotated tag v0.2.0 resolves 3facd8aa6c8527c48d739adf713dbac014793294; package metadata 0.1.1

access.accessNotes: Apache-2.0 source, tests, policy examples and history were freely accessible. The locked Python environment installed without registration.

evidence.summary: Cerbos FastMCP is a concise server-side authorization middleware and useful negative comparator. In its locked Python 3.12 environment, 36 tests passed and three live-PDP integration tests skipped. It denies missing principals and PDP errors, authorizes tool calls with name/arguments/source, and filters tool listings through top-level and per-tool checks. It overrides listing for prompts/resources but not their retrieval. Controlled `get_prompt`, `read_resource` and resource-template-list requests reached downstream with zero PDP calls. A second vector allowed a low-value transfer, mutated the middleware context after the decision, and executed high-value attacker arguments. The sample policy failed compilation on current Cerbos 0.55 due to an invalid constant name. The implementation is native Cerbos gRPC, not AuthZEN, and emits no immutable-operation permit, result/effect evidence or complete-mediation proof.
evidence.technicalContribution: A typed FastMCP middleware that resolves a token-derived Cerbos principal, maps tool/list operations into Cerbos resource actions and converts PDP failures or denials into MCP authorization outcomes.
evidence.methodology: The repository was pinned at main 3bdaef615dd33ab18b20b48d311335459b52b54c and its tag/history, lock, middleware, tests, examples, CI and policies were inspected. The locked suite ran on Python 3.12; inherited FastMCP hooks were enumerated and controlled denying-PDP bypass calls were executed. A post-decision mutable-context substitution was reproduced. The sample policy was compiled with digest-verified Cerbos v0.55.0. The live example server started, but full integration tests could not run because the bundled policy did not start the current PDP.
findings: Thirty-six tests passed and three live-PDP tests skipped in the pinned environment.
Tool call and list checks fail closed on missing principal, denial and PDP exception.
Prompt/resource listing is protected, while prompt retrieval, resource reading and resource-template listing inherit pass-through hooks and made zero PDP calls.
Arguments can change after the boolean decision and before the next middleware executes.
The bundled policy fails the current Cerbos compiler, so unit success did not establish current integration viability.
Tag/package version ambiguity and the native vendor API reduce interoperability and release clarity.
limitations: Early first-party repository with no visible adoption or independent audit.
The controlled in-process mutation demonstrates an unsealed composition seam, not a proven unauthenticated remote exploit.
Only the reviewed FastMCP 2.12.3/MCP SDK 1.14.1 path was exercised; other framework versions may differ.
No standard AuthZEN/COAZ mapping, generic current MCP method registry, atomic consumption, result/egress policy, receipts or effects are implemented.
incentives: Cerbos benefits from showing simple MCP integration and PDP adoption. Small public source and tests improve transparency, but README coverage and current-compatibility claims remain first-party.

quality.rationale: Direct MCP relevance, readable code and reproduced positive/negative behavior justify supporting inclusion. Incomplete hook coverage, mutable execution, skipped integration, current policy incompatibility, version ambiguity and first-party alpha maturity sharply limit the score.

recommendation.preferredAction: Use Cerbos FastMCP as a reference and negative-vector seed, not an unchanged dependency; generate full MCP coverage, move the public seam to final AuthZEN/COAZ, seal the evaluated operation, and require two-PDP live tests.
options: Extract its principal/list/failure patterns into a Warrantor adapter and add the assurance boundary; recommended.
Fork and repair the middleware while accepting FastMCP/Cerbos version ownership.
Adopt unchanged and accept retrieval bypasses and operation substitution; reject.

architecture: Separate framework hook adapters from the transport-neutral Warrantor PEP and receipt state machine.
implementation: Generate method coverage, freeze the canonical operation, compile policies on every supported PDP version and exercise live integrations in CI.
business: Do not claim full MCP authorization from tool/list middleware coverage.
regulatory: A PDP call without retrieval coverage and exact-operation evidence is incomplete audit-control evidence.
academic: Use the bypass/mutation cases in an authorization-middleware completeness benchmark.
content: Show why list authorization and content authorization require separate hooks and evidence.

verification.notes: 36 tests passed, 3 live-PDP tests skipped; current Cerbos policy compilation, three inherited-hook bypasses and post-decision mutation were reproduced. See artifact-review-authzen-pdps-mcp-gateways.md.

sources.title: Vengtoo MCP Gateway v0.1.1

access.accessNotes: The two-commit Apache-2.0 source, tests, package lock, roadmap and security policy were freely accessible. Closed Vengtoo cloud behavior was not required for local tests and was not audited.

evidence.summary: Vengtoo MCP Gateway v0.1.1 is an early but real tool-call proxy/PEP. It multiplexes spawned stdio downstreams behind stdio or HTTP ingress, performs per-call external authorization, filters per-subject tool visibility, restores blocked/pending state behind a startup gate, detects nested schema drift, separates HTTP caller identities and strips gateway/ambient credentials from downstream environments. All 52 native tests, TypeScript type-check and build passed. Yet its nominal AuthZEN body uses `resource.name` and `resource.attributes`, not final 1.0 `id` and `properties`; both digest-verified Cerbos and OpenFGA releases returned HTTP 400. Controlled HITL polling repeated the legacy request without echoing the approval ID or sending `X-Request-ID`. Only tools are proxied, current identity is static bearer mapping, dynamic tool updates and remote downstreams are absent, and audit serialization omits arguments despite the README while recording no policy revision, permit, result or effect. It is strong supporting implementation evidence and a release-corpus seed, not a production dependency.
evidence.technicalContribution: An open MCP tool proxy with call-time external authorization, per-caller HTTP sessions, tool discovery and namespacing, drift/pending/block governance state, fail-closed startup/call behavior and local structured decision logging.
evidence.methodology: The v0.1.1 tag/commit was pinned and source, package lock, tests, HTTP/session code, authorization body, list filtering, startup restore, state, drift, audit, roadmap and security policy were inspected. `npm ci`, all 52 tests, TypeScript type-check and build were executed. The built `authorize()` function was pointed at live Cerbos v0.55.0 and OpenFGA v1.19.0 endpoints. A controlled pending-then-approved server captured both polls and headers. Native tests were interpreted at their actual scope rather than as AuthZEN conformance.
findings: All 52 repository tests, type-check and build passed at the pinned release.
Call-time PDP errors and startup-gate timeout deny, while blocked/pending tools remain separately enforced.
The gateway's request failed against both selected final AuthZEN PDPs because resource ID/properties use obsolete names.
The tool route entry is captured before awaiting the PDP, reducing a simple mapping-swap vector.
HITL polls do not carry the returned approval ID or a stable request ID and no atomic permit is consumed.
Tool visibility fails open by default on batch authorization error, although invocation remains protected.
The local audit entry omits arguments, result/effect and policy/permit identity despite broader README wording.
limitations: Only tools are mediated; resources, prompts, sampling, elicitation and result guardrails are not current capabilities.
Downstream MCP servers are startup-spawned stdio processes; remote downstreams, restart resilience and dynamic list changes are roadmap.
Static bearer identity lacks the MCP OAuth discovery, audience, expiry and revocation properties planned for a later grade.
The cloud PDP, decision log, policy system, approval matching and commercial control plane are closed and unreviewed.
Two commits, no visible adoption and no independent audit provide very low maturity evidence.
Direct reachability of downstream servers can bypass the gateway unless deployment topology prevents it.
incentives: Vengtoo benefits commercially from gateway and cloud adoption. Publishing a locked open gateway, tests, roadmap and security policy is positive; product claims and closed-service behavior remain first-party.

quality.rationale: A strong native suite, reproducible build and unusually relevant real gateway mechanics earn supporting status. Failed final-AuthZEN interoperability, two-commit maturity, narrow coverage, closed-service boundaries and missing evidence binding prevent higher promotion.

recommendation.preferredAction: Reject v0.1.1 as an unchanged dependency, import its startup-gate, route-capture, caller-separation, environment-filtering and drift-state patterns into the negative corpus, and monitor remediation of final AuthZEN, OAuth, coverage and evidence gaps.
options: Use as reference-only and contribute protocol corrections upstream; recommended.
Fork for a bounded prototype and own final AuthZEN, MCP coverage and durable-evidence changes.
Deploy unchanged and accept legitimate-call denial plus material assurance gaps; reject.

architecture: Keep the tool PEP topology but require downstream isolation and a transport-neutral assurance state machine.
implementation: Replace legacy fields, discover/pin endpoints, add operation/approval digests and atomic consumption, and cover every supported MCP primitive.
Make audit arguments/results/effects durable and reconcile expected events across crash points.
business: Treat nominal AuthZEN support as a tested procurement requirement, not a URL or README label.
regulatory: Static bearer identity and local incomplete logs are not sufficient evidence for accountable enterprise agent actions.
academic: Use the green-native/red-interop result in research on cross-implementation authorization conformance.
content: Publish a constructive case study showing why native tests and final-standard interop are distinct gates.

conflicts: OpenID Authorization API 1.0 final resource field names

verification.notes: 52/52 tests, type-check and build passed. Live Cerbos/OpenFGA final endpoints both rejected its request shape; controlled HITL polling omitted approval/request correlation. See artifact-review-authzen-pdps-mcp-gateways.md.

sources.title: Make Agent Defeat Agent: Automatic Detection of Taint-Style Vulnerabilities in LLM-based Agents

access.accessNotes: The official paper, presentation page and GitHub source were freely accessible. The Zenodo metadata record was public but its files were restricted during this review; no project-level license was located at the repository root or through GitHub metadata.

evidence.summary: AgentFuzz is the strongest reviewed source for capability-elicited attack generation against open-source LLM-agent applications. It combines CodeQL-derived source-to-sink paths, LLM-generated functionality-specific natural-language seeds, semantic and distance feedback, seed prioritization, and functionality/argument mutation. The USENIX page reports 34 high-risk zero-days across 20 applications, 33-times higher precision than the comparison approach and 23 assigned CVEs. The full paper reports 100% precision and 97.14% recall in its constructed evaluation, but the recall ground truth is not a complete independently labeled vulnerability universe: positives pool AgentFuzz and LLMSmith discoveries while only a sample of negatives is manually checked. Later project material refers to 27 CVEs, so the count is version-sensitive. Pinned artifact compilation completed with extensive warnings in bundled py-conbyte; no native tests or project-level license were located and the full campaign requires CodeQL, target applications and an external model endpoint. AgentFuzz should seed Warrantor's attack generator and application/PEP/egress cases, but its taint-sink success condition is not an authority-substrate, complete-mediation or final-effect proof.
evidence.technicalContribution: A directed greybox fuzzer that uses static source-to-sink distance plus semantic/functionality feedback to synthesize and mutate natural-language prompts capable of triggering taint-style vulnerabilities in LLM-agent applications.
evidence.methodology: The paper evaluates AgentFuzz against 20 open-source agent applications and a prior approach, constructs functionality-aware seeds and mutations, manually validates reported vulnerabilities, compares precision/recall/time-to-exposure and reports real vulnerability/CVE outcomes. This review inspected the paper and pinned repository at 0fc9960fd126b20cb0d19b4aec4b1266855d44f0, counted tracked artifacts, compiled the Python tree, inspected setup, outputs, licensing, archive metadata and test standing, and bounded the ground-truth and CVE-count claims. The paid/full target campaign was not rerun.
findings: The official proceedings page reports 34 high-risk zero-days in 20 applications and 23 assigned CVEs.
The approach links source-guided distance to natural-language semantic/functionality mutation, making it more relevant to capability-elicited corpora than prompt lists alone.
The reported 100 percent precision and 97.14 percent recall describe the authors' constructed oracle, not exhaustive independent vulnerability ground truth.

The paper reports an average 0.69 million tokens per application, a maximum cost of USD 6.90 under January 2025 pricing and average time to exposure of 121.8 minutes, making campaign cost and model drift material reproduction variables.
Project versions disagree on 23 versus 27 CVEs, so citations must carry source/version/date.
Compilation succeeded with numerous warnings in a bundled dependency, but no release test gate or project-level license was found.
limitations: Source access and CodeQL-compatible language/application structure are central to the reviewed technique; closed systems and non-Python targets require different instrumentation.
An LLM call reaching a sensitive sink does not establish that an authority substrate admitted an unauthorized effect, and may over- or under-approximate runtime exploitability.
Vulnerability confirmation, responsible-disclosure state and CVE assignment evolve over time and require per-case validation.
External model endpoints, prices and behavior make the full experiment costly and mutable.
The mutable GitHub source is available, but the named Zenodo archive files were restricted and no root license was located.
incentives: Academic authors benefit from first-framework and high-vulnerability-yield framing, but top-tier peer review, public source and real coordinated-disclosure outcomes make the claims unusually inspectable.
No direct product-sales incentive was identified; vulnerability counts still create publication and visibility incentives.

quality.rationale: Top-tier peer review, deep source-guided method, real vulnerability outcomes, open code and exceptional corpus relevance make this essential. Reproducibility is reduced for model/API dependence, incomplete licensing/archive access, absent tests, compiler warnings and a constructed rather than exhaustive oracle.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt AgentFuzz's source-guided seed, feedback and mutation concepts, then redefine success around named authority invariants, exact final-wire operations and observed effects rather than a generic sensitive sink.
options: Integrate its attack-generation ideas into a standalone Warrantor corpus; recommended.
Contribute a substrate-conformance profile upstream while accepting its source/language and experiment dependencies.
Use the published vulnerability prompts as a static regression set only; fastest but weakest.

architecture: Expose a typed map from capabilities and sensitive sinks to W1-W6 invariants and authoritative effect points.
implementation: Add cross-language instrumentation, deterministic negative vectors, adaptive mutation and signed run receipts; pin target commits and model/provider state.
Verify every imported CVE case against the affected version and disclosure record before using it as product evidence.
business: Use real vulnerability classes to demonstrate relevance, but do not market the paper's recall/CVE totals as Warrantor performance.
regulatory: Map attack cases to technical controls without claiming that a fuzzing result proves compliance.
academic: Compare taint-sink discovery with unauthorized-effect discovery and cross-implementation transfer.
content: Explain why source-guided agent fuzzing is a corpus input rather than an authority proof.

verification.notes: Paper and source inspected; commit 0fc9960fd126b20cb0d19b4aec4b1266855d44f0 compiled with bundled-dependency warnings. No native suite or root license found; full vulnerability campaign not rerun. See artifact-review-agent-attack-corpora.md.

sources.title: Les Dissonances: Cross-Tool Harvesting and Polluting in Pool-of-Tools Empowered LLM Agents
sources.publisher: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium

access.accessNotes: The NDSS paper, slides and MIT-licensed Chord artifact were freely accessible. The locked environment installed, although substantive live scans require multiple external service credentials.

evidence.summary: Les Dissonances is essential evidence that security properties emerge across tool sequences, not only inside one tool. It defines Cross-Tool Harvesting and Polluting, where a malicious or vulnerable tool hijacks task control flow to collect or corrupt information from predecessor or successor operations. Chord dynamically scans tool interactions in LangChain and LlamaIndex. The canonical NDSS paper evaluates 66 real-world tools and reports 75% vulnerable to XTHP. Earlier arXiv/repository materials refer to 73 tools and different harvesting/polluting rates, so the conference result must be cited separately. The MIT artifact is unusually compact and locked: compilation passed, its 238-package frozen environment installed and package imports passed, but no native tests were found and reproducing the scan requires third-party/API credentials. The result directly requires W4 to model typed sequence/information-flow edges and W5 to enforce across a workflow, but it is not proof of a complete authority substrate.
evidence.technicalContribution: A systematic threat model and dynamic scanner for cross-tool control-flow and information-flow vulnerabilities in pool-of-tools LLM-agent frameworks, covering predecessor/successor harvesting and pollution.
evidence.methodology: The paper derives XTHP attack vectors, builds Chord, analyzes real LangChain and LlamaIndex tools and evaluates attack feasibility and defenses. This review used the canonical conference paper, pinned commit 8ac19e8bd5fdca0a7c21bfe46b3e16e943f07831, compiled the source, installed its frozen environment, imported the package, inspected data/results/dependencies and compared conference and earlier sample/result versions. Live third-party scans were not run.
findings: The NDSS abstract reports 75 percent of 66 evaluated tools vulnerable to XTHP.
The vulnerable unit is often a relationship in task control flow, so independent per-tool authorization can miss the exploit.
The reviewed data contains 148 LangChain tool-map entries, 160 queries in one set and 32 in another plus malicious-tool/argument definitions.
The frozen environment is installable but resolves 238 packages and a large GPU-enabled Torch/CUDA stack, imposing high smoke-test cost.
Earlier 73-tool results are a different version and must not be blended with the 66-tool conference sample.
limitations: The evaluation covers two agent frameworks and a bounded tool sample; population prevalence cannot be generalized to every stack.
Vulnerability classification and empirical rates are author-produced and the credentialed scan was not independently rerun.
No native automated test suite was found despite the lockfile and existing result files.
XTHP detection does not prove correct policy compilation, multi-principal authority or complete effect mediation.
incentives: Academic novelty and prevalence incentives favor strong attack framing, while peer review, an open locked artifact and versioned results improve inspectability.
No direct commercial sales incentive was identified.

quality.rationale: Top-tier peer review, a novel cross-tool threat model, open locked artifact and direct W3-W5 relevance make this essential. Framework/sample limits, author-produced labels, absent tests, credential requirements and version drift bound the result.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt XTHP's cross-tool relationship classes and Chord fixtures, then express them as typed policy, permit, egress and effect invariants across Warrantor implementations.
options: Port semantic attack families into the Warrantor corpus and retain Chord as an external comparator; recommended.
Extend Chord directly with authority assertions while accepting its framework and dependency footprint.
Use the paper only as threat documentation; lowest effort but loses executable coverage.

architecture: Represent predecessor/successor control and information-flow edges as first-class authorization and egress inputs.
implementation: Build credential-free deterministic fixtures plus live framework profiles and pin every result to the conference or artifact version.
business: Position workflow-level containment as a response to per-tool allowlist limits, not as proof that 75 percent of all enterprise tools are vulnerable.
regulatory: Use cross-tool data-flow cases as technical privacy/security evidence, not legal compliance conclusions.
academic: Measure transfer of XTHP vectors across MCP, direct SDK and policy-engine implementations.
content: Publish a cross-tool explainer centered on why individually trusted tools can compose unsafely.

verification.notes: Conference paper and commit 8ac19e8bd5fdca0a7c21bfe46b3e16e943f07831 inspected; compilation, frozen install and imports passed. Full credentialed scans were not run. See artifact-review-agent-attack-corpora.md.

sources.title: Agent Security Bench (ASB): Formalizing and Benchmarking Attacks and Defenses in LLM-based Agents

access.accessNotes: The official ICLR paper and MIT source were freely accessible. The pinned current tree includes unresolved merge-conflict markers and no reviewed deterministic full-stack lock.

evidence.summary: ASB is an influential broad taxonomy and benchmark, not a safe unchanged oracle. The ICLR abstract describes ten scenarios and agents, more than 400 tools, 27 attack/defense types, 13 model backbones and seven metrics, including prompt injection, memory poisoning, a Plan-of-Thought backdoor and mixed attacks. It reports a highest average ASR of 84.30%. A later full-method benchmark critique found that ASB forcibly inserts attacker tools into selected tool subsets and counts invocation of those tools as success. In its GPT-4o experiment, removing that intervention changed the relevant ASR from 73.58 ± 2.70 to 9.25 ± 0.25. It also found utility could be gamed through tool-set membership without semantic or sequence-correct completion. Artifact inspection reinforced the concern: pinned main commit 1f561dccf92d55302368fa67679b4ba9d9c8fdc4 fails Python compilation due to literal unresolved merge-conflict markers and exposes no credible repository-wide release suite. Warrantor should use ASB's taxonomy and scenarios, preserve the contradiction, and independently rebuild or adjudicate every oracle.
evidence.technicalContribution: A unified formalization and empirical benchmark of attacks and defenses across agent system prompts, user prompts, tools and memory, with broad scenario, model and metric coverage.
evidence.methodology: The ICLR study implements ten scenario agents and hundreds of tools, applies ten prompt-injection attacks, memory poisoning, Plan-of-Thought backdoors, mixed attacks and eleven defenses across 13 LLMs, and reports security/utility metrics. This review inspected the official paper and current MIT repository, pinned its commit, compiled the source, enumerated data/config/test/reproducibility assets and reconciled the later firewall paper's method-level critique and revised results. Hosted experiments were not rerun because the current artifact fails the first mechanical gate and depends on external models/APIs.
findings: ASB provides unusually broad attack, defense, scenario and model taxonomy.
Its official abstract reports a highest average attack success rate of 84.30 percent.
A later study identifies forced attacker-tool injection as benchmark-induced control-flow manipulation and reports 73.58-to-9.25 percent ASR after correction in one GPT-4o setting.
The utility metric can reward calling all expected tools without semantically correct ordered completion and can conflate attacker-tool presence with task failure.
The current repository contains unresolved merge-conflict markers and no credible release-wide test gate.
limitations: The benchmark mainly observes agent/workflow behavior, not exact PDP decision, permit, final-wire and external-effect invariants.
The strongest headline depends heavily on benchmark construction, model/version and attack selection and is not a deployment prevalence estimate.
The current repository cannot pass a clean compilation gate and lacks a reviewed full environment lock.
Original authors and the later critics both have publication incentives; corrected results require independent reproduction and adjudication.
incentives: The authors benefit from comprehensive-benchmark and high-vulnerability framing; peer review and open source provide transparency but do not eliminate co-designed oracle bias.
The later critique supplies independent challenge evidence but also promotes its own firewall design, so both must be retained.

quality.rationale: Peer review, breadth and direct relevance justify high-quality inclusion. Known benchmark-induced inflation, coarse utility semantics, current source conflict markers, absent release tests and model dependence prevent essential status.
