sources.title: Prompt Injection Attack to Tool Selection in LLM Agents
sources.publisher: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium

access.accessNotes: The official paper, slides and video were freely accessible. No author-controlled code or dataset repository was located through the paper and bounded searches, so published effect sizes remain unreproduced.

evidence.summary: ToolHijacker establishes that tool descriptions, retrieval indexes and registry metadata are part of the security boundary. In a no-box setting, an attacker injects a crafted malicious tool document into a library so a retrieval-plus-selection pipeline chooses the attacker's tool for a target task. The paper formulates document construction as an optimization problem, applies two-phase optimization, compares against manual and automated prompt-injection attacks, and evaluates StruQ, SecAlign, known-answer detection, DataSentinel and perplexity-based defenses. The official NDSS abstract concludes the evaluated defenses are insufficient. The study does not test a deterministic default-deny PEP or downstream effect boundary, and no official public code artifact was located. Warrantor should reimplement the attack semantically against tool origin, document digest, identifier/version resolution and allowlist/provenance gates; it should not claim reproduction of the authors' effect sizes.
evidence.technicalContribution: A no-box optimization attack that poisons a tool-library document to manipulate retrieval and selection toward an attacker-controlled tool, plus an evaluation of prevention and detection defenses.
evidence.methodology: The paper formalizes the target-task/tool-selection objective, generates malicious tool documents using a two-stage optimization process, tests selection effectiveness against baselines and evaluates prevention- and detection-based defenses. This review inspected the official proceedings paper/page and bounded artifact searches. No code was available to execute, so the Warrantor use is threat/case design rather than reproduced performance.
findings: Tool metadata can be an executable influence channel even when the attacker has no model or agent internals.
Retrieval and selection are distinct attack stages and must be tested separately from execution authorization.
The evaluated model-level prevention and detection defenses did not eliminate the attack in the authors' experiments.
A correctly enforced authority and egress layer must remain safe after the model chooses an attacker-preferred tool.
limitations: No public artifact was located, materially limiting reproduction and adaptation confidence.
Effectiveness depends on the model, embeddings/retriever, candidate corpus, prompts and target tasks.
Selection of a malicious tool is not itself proof that an unauthorized operation or effect occurred.
The study does not measure registry signatures, provenance-gated enrollment, deterministic allowlists or complete egress mediation.
incentives: Academic novelty and attack-effectiveness incentives favor strong framing, while NDSS peer review and full methods improve credibility.
The absence of an executable artifact leaves implementation details and negative results less inspectable.

quality.rationale: Top-tier peer review, clear threat model, broad defense comparison and direct registry/PEP relevance justify a high score. No public artifact and the selection-versus-effect boundary prevent essential status.

recommendation.preferredAction: Independently reimplement minimal semantic ToolHijacker cases against Warrantor's registry and selection pipeline, then assert that provenance, authorization and egress controls prevent effects even after a wrong selection.
options: Reimplement and contribute an open conformance vector set; recommended.
Wait for an official artifact while keeping registry controls untested; defer but risky.
Treat tool allowlisting alone as sufficient; reject.

architecture: Bind tool document, origin, identifier, version, schema and retrieval-index state into notarized enrollment and authorization.
implementation: Test name collisions, description changes, rug pulls, embedding/retrieval mutations and selected-versus-executed identity.
business: Make provenance-gated tool enrollment a procurement feature without implying prompt defenses are useless in every setting.
regulatory: Record tool provenance and change approvals as audit evidence where deployment policy requires them.
academic: Study whether registry provenance plus deterministic PEPs convert selection compromise into harmless failure.
content: Explain why tool descriptions are security-sensitive supply-chain material.

verification.notes: Official NDSS page and full paper inspected; no author-controlled implementation artifact located in bounded searches. See artifact-review-agent-attack-corpora.md.

sources.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP): Security Design Considerations for AI-Driven Automation
authors: National Security Agency Artificial Intelligence Security

access.accessNotes: The official press release and 17-page PDF were freely accessible. The paper is public government guidance and does not include a conformance artifact.

evidence.summary: NSA's current MCP security paper is the highest-authority operational guidance in this review. It states that MCP's rapid spread outpaced its security model and details optional or absent authentication, ambiguous bearer/session lifecycle, insecure serialization, poor approval flows, implicit trust, dynamic discovery, context leakage, inconsistent implementation, inadequate logs and real-world attack patterns. It recommends explicit trust zones, origin and authorization checks, a filtering outbound proxy or DLP, schema/context validation, least-privilege OS sandboxing, signatures bound to time/context, replay protection, untrusted-output filtering, exact parameter/identity/result-hash logging, inventory, vulnerability tracking and network scanning. These recommendations strongly support W1-W5 requirements and enterprise messaging. They do not constitute a controlled efficacy study, formal proof, conformance suite or evidence that Warrantor uniquely or completely meets them.
evidence.technicalContribution: A government threat-and-control architecture for production MCP, integrating protocol, implementation and operational risks with concrete recommendations across identity, validation, isolation, egress, message integrity, monitoring and vulnerability management.
evidence.methodology: The document synthesizes the MCP specification, public implementation patterns, incidents and security research into a 17-page design-consideration paper. This review inspected every section, mapped threat/control statements to W1-W6 and checked the official publication/press metadata. No empirical artifact exists to reproduce.
findings: The guidance says session-to-identity association and access controls are implementation choices rather than guaranteed protocol properties.
It recommends destination/method-specific outgoing proxy or DLP controls to reduce exfiltration.
It recommends OS-level isolation such as AppContainers, seccomp, AppArmor or SELinux and least-privilege denial of unneeded paths.
It recommends binding messages to time/context with expiry and replay metadata and treating each tool output as untrusted input.
It recommends logs containing exact parameters, identities and, where feasible, cryptographic hashes of results.
limitations: The paper is guidance, not peer-reviewed original research or a quantified control-effectiveness experiment.
Examples are synthesized from external sources and do not establish population prevalence.
Recommendations do not define a portable policy language, exact delegation algebra, evidence completeness model or conformance oracle.
United States national-security provenance increases authority for high-assurance practices but does not create legal applicability in India or GCC jurisdictions.
incentives: NSA's mission favors conservative, defense-in-depth guidance for high-stakes environments rather than product promotion.
Government authority does not eliminate the need to verify cited incidents and test implementation efficacy.

quality.rationale: Exceptional authority, timeliness, breadth and direct MCP/Warrantor relevance merit high-quality inclusion. It is guidance rather than reproducible original research, so it does not reach essential despite its operational value.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt the paper as a minimum MCP threat/control checklist and enterprise requirement source, then translate every recommendation into a versioned, testable Warrantor invariant without claiming the guidance proves efficacy or novelty.
options: Create a traced NSA-to-Warrantor control/conformance profile; recommended.
Use the paper only in architecture documentation without executable tests.
Treat MCP authorization alone as sufficient; reject.

architecture: Define explicit client/server/tool/model/user trust zones and separate identity, policy, egress, sandbox and evidence boundaries.
implementation: Add destination/method egress rules, OS sandbox profiles, schema/context validation, replay/time binding, output inspection and exact invocation logs.
business: Use NSA guidance to frame enterprise requirements, especially regulated/high-assurance buyers, while avoiding endorsement language.
regulatory: Map the technical controls separately to each relevant jurisdiction; do not transpose US guidance into legal obligations elsewhere.
academic: Evaluate which recommended layers independently and jointly reduce unauthorized effects under adaptive attacks.
content: Publish a control-by-control MCP architecture explainer with implementation and evidence gaps.

verification.notes: Official 17-page version 1.0 PDF and release notice inspected and mapped; no experiment or conformance artifact exists. See artifact-review-agent-attack-corpora.md.

evidence.summary: NIST CAISI provides the most actionable reviewed benchmark-methodology guidance with an executable extension. It fixed AgentDojo scenarios, added asynchronous/Inspect integration and added remote-code-execution, mass-exfiltration and automated-phishing tasks. Its experiments derive four rules: shared suites require continuous repair, attacks must adapt to the evaluated defense, task-specific consequence matters and repeated attempts change risk. NIST reports a held-out adaptive attack raising ASR from 11% to 81%, and 25 repeated attempts raising average ASR from 57% to 80%. The pinned archived repository installed from its lock. Sixteen tests passed and four skipped with 12 warnings; the four async tests skipped because no async pytest plugin was configured, so the green result is incomplete. The work should define Warrantor evaluation protocol, but AgentDojo task outcomes are not authority-substrate or final-effect proof.
evidence.technicalContribution: A government-led extension of AgentDojo into Inspect with repaired scenarios and high-impact RCE, exfiltration and phishing tasks, paired with empirical guidance on adaptive, stratified and repeated-attempt evaluation.
evidence.methodology: CAISI tested upgraded Claude 3.5 Sonnet in four AgentDojo environments, developed attacks on a random Workspace subset with held-out user-task testing, transferred attacks across environments, stratified injection tasks and repeated selected attacks 25 times. This review inspected the blog and pinned commit a491020fd14e87bcc19b2eb77fe307d8b329b05d, installed the frozen development environment and ran the native test directory with capture disabled after isolating a PTY capture error.

AgentDojo's simulated task success is not identical to a policy-enforcement or external-effect invariant.

Government authority still does not remove model/provider drift or the need for independent replication.

quality.rationale: Government authority, transparent experimental framing, direct artifact, high-impact cases and decisive adaptive/repeated-attempt lessons justify high-quality status. Blog-level reporting, model drift, archived bulk and skipped tests prevent essential status.

sources.title: Indirect Prompt Injections: Are Firewalls All You Need, or Stronger Benchmarks?
sources.venue: arXiv; presented at NeurIPS 2025 Lock-LLM Workshop

access.accessNotes: arXiv abstract, PDF, HTML and project page were freely accessible. An OpenReview submission remained under review in the inspected record; no accepted ICLR status or public code repository was verified.

evidence.summary: This preprint is the strongest reviewed challenge to current agent-security benchmark validity. It tests a tool-input minimizer and tool-output sanitizer across AgentDojo, ASB, InjecAgent and tau-Bench, initially saturates the static public attacks, then identifies benchmark bugs, weak success/utility measures and attack weakness. Most importantly, it shows that ASB force-injects attacker tools into selected subsets: removing that manipulation changes a GPT-4o ASR from 73.58 ± 2.70 to 9.25 ± 0.25. It also demonstrates that adaptive cascades can break defenses that appear perfect on static suites, adding formatted, second-order semantic and defense-aware mutations. Its durable value is methodological: benign utility, utility under attack and ASR must be co-reported; attacks must not alter the path under test; task success must be semantic and ordered; and adaptive holdouts are required. The paper is not verified as an accepted ICLR contribution, and no public corrected code artifact was located, so its numerical results still need independent reproduction.
evidence.technicalContribution: A modular minimize-and-sanitize tool-boundary defense, a method-level audit/correction of four agent benchmarks and a three-stage adaptive cascade attack protocol designed to expose failure after static attacks are saturated.
evidence.methodology: The authors evaluate two LLM firewalls across four public benchmarks and multiple models, report benign utility, utility under attack and ASR, inspect and correct AgentDojo/ASB benchmark mechanics, and escalate attacks through formatted, second-order and defense-aware adaptive stages. This review inspected arXiv v2's full HTML/PDF, tables, threat model, limitations and project/OpenReview standing, then searched for the claimed corrected artifacts. No public source repository was located.
findings: Forced attack-tool injection can dominate ASB's measured ASR; the reported corrected GPT-4o comparison is 73.58 versus 9.25 percent.
Static public benchmarks can be saturated by a simple sanitizer while adaptive second-order and defense-aware attacks recover failures.
ASB utility can reward unordered tool-set calls, and AgentDojo utility/injection placement can erase task-critical content or use brittle state deltas.
Security, benign utility and utility under attack must be reported together.
Defense cost, latency, token use and privacy exposure remain material even when ASR improves.
limitations: The canonical source is a preprint/workshop paper; accepted ICLR status was not verified.
No public code/corrected-benchmark repository was located despite the release statement, preventing independent artifact confirmation in this wave.
The threat model assumes a benign user and compromised tool outputs, excluding malicious principals, compromised PEPs and alternate effect channels.
The authors promote their own firewall approach while auditing competitor benchmarks, so incentives and independent replication matter.
Model-driven sanitization is probabilistic defense in depth and cannot replace deterministic authorization/egress boundaries.
incentives: The authors and ServiceNow benefit from showing a simple effective defense and flaws in prior benchmarks; the paper's adaptive self-challenge is positive but does not remove product/publication incentives.
Open full methods make the critique inspectable, while missing public code lowers confidence in corrected results.

quality.rationale: Detailed disconfirmation, benchmark corrections, multiple metrics and adaptive attacks make this high-value evidence. Preprint status, self-promoted defense, narrow threat model and missing public artifact cap authority and reproducibility.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt the benchmark-integrity requirements and adaptive cascade structure, independently reproduce the corrected cases, and treat minimization/sanitization as defense in depth behind deterministic authority and egress enforcement.
options: Recreate the corrections in a pinned Warrantor harness and seek independent adjudication; recommended.
Wait for public author code while applying the methodological requirements now.
Use the paper's firewall as the sole containment layer; reject.

architecture: Keep probabilistic tool-boundary filters outside the trusted authority oracle and verify downstream effects independently.
implementation: Forbid forced attack exposure, require semantic ordered utility and implement private adaptive holdouts with cost/privacy metrics.
business: Use the 73.58-to-9.25 case to justify benchmark diligence, not to dismiss all benchmark evidence.
regulatory: Document benchmark construction and excluded trials so risk evidence is auditable and not selectively optimistic.
academic: Independently reproduce corrected ASB/AgentDojo and compare substrate-level mutations against the adaptive cascade.
content: Publish a careful benchmark-integrity explainer showing how mechanics change the headline without accusing authors of fabrication.

verification.notes: arXiv v2 full methods/tables and project/OpenReview standing inspected. No public code repository or accepted ICLR status verified. See artifact-review-agent-attack-corpora.md.

sources.title: Virtual Patching Cheat Sheet

evidence.summary: OWASP supplies the decisive direct counterexample to CLM-0009's universal wording. It defines virtual patching as an enforcement layer that prevents exploitation without changing application source and explicitly documents automated conversion of vulnerability-scanner XML into protection rules, including ZAP-to-ModSecurity CRS, ThreadFix and commercial WAF imports. It also defines a governed preparation, identification, analysis, creation, implementation/testing and follow-up lifecycle; stresses exploit-agnostic protection, false-positive/false-negative analysis, logging, ticket/rule IDs and operational pre-authorization. It does not define agent evaluation receipts, action-class semantics, cryptographic per-rule approval, permit-to-effect binding, expiry-by-reproduction or regression-corpus linkage.
evidence.technicalContribution: A practical, threat-aware virtual-patching lifecycle that includes automated vulnerability-finding conversion into enforceable protection rules and operational controls for safe deployment.
evidence.methodology: This review inspected the current OWASP page and source, traced its explicit automated-patch examples, separated documented process from implementation claims, and compared every lifecycle stage with Warrantor R10.

The lifecycle includes testing, false-positive/negative analysis, rule/ticket traceability and follow-up.
Exploit-specific signatures can overfit, so protection-level design matters.

Examples focus on web-application vulnerabilities and WAF-style enforcement rather than agent tool authorization.
Named implementations and links may age independently of the continuously maintained page.
No portable signed evidence or cross-stack conformance model is defined.
incentives: OWASP's public-interest mission and noncommercial publication reduce direct sales bias, while community guidance still requires implementation-specific validation.

quality.rationale: Direct claim disconfirmation, concrete examples, mature lifecycle and independent OWASP authority make this high-quality. Guidance-level methodology, web focus and absent portable evidence limit essential status.

options: Use the lifecycle as R10's operational foundation and profile it for agent actions; recommended.
Reference it only and independently recreate the process; avoidable duplication.
Continue claiming no finding-to-protection prior art; reject.

sources.title: CACAO Security Playbooks Version 2.0

access.accessNotes: Current and immutable CS01 HTML/PDF were freely accessible; the authoritative artifact is the OASIS work product.

evidence.summary: CACAO 2.0 is the strongest open normative substrate for portable security-response workflows. It defines playbooks, sequential/parallel/conditional/temporal workflow steps, commands, authentication types, agents, targets, extensions, markings, versioning, permanent revocation and optional digital signatures. Playbooks can be manually or automatically triggered by events or observations and can call other playbooks. sources.title: Using Vulnerability Assessment Tools with a Security Policy
sources.venue: BIG-IP Advanced WAF / Application Security Manager Documentation

publication.version: current documentation applying through BIG-IP ASM 21.0.0

access.accessNotes: The current chapter and companion declarative-policy chapter were freely accessible. F5 labels the mechanism as applicable to current BIG-IP ASM versions through 21.0.0 and updated both chapters on 2026-07-07.

evidence.summary: F5 BIG-IP ASM is the strongest reviewed shipping counterexample to the broad attack-to-policy nonexistence claim. It imports XML findings from named web-application scanners or a generic schema, suggests security-policy updates for the discovered vulnerabilities, classifies findings as automatically or manually resolvable, exposes the planned changes, supports Resolve and Resolve-and-Stage, permits per-finding ignore/accept choices, applies the resulting policy, and directs operators to retest. A seven-day enforcement-readiness period, traffic samples, learning scores, staging, transparent/blocking modes and recorded illegal requests provide substantial operational controls. The current documentation also exposes a critical safety tension: Real Traffic Policy Builder can override scanner-derived protections by allowing methods/uploads or disabling signatures. This is a direct prior-art challenge, not a complete Warrantor substitute: it is web/WAF-specific, has no portable adversarial-evaluation receipt, cryptographic per-candidate approval, exact action-class IR, independently verifiable effect receipt, mandatory expiry, cross-engine equivalence or regression/safety-case closure.
evidence.technicalContribution: A production scanner-to-WAF-policy workflow with generic and vendor-specific finding import, per-vulnerability resolution, staging, retest, enforcement readiness, traffic learning and declarative JSON policy deployment.
evidence.methodology: The current vulnerability-assessment chapter was inspected end to end, including scanner integration, import, resolution, staging, suggestion review and enforcement. The companion declarative-policy chapter was inspected for JSON, source-control and CI/CD semantics. No licensed appliance was executed.
findings: Scanner output is ingested into a real production security-policy workflow rather than remaining advisory evidence.
Automatically resolvable findings can update policy directly or enter staging before blocking.
Operators can inspect proposed changes, ignore findings, retest protection and review traffic samples.
Automatic traffic learning may weaken scanner-derived protection, so suggestion precedence and negative conformance tests are security-critical.
limitations: First-party documentation establishes product behavior and workflow, not independent effectiveness or false-positive rates.
The mechanism is scoped to BIG-IP ASM/Advanced WAF and web-application vulnerability classes.
The reviewed workflow does not authenticate findings or approvals cryptographically and does not prove exact enforcement effects.
No mandatory expiry-by-reproduction, cross-engine semantic profile or automatic regression-corpus binding is documented.
incentives: F5 has a commercial incentive to emphasize integration and efficacy; detailed procedural documentation is authoritative for interfaces but not independent assurance.

quality.rationale: This is current, unusually detailed first-party procedure for a direct production counterexample with staging and retest controls. Closed-product access and vendor bias cap reproducibility and independence.

recommendation.preferredAction: Adopt F5's finding-review-stage-retest lifecycle as a mandatory comparator and adapter target, while adding authenticated evidence, narrow typed policy, exact effect receipts, expiry and regression closure.

Use F5 declarative JSON as one W4 target while preserving a vendor-neutral intermediate representation.

sources.title: Datadog App and API Protection Policies and Automated Response

access.accessNotes: Current public application and workload protection documentation was freely accessible without an account; product execution requires a Datadog service and instrumented workloads.

evidence.summary: Datadog provides a strong commercial application/runtime response comparator. App and API Protection can turn a Security Signal into automatic IP or user blocking for a configured duration, distribute denial configuration through Remote Configuration to instrumented services, block in the SDK or push the indicator to AWS WAF, Cloudflare or Fastly, and expose every blocked trace in Trace Explorer. Operators can preview matching traces for custom WAF rules, choose monitoring/blocking/disabled modes, auto-update or pin a managed policy version, rescind or extend denylist entries and use a global off switch. It does not automatically infer the narrowest policy from an arbitrary adversarial evaluation; most responses use configured rule-to-action mappings or indicator denylisting. It has no portable candidate approval receipt, cross-engine semantic proof, immutable finding-to-effect chain or automatic regression closure.

sources.title: US8572750B2 — Web Application Exploit Mitigation in an Information Technology Environment
sources.publisher: United States Patent and Trademark Office

access.accessNotes: Full text and bibliographic history were freely accessible. Google Patents listed a 2011-09-30 priority date, IBM as original assignee, Finjan Blue as current assignee and active status; those legal-status fields are aggregator evidence, not a legal opinion.

evidence.summary: This patent is decisive historical prior-art evidence against broad attack-to-policy novelty, though not proof of a shipped implementation. It describes establishing baseline request/response behavior, mutating requests to reproduce web vulnerabilities, recording variant request/response pairs and scan metadata, mapping request elements into a generic virtual-patch schema, deriving logical pattern expressions from exploit-vector permutations, converting the generic schema to device-specific interfaces, deploying rules/signatures to IPS, firewalls, AAA and other security devices, using change management as an allow/deny control, and initiating rescans until the vulnerability is no longer exploitable. It also permits manual false-positive classification and checks whether existing infrastructure already mitigates the vulnerability. The disclosed loop closely resembles finding → generalized candidate → target lowering → change control → deployment → reproduction. It lacks modern cryptographic receipts, explicit canary/rollback/expiry state, action-class semantics, cross-engine equivalence evidence, empirical evaluation, source code and proof that any commercial system implemented the disclosure.
evidence.technicalContribution: A disclosed scanner-to-virtual-patch feedback loop with exploit generalization, generic-to-device policy mapping, change-management control, multi-device deployment and confirming rescan.
evidence.methodology: Bibliographic fields, detailed description and claims were inspected in the public patent record. Patent disclosure was treated as prior-art/claimed-mechanism evidence only, not implementation or legal-advice evidence.
findings: The public priority date predates Warrantor by more than a decade.
The disclosure explicitly links successful vulnerability reproduction to generated and deployed protection rules.
A generic virtual-patch schema is converted to specific device interfaces, strongly bounding cross-target compiler claims.
Rescan and change-management controls anticipate parts of R10 but do not supply its modern evidence guarantees.
limitations: A patent is a claimed disclosure, not evidence that a working product shipped or that every claim is valid or practiced.
Google's legal-status/assignee fields require official-register and counsel verification for consequential decisions.
No code, benchmark, independent replication, receipt protocol or agent-specific action semantics are provided.
The disclosure predates the main window and is retained only as indispensable prior art.
incentives: Patent applicants are incentivized to claim broadly; detailed technical disclosure has high prior-art value but lower implementation credibility.

quality.rationale: The official publication and unusually exact lifecycle make it powerful prior-art evidence. Patent incentive, absent implementation and negligible reproducibility limit it to supporting status.

recommendation.preferredAction: Use this record to retire broad novelty language and commission a claim-chart/FTO review before patent-sensitive commercialization; do not treat it as an implementation baseline.

sources.title: US7895649B1 — Dynamic Rule Generation for an Enterprise Intrusion Detection System

evidence.summary: This early patent record materially bounds claims around automatic rule generation, expiry and integrity. Its claims describe aggregating sensor packet flows, detecting an attack, automatically generating and distributing a response message that identifies or impedes the attack, assigning a generation date, automatically removing messages older than an aging threshold, computing a verification value for the generated response and enabling sensors to reject unverifiable communications. It also covers staged attack detection and generation of response messages for later stages. The disclosure anticipates attack-derived enforcement rules, automatic expiration and signed/hashed distribution decades before Warrantor. It does not show a successful adversarial-evaluation finding, narrow semantic agent action class, human approval, canary rollout, observed external effect, rollback receipt, regression generation, implementation or independent performance evidence. A verification value protects message integrity/authenticity in the described system; it is not by itself a complete Warrantor receipt.

sources.title: EP3035637B1 — Policy-Based Network Security

It describes detecting and characterizing threats, selecting a mitigation scheme, filtering its response actions through corporate, legal or governmental policy to produce an allowed set, optionally requiring user or automatic approval, ordering actions by prerequisites, executing them, monitoring whether the threat remains and selecting a new plan when the first response is insufficient. This strongly bounds Warrantor claims around authority-aware action selection, policy filtering, approval and effect-driven replanning. It does not specify agent action-class semantics, a portable candidate IR, cryptographic per-transition receipts, cross-engine equivalence, mandatory expiry, rollback evidence, regression-corpus synthesis, implementation or empirical efficacy.

sources.title: Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework Schema 1.9.0

evidence.summary: OCSF 1.9 is the strongest current operational-event foundation for SAFE. Its record-integrity profile carries attestations, fingerprints, multiple signatures, authority and previous-event linkage. A pinned local compilation produced the decisive negative result for X9: class UID 3003 resolves to Authorize Session in Identity and Access Management, not Incident; X9 activities 4–6 are invalid for that class; its arbitrary top-level fields are unknown; and required metadata/class attributes are missing. OCSF supplies vocabulary, not proof of truthful reporting, exhaustive mediation, confidential exchange governance or complete evidence capture.

It defines HTTPS REST discovery, API roots, collections, manifests, object retrieval and addition, pagination, media types, status resources and error handling for cyber-threat intelligence exchange. It proves that collection-oriented interoperable transport is mature prior art and offers a viable optional SAFE delivery profile for STIX projections. TAXII does not determine whether a report is required, truthful or complete, does not define AI incident fields, trust-group governance or reporter protection, and does not turn collection access into per-record delegated authority. Idempotency, revision concurrency, acknowledgements and Warrantor receipt binding need a tighter profile.

Institutional governance, content semantics and cryptographic event assurance remain out of scope.

Access control and HTTPS do not prove event authority, integrity lineage or receiver handling compliance.

SAFE should carry a normalized TLP marking with source and effective audience, combine it with richer IEP policy and recipient groups, and separately enforce access and produce handling receipts.

evidence.summary: ContainmentBench separates endpoint compliance, logged propagation, recovery instrumentation and authorized structured-action utility after injection. findings: The main study reports 17,640 rollouts over 504 synthetic scenarios.

Reported authorized completion was 0.1642 for taint-only, 0.8567 for trusted-ledger and 0.9233 for a strong tool-boundary baseline.
Transfer to another model/common JSON setting produced violations under one intent-ledger configuration.
limitations: Synthetic study with primarily one model family.
Non-adaptive payloads and assumed-correct structured ledger.
Logged propagation is instrumentation-dependent, not an independent external-effect oracle.

sources.title: VIGIL: Runtime Enforcement of Behavioral Specifications in AI Agent Skills

evidence.summary: VIGIL is strong current W3/W4 prior art for converting behavioral specifications into typed finite-trace safety policies, compiling them into SMT constraints and blocking pending calls before a violating transition. Its central assumption is a complete trusted tool-call collector; opaque behavior inside scripts and non-tool process, network or external-effect paths remain outside the monitor.

sources.title: Wasmtime Security and Sandboxing Model

publication.version: Wasmtime 47 documentation and repository state inspected 2026-09-01

access.accessNotes: Official security documentation and open repository were freely accessible.

evidence.summary: Wasmtime provides a strong open sandbox substrate for untrusted WebAssembly with linear-memory isolation, typed control transfer, explicit imports/exports, capability-oriented WASI access and defense-in-depth measures. The documentation also makes the embedding boundary clear: host functions, configured resources, epoch interruption, terminal handling and platform mitigations determine real authority. Warrantor's exact sandbox-runtime package passed seventeen tests under Rust 1.95 but failed to build under the default Rust 1.93.1 because Wasmtime 47 requires Rust 1.94 or newer.
evidence.technicalContribution: A production-grade WebAssembly runtime security model and implementation with explicit embedder-controlled capability, resource and interruption boundaries.
evidence.methodology: Official security and Store/resource documentation were inspected. The repository's exact dependent package was built and tested under a compatible Rust toolchain, and default-toolchain incompatibility was reproduced.
findings: WebAssembly guest memory and control transfer are isolated by the runtime model.
WASI filesystem access can be capability-scoped.
Guest authority is determined by explicit imports and host functions.
Resource growth limits and epoch interruption require embedder configuration.
The Warrantor package passed 17 tests with Rust 1.95.
The default Rust 1.93.1 toolchain cannot compile Wasmtime 47's minimum requirement.
limitations: Sandbox guarantees do not make imported host functions or surrounding services safe.
Network, identity, persistence and distributed target sets require separate controls.
Defense-in-depth features are platform/configuration dependent.
A green package test suite is not escape certification.
incentives: The Bytecode Alliance documents its own runtime and security posture; authoritative implementation detail is strong but not independent assurance.

quality.rationale: Exact dependency relevance, authoritative depth and local package reproduction are strong; vendor/contributor authorship and embedder-dependent guarantees prevent essential classification.

Use for non-security extensions only.

content: Explain sandbox substrate versus stop assurance.
